The manuscript is twelve duodecimo leaves. Edwards' notation at the top of the first page indicates that the sermon was preached second time on an unspecified date.

<!-- p. 359 -->

### Living Unconverted Under an Eminent Means of Grace

Jeremiah 6:29–30.[^017-note2]

> *The bellows are burnt, the lead is consumed of the fire; the founder melteth in vain: for the wicked are not plucked away. Reprobate silver shall men call them, because the Lord rejected them*.

Jeremiah was one of the last prophets that was sent to warn Judah and Jerusalem before their destruction. He lived to see their destruction and captivity into Babylon. He speaks abundantly in this prophecy of that destruction, warning the people of it and pressing it upon them, that they would reform their evil ways, that they might escape it.

He is upon this subject in this chapter, setting forth [the] greatness of the sin and obstinacy of the people and foretelling their destruction. They had had many prophets to warn them and declare the word of God to them, but they had turned a deaf ear to them all; and they filled up the measure of their sin and obstinacy by their treatment of the prophet Jeremiah.

God tells him that he had set him as a tower and fortress amongst the people, to try their ways, in the Jeremiah 6:27; and God compares his trying of them by the threatenings and warnings of his word to the trials of metals in the fire. He had said in [the] verse foregoing the text that they were brass and iron. Jeremiah 6:28, "They are grievous revolters, walking with slanders: they are brass and iron; they are all corrupters"; that is, they are a base metal, they are not true silver and gold, as God's true and faithful people are, but they are like the baser sort of metals. To the same purpose is that, Ezekiel 22:18, "Son of man, the house of Israel is to [me] become dross: all they are brass, and tin, and iron, and lead, in the midst of the furnace; they are even the dross of silver."

<!-- p. 360 -->

The way of trying of gold and silver was in furnaces of fire, as we have often mention of it in God's Word. 'Tis this is alluded to in our text, where the case is represented thus: that God had been by his prophets trying of these metals in the fire, to see if he could not extract some gold and silver out of it, for metals, when they are tried in furnace, that that is base metal will be consumed of the fire, and what remains will be only pure metal. The prophets had been blowing the fire so long that the bellows were burnt out, and yet they could extract no good silver; it all proved to be lead.

"The lead is consumed of the fire." As I said before, when they tried metals, the baser part would be consumed and the purer part would remain; but it was all consumed, it all proved lead, and so consumed of the fire. So that the founder melted in vain: he gets nothing by it; he put something into the fire, but he gets nothing out: all that he put in is consumed of the fire.

"The wicked are not plucked away." That is, if they were not wicked, they would bear the fire, and so the founder would have something to take out. But they are all refuse metal that burns up in the fire, and so they ben't plucked out of the fire no more.

"Reprobate silver shall men call them"; that is, refuse silver. The meaning of the word "reprobate" is "rejected," or "disapproved." By reprobate or refuse silver means hypocrites, that have a gloss like silver, but when they come to be tried in the fire prove but lead and dross; and therefore God will not accept of them, but they shall be consumed of the fire.

Thus it was with Judah and Jerusalem. God had been a long time trying if he could not make something of them. He had sent his former prophets to try them, to see if they could not, by blowing, extract some silver and gold from amongst them, but they had tried as long as they lived. The prophets, they did not live forever, and God had tried till he was weary; but now his patience was worn out, and his former prophets were dead, and they sought Jeremiah's life, so that the bellows were as it were burnt out.

#### Doctrine.

#### It argues great danger of being finally left of God, when sinners have lived long unconverted under eminent means of conversion.

And that upon these three accounts:

I. Their sins are abundantly more aggravated than other men's.

<!-- p. 361 -->

II. Their hearts are more hardened against means of grace than other men's.

III. They have resisted the Holy Ghost more than others, and so will be more likely to be finally left by him.

[*Reason*] I. Their sins are much more aggravated than other men's. All those that live under the gospel, that enjoy the means of grace, let them [be] more or less eminent: if they continue impenitent, their sins are much greater than the sins of other men, much greater than the sins of the heathen that worship the sun, moon and stars and bow down to all the host of heaven, and to images, and worship the devils; that are in brutish ignorance and have a brutish, sottish way of worship. God gives us to understand in his Word that he is nothing near so much provoked with their sins as he is with the sins of them that live under means of grace. Amos 3:2, "You only have I known of all the families that are in the earth: therefore will I punish you for all your iniquities"; that is, "You only have I acknowledged for my people, and have brought you near to myself."

The heathen nations that were round about Canaan, they lived in idolatry and witchcraft, in lust and cruelty and all ways of vice; they wholly rejected the true God and his religion. But yet God was not so angry with them as he was with Jerusalem, nor did he punish them so severely. Daniel 9:12, "And he hath confirmed his words, which he spake against us, and against our judges that judged us, by bringing upon us a great evil: for under the whole heaven hath not been done as hath been done upon Jerusalem."

God had rather that men were quite cold than lukewarm. That is, he had rather that they should be heathen than wicked professors of Christianity. God cannot endure such wicked men; they are exceeding loathsome to him; he will spew them out of his mouth (Revelation 3:15–16).[^017-note3] And the Apostle tells us, 2 Peter 2:21, that we had better not have known the way of righteousness, than, after we have known, "to turn from the holy commandment delivered unto them."

And for the same reason, those that have lived in sin under the best and most eminent means, their sins are abundantly greater and more heinous and provoking unto God than the sins of those that have lesser advantages.

We have instances in Scripture of it. Chorazin and Bethsaida and Capernaum were cities that enjoyed extraordinary and very eminent

<!-- p. 362 -->

means of grace. Other cities of the land also lived under means of grace: they had Moses and the prophets; yea, sometimes Christ and his disciples were in other cities. But in these cities, Christ was wont more commonly to converse, to preach and work miracles, and therefore Christ denounces a special woe against them. Matthew 11, beginning with the twentieth verse:

> Then began he to upbraid the cities wherein most of his mighty works were done, because they repented not: Woe unto thee, Chorazin! woe unto thee, Bethsaida! for if the mighty works, which were done in you, had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. But I say unto you, It shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon at the day of judgment, than for you. And thou, Capernaum, which are exalted unto heaven, shalt be brought down to hell: for if the mighty works, which have been done in thee, had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. But I say unto you, That it shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom in the day of judgment, than for thee.

Not that there were none converted in these cities by Christ's preaching and miracles. He had commonly a great many hearers that had a seeming delight to hear him. Multitudes used to flock after him, and throng and crowd him sometimes, so that he could not find time to eat his bread. And there were some that did sincerely believe on him. Christ was not altogether without success among them in his preaching, but the effect was nothing to the means, nothing such as God expected; and God was therefore exceeding angry with them, to destroy them with such a dreadful destruction as he threatened.

So it was with Jerusalem. They enjoyed eminent means of grace. Christ was often there: he would often have gathered her children as a hen gathers her chickens under her wings. And there were some there also converted, but the bulk of them would not, and rejected Jesus Christ and despised his gospel; and therefore God was so provoked, that a little after he destroyed them in such a manner as gave the most remarkable tokens of God's vengeance that ever was seen in any temporal destruction. They had such tribulation as Christ foretold that never was, nor ever should be, on any nation (Matthew 24:21).

So it was with Jerusalem before its first destruction. They enjoyed distinguishing means of grace. Samaria and the Ten Tribes that were carried away captive by Salmanesser had great means of grace; they

<!-- p. 363 -->

had many prophets sent to them, to warn them before their destruction. But Jerusalem had greater because it was the city that God had chosen, and there was the temple where God dwelt. And therefore God tells Jerusalem that Samaria had not committed half her sins. Ezekiel 16:51, "Neither hath Samaria committed half of thy sins; but thou hast multiplied thine abominations more than they." How was it that Jerusalem's sins were so much greater than Samaria's? Samaria left the true worship of God in Jeroboam's time and never returned to it anymore till the captivity by Salmanasser. They worshipped the calves at Bethel and Dan and had not one reformation. Of all the kings they had, they had not so much as one good one, whereas Jerusalem had several good kings, several reformations, and they worshipped God in the temple, in the place that he chose. But here was the difference: Jerusalem had greater means than Samaria had, and therefore God reckons Samaria's sin not one half of Jerusalem's sins.

God, in Ezekiel 16:46–47, tells them that what Sodom and Samaria had done was a little thing in comparison of what Jerusalem had done. "And thine elder sister is Samaria, she and her daughters that dwell at thy left hand: and thy younger sister, that dwelleth at thy right hand, is Sodom and her daughters. Yet hast thou not walked after her ways, nor done after their abominations: but, as if that were a very little thing, thou wast corrupted more than they in all thy ways."

And so it surely is nowadays. They that live impenitent under the most powerful and eminent means of grace, they have a great deal more to answer for than others that have lived under less advantages. Those that have lived under eminent gospel means, they have greater advantages than even Jerusalem itself. If Sodom's sins and Samaria's sins were not half Jerusalem's sins, Jerusalem's sins were not half so great as the sins of some that live under great gospel light.

The sins of them that live under eminent [means] are much greater than others', principally upon these three accounts: they sin with more presumption, with more obstinacy, and more ingratitude.

*First*. Their sin is attended with greater presumption. They sin against clearer knowledge. They that sin, and distinctly know that they do sin, they sin with horrid presumptions and must be more especially provoking. He that knows his Lord's will, and don't do it, "shall be beaten with many stripes" [Luke 12:47].

They that have lived long under eminent means, they know better than others what sort of God that is they sin against and what authority they contemn, and what threatenings they despise and run the venture

<!-- p. 364 -->

of, and what reason there is that they should not sin; and therefore they sin with a high hand. When men sin through ignorance, God is willing to make allowances and more easily forgives; but [not] when they sin presumptuously. Numbers 15:27–28, Numbers 15:30–31, "If any soul sins through ignorance, then he shall bring a she-goat of the first year for a sin offering. And the priest shall make an atonement" for him. "But the soul that doeth ought presumptuously, whether he be born in the land, or a stranger, the same reproacheth the Lord; and that soul shall be cut off from among his people. Because he hath despised the word of the Lord, and hath broken his commandment, that soul shall utterly be cut off; his iniquity shall be upon him."

Paul tells us how great a sinner he was, how he persecuted the church of God. But, says he, "I obtained mercy, because I did it in ignorance and unbelief" (1 Timothy 1:13), intimating that sins that are committed against knowledge are not so easily forgiven. So Christ prays the Father to forgive his crucifiers because they knew not what they did. But men that have lived in sin under eminent means of grace, they know what they did.

Sinning against such light is as it were rebelling against God to his face. Let us consider how provoking would it be to a master or a prince to have a servant or subject despise his authority and disobey his commands openly to his very face, especially if his positive command were joined to warnings and threatenings.

Those that have lived in sin under eminent means, their sin has broken through many greater restraints than other men's. Their sin has been more victorious. He has had more powerful restraints than other men; he has more warnings and more conviction set before him. Sin that is so victorious over restraints must needs appear greater and more heinous.

*Second*. They [that] have lived long unconverted under eminent means, they have sinned with very great obstinacy. If a man sins once willfully against light and knowledge, it is very provoking; but abundantly more so when they [show] obstinacy under repeated commands, and repeated reproofs and threatenings, and repeated endeavors to bring him to obedience. And there is nothing is a greater sign of men's approaching ruin than obstinacy under powerful means and endeavors to bring them to repentance. Proverbs 29:1, "He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy."

And we have abundancy of instances of it in Scripture: God did not

<!-- p. 365 -->

destroy the old world till he had often reproved them by Noah; nor Sodom till he had sent them Lot, a preacher of righteousness; nor Pharaoh and the Egyptians till they had been often reproved by Moses and in God's providence; nor Saul till he had often reproved him by Samuel and otherwise; nor Samaria, nor Jerusalem, nor Chorazin and Bethsaida, etc.

*Third*. They that continue unconverted under such eminent means, their sin is greater because it is aggravated by a greater ingratitude. Those to whom God gives extraordinary means, they are highly favored and privileged by the distinguishing mercy of God above others. They are exalted up to heaven, as Christ speaks of Capernaum [Matthew 11:23]. God is so gracious to them as to give the best means, and privileges them above their neighbors. And therefore when they continue impenitent, they abuse [the] distinguishing mercy of God: and what is more provoking than to have kindness abused and trampled on? Seeing therefore that those who have long continued impenitent under eminent means of grace, their sin is so much greater and more provoking than the sin of others, they are in greater danger of eternal ruin; their sin is seldomer pardoned.

*Reason* II. Another reason why such are in greater danger of being finally ruined, is that they are more hardened against means than others.

'Tis always the effect of God's word, either to harden or to soften. It opens the eyes of some, and turns them from darkness unto light. The eyes[^017-note4] of others are closed by it. Isaiah 6:10, "Make the heart of their people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and convert, and be healed." Isaiah was commanded to do this no other way, but only going and preaching the word of God to them.

The light of the gospel enlightens some, and others it strikes blind. It brings scales over their eyes, as the light which Paul saw did upon his eyes. And the better and more powerful the means are, the more effectually do they harden if they don't soften. There can be no more effectual way to harden a man than for him to go and live in sin under some eminent minister. They that have been used to powerful preaching, and are used to hear and stand it out, they grow sermon proof.

If a man has been used to more ordinary means, and that don't

<!-- p. 366 -->

convert him, there is some hope that he may be profited by extraordinary means; but they that have stood it out under eminently powerful means, they are more effectually hardened against that that is inferior. They that have been used to encounters with lions, and to conquer them, won't be afraid of weaker animals. They that have been used the roaring of cannons, won't be likely to be much moved with the noise of small arms.

They that have been used to eminently powerful means, and have stood it out to the last as long as those means lasted, they have got the victory over means of grace. They have been used to the battle, and they have been used to conquer; and they that have been used to conquer, they grow bold in sin. Their sin will not be very easily conquered, and especially when they have been used to conquer champions.

*Reason* III. [The third] and last reason of the doctrine is that such as have lived long unconverted under eminent means, they commonly have been more used to resist the Holy Ghost than others, and therefore are in more danger of being finally left by the Holy Ghost. God very commonly gives strivings of his Spirit together with eminent outward means of grace. Those that live long under a powerful ministry do experience more or less of the awakening motions and strivings of God's Spirit, however stupid they may come to be at last.

And those that, notwithstanding these strivings, continue impenitent, 'tis because they have resisted the Holy Ghost: and that is the way to provoke the Holy Ghost finally to leave them. Thus did the Jews in Christ's and the apostles' times provoke God finally to leave and forsake them. Acts 7:51, "Ye stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost." Their long resisting God's Spirit made him so dreadfully to destroy them.

### Application.

[The] *Use* [is] of *Awakening* to the unconverted of this town. There have [been] few places that have enjoyed such eminent powerful means of grace as you of this place have enjoyed. You have lived all your days under a most clear, convincing dispensation of God's word. The whole land is full of gospel light, but this place has been distinguishingly blessed of God with excellent means for a long time under your now deceased minister.

And it argues a dismal degree of obduracy and blindness, that persons could stand it out under such a ministry. In what a clear and

<!-- p. 367 -->

awakening manner have you hundreds of times had your danger and misery in a natural condition set before you! How clearly have you had the way of salvation shown to you, and how movingly have you had the encouragements of the gospel offered to you!

Such as can live all their days under such means of awakening and of conversion, and have stood it out and have been proof against such preaching, are undoubtedly of exceeding hard hearts. They that are still unawakened, doubtless their hearts are much harder than if they had not lived under such great advantages. Powerful preaching, if it don't awaken, it hardens more than other preaching.

Those means are now gone; you'll have them no more. You have stood it out until the bellows are burnt. You had the preaching, the calls and warnings of your eminent deceased minister till he was worn out in calling and warning and exhorting of you. God was so gracious, and so loathe that you should perish, that he continued his ability of preaching to wonderment. But the founder melted in vain as to you. He did not cease blowing till the bellows were worn out, as it were burnt out, in vain, trying if he could not extract some true silver from amongst the lead. He was very loathe to give you over till he had persuaded, and God seemed loathe to give you over by continuing of him so long to call upon you and warn you. But how many wicked are there that are not yet plucked away? And it truly looks with a dark aspect upon them. They have reason to be afraid whether ever they shall be plucked away, and that for these reasons:

*First*. They have missed a precious opportunity which God put into their hands. It was a great price[^017-note5] that God put into your hands, by ordering it to be your lot to live under such a ministry. God was nigh to you; you lived under a burning and shining light. This opportunity has been continued beyond what you could expect, but yet you have let it slip. You have not improved the price that God put into your hands.

Solomon tells us that to everything there is a season and a time [Ecclesiastes 3:1–2]. God gives men some special opportunity for every purpose and every business, wherein, if they set themselves about it in good earnest, they may much more easily succeed in it than at another time. So there is a time to be converted in, when God is near and when men are under more special advantages for that work. But, as Solomon observes, the misery of man is great upon him, because he knows not his time. Ecclesiastes 8:6–7, "Because to every purpose there is time

<!-- p. 368 -->

and judgment, therefore the misery of man is great upon him. For he knoweth not that which shall be: and who can tell him when it shall be?" Your misery therefore is great upon you, that you did not improve that time which you don't know but was your only time. You promised yourself good opportunity hereafter, but you know [not] that which shall be, and who can tell you when it shall be. And Ecclesiastes 9:12, "For man also knoweth not his time: as the fishes that are taken in an evil net, and as the birds that are caught in the snare; so are the sons of men snared in an evil time, when it falleth suddenly upon them." Men that don't know their time and improve their opportunity, they promise themselves future opportunity; but their[^017-note6] destruction overtakes them at once when they think nothing of it, as a bird that is carelessly feeding is caught by the snare when they suspected no evil, and as the fishes are encompassed with the net while they are briskly playing in the water. It may therefore justly be a terrifying consideration, that you have missed such an opportunity as you have had.

*Second*. This will appear if we consider the end why God sends eminent ministers to a place and continues them there. He does it that his elect people that are there may be gathered in. Sometimes God sends some eminent messengers to a place only because he has one elect vessel there. Thus Christ must needs go to Samaria, a place where he was not wont to go, only to convert the woman of Samaria. So when he went to the coast of Tyre and Sidon, it seems to be for nothing else but to show mercy to the woman of Canaan. And when he went over into the country of the Gadarenes, it seems to be on purpose to deliver and convert him that was possessed with a legion of devils.

So when God has many elect in a place, God usually sends some eminent minister to be there to gather them in. Thus Paul continued a year and six months at Corinth by God's direction, because God told him he had much people in that city (Acts 18:10). Thus when Paul assayed to go into Bythinia, the Spirit suffered him not (Acts 16:7). It was because God had not any work for him to do there, any people to gather in; but he was commanded to go and preach at Macedonia, for God had many elect to be gathered in there, as appeared by the effect of his preaching among them. Acts 16:9, "And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; there stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia and help us."

And God sent Mr. Stoddard to this place because he had an elect

<!-- p. 369 -->

people here, and he continued him till he had done the work his Master designed him for. Many have been gathered in by his ministry, and it looks darkly upon you that are left, especially you that have lived unconverted a long while under his ministry.

If you hope that God will bless those means that may be used for time to come, if God does do so, it would be very just if he should resolve that none of you who have stood out against the calls and warnings of your former minister should have any benefit of it, but that his blessing of the means of grace for time to come should be upon your little ones, the rising generation that have not been guilty of despising and being unprofitable under those eminent means that you have despised.

The children of Israel in the wilderness enjoyed eminent means of grace. They see all God's wonders in Egypt and how he had brought them out with an outstretched arm, and they had seen God's miracles at the Red Sea and had heard God speaking from Mount Sinai, but they yet continued disobedient and stiff-necked. Therefore God swears in his wrath that none of them but Joshua and Caleb should enter into Canaan; but their little ones, that had not been guilty of contemning those eminent means, they should enter in. So it would be most just if God should deal with you that have despised and been obstinate under these powerful means you have enjoyed.

*Third*. God sometimes takes away his Spirit from a people when he takes away eminent means of grace. Thus it was in Christ's time: while Christ lived among them, the Jews enjoyed eminent means of grace, and God's Spirit strove with them; but when Christ died, the Spirit of God left them and their day of grace was past. Christ, when he was going up to Jerusalem to be crucified, he laments over the city, and says, "If thou hadst known, even thou, at least in this thy day, the things which belong unto thy peace! but now they are hid from thine eyes" [Luke 19:42]. These eminent means of grace were at an end, and so their day of grace was at an end. There were eminent means afterwards by the preaching of the apostles and their miracles, but yet God put an end to their day of grace because they had outstood those eminent [means]. So that whatever endeavors may be used with sinners for time to come, yet those that have long continued obstinate under so powerful a ministry are in great danger of being left by the Spirit of God.

We have another instance in Israel after Joshua's time. Judges 2:7, "The people served the Lord all the days of Joshua, and of the elders

<!-- p. 370 -->

that outlived Joshua, who had seen all the great works of the Lord, that he did for Israel." But when they were dead, they soon departed from God, and God departed from them.

Sinners therefore that have long continued in this town so have great reason to be startled by the consideration of what they have enjoyed and what condition they are now in. Consider how dreadful your punishment will be if you continue impenitent to the last. Woe to them that go to hell out of Northampton and that lived under Mr. Stoddard's ministry! We are ready to wonder at the wickedness we hear there is in some parts of the world, in the West Indies and in other places; but they han't one half of the sins to answer as obstinate sinners will have that go from this place.

And how dreadful is the case of those vicious persons that yet continue unreformed. How doleful will the punishment of drunkards be that have been unreformed by all means they have enjoyed and that yet continue unreformed.

The many powerful awakening sermons that you have heard won't be forgotten, though you have so little regarded them. They'll all be remembered, and you must hear 'em rehearsed again. Though you was so quiet under 'em when you heard 'em, yet when you hear 'em again, you will not be so quiet; they'll be thunder to you. Every word will pierce your heart through and through with torments.

<!-- p. 371 -->

John Williams of Deerfield on June 12.

### The Threefold Work of the Holy Ghost

As the title suggests, *The Threefold Work of the Holy Ghost* is an exploration of the various offices of the third person of the Trinity, though the second person and the nature of justifying faith also receive extended attention. Coming in the midst of a very productive period, this major and lengthy effort reflects surrounding sermons such as *None Are Saved by Their Own Righteousness* and *The Sacrifice of Christ Acceptable* and in many ways is a gathering of Edwards' theological and pastoral concerns.

We know that the nature of the Trinity preoccupied Edwards during the first half of 1729 because this discourse is as detailed an account of the relationships between the persons of the Trinity as we can find in Edwards' writings to this point in his life. It anticipates his *Essay on the Trinity*, begun in early 1730. The content of this discourse shows that Edwards was a close student of the debate over the Trinity that had been engaging European theologians since the end of the seventeenth century.[^018-note1] In response to anti-trinitarian views of the subordinate roles of the second and third persons, Edwards affirms the eternal and equal cooperation of the Son and Holy Ghost with the Father. The idea for this discourse, which at seven preaching units is longer than the *Essay* in its original form, had been germinating in Edwards' mind since he laid out the basic tripartite structure of it in "Notes on the Scripture" no. 134, written in late 1728. In that entry, he explains that the three offices of the Holy Ghost, paralleling John 16:8, the text of this discourse, are to convince the world of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment: making the world aware of the necessity of receiving Christ, the sufficiency of his righteousness, and his power as a judge and deliverer.

Edwards probably completed writing and began delivering *The Threefold Work* in April 1729 before his trip to New Haven in the following month, and he may even have had a preaching unit or two to deliver when he returned. The discourse is divided into three propositions,

<!-- p. 372 -->

each followed by an application, with a "General Improvement" at the end. It begins with a demonstration of how the Holy Ghost "confers the benefit" of Christ's salvation by making individuals "partakers" of Christ's righteousness. Through an "eternal consultation and agreement," the Trinity set in motion the covenant of redemption. In this covenant, the Holy Ghost performs his offices not as an inferior member of the Trinity, but as an equal of the Father and Son. The Holy Ghost is Christ's messenger, but this for Edwards does not constitute subordination. As he observed several months earlier in "Miscellanies" no. 376, that fellowship with the Father and Son *"consists* in our communion of the Holy Ghost with them"; so in this sermon Edwards portrays the Holy Ghost as the convincer of sin, influencing the hearts of believers as an "indwelling principle."

If Edwards concentrates on the Trinity in the doctrinal sections of this discourse, in the applications he turns to identification of the signs of grace as marks of the respective works of the Holy Ghost in believers' hearts. Reflecting his collation of Scripture texts in his "Signs of Godliness" notebook, in the application to the first sermon Edwards begins to draw very fine distinctions between the "certain signs" of grace and mere delusions. Having "fears and concerns," or being affected by a certain passage of Scripture or by preaching, does not necessarily mean that such affections come from God, for Satan is also active when God's Spirit is present. As a general rule, Edwards tells his people that when convictions are "agreeable to truth, and make men more careful to avoid sin and to use the means of God's appointments for salvation, there need be no scruples."

The second office of the Holy Ghost is to convince the world of righteousness, or to make believers partakers of Christ's righteousness by applying Christ's redemptive sacrifice. The third preaching unit establishes a distinction between Christ's negative (or passive) and his positive (or active) righteousness offered in atonement. Here Edwards asserts Christ's "sufficiency" or satisfaction for sin against anti-trinitarians who "deny that Christ's active obedience to God's law is imputed to believers." Allowing for individual righteousness apart from righteousness (or justification) in Christ is for Edwards tantamount to works-righteousness. Therefore he is at pains to establish Christ's divinity and the intimate connection of the Father and Son in the redemptive process. Christ, and Christ alone, "is he in whom we have justification." Christ removes guilt by the negative righteousness achieved through his suffering, but this is not enough to admit others

<!-- p. 373 -->

into heaven. Drawing on "Miscellanies" no. 381, "Christ's Righteousness," Edwards seeks to demonstrate that "the positive precepts of the law" that Christ obeyed need not have been the same law that was given to Adam. Rather, the important thing was that he perfectly obeyed. By this positive righteousness, he purchased heaven for believers.[^018-note2]

For Edwards, those who do not put their faith wholly in the sufficiency of Christ's righteousness, as applied by the Holy Ghost, are guilty of mocking the eternal plan of redemption that the Trinity devised. Amplifying the theme of *None Are Saved by Their Own Righteousness*, Edwards points out that an individual who thinks his own righteousness is wholly or partially sufficient perverts the covenant of redemption as "a frivolous notion," and as much as states that the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost "busied themselves about it needlessly," or merely to "surprise and amuse the world." If human righteousness is at all acceptable, then God the Father is guilty of cruelty for making his Son go to his death, God the Son committed "the most egregious folly" for dying to no purpose, and God the Holy Ghost comes "to convince men of lies."

Edwards goes on to explain that Christ's righteousness can be looked upon as belonging to believers because of his union with God and humankind by being united to both in nature and love. But it is the Holy Ghost that gives the conviction of this truth by "convincing of the reality and suitableness of it." The effects of true conviction include a "yielding" and "consenting" of the soul, committing oneself to Christ, and "calmness of mind." In these things, Edwards states, drawing on his "Faith" notebook, consists "saving, justifying faith."

Finally, the Holy Ghost operates to make individuals see the sufficiency and excellency of Christ as ruler and deliverer. As ruler, he gives laws, influences hearts, and judges souls at death. As deliverer, he redeems from Satan, from worldly afflictions, and from death and the grave. The Holy Ghost gives conviction of these attributes of Christ, as well as of his excellency as Lord and king. When a person is convinced of Christ's glory as Lord and king, obedience to God's commands no

<!-- p. 374 -->

longer comes from "slavishness," or "from fear of his wrath," but rather from a new principle of love and gratitude.

In his "General Improvement of the Whole," Edwards reiterates the importance of the Holy Ghost in the work of redemption. Christ is the judge and deliverer, but without the Spirit to convince of this, the Word is a "dead letter." The people of God therefore have earnestly to seek the Spirit if God's presence is to be among them. In his conclusion, Edwards makes the discourse applicable to the situation of the church: its members have to pray for the Spirit to visit them, as in times past, to have true conviction of sin, righteousness, and judgment.

∗ ∗ ∗

The manuscript is fifty-four duodecimo leaves. Its ink varies from dark to light brown, and fluctuations in ink viscosity indicate that this was not written in one effort, but as needed, over at least a two to three week period. That this was a series of regular sermons rather than something intended for the weekly lecture is confirmed by the existence of applications for each of the three overall portions, as well as the General Improvement at the very end.

The style of the sermon marks a transition for Edwards. Perhaps due to the demanding and lengthy nature of the discourse, he used abbreviations more than ever before. While parts of the discourse are fully written out, others are written in a sometimes terse, sometimes fragmentary manner. Scattered sections amount to nothing more than lists of points contained in mere words or phrases meant to be expounded extemporaneously. The uneven nature of the sermon's composition may reflect Edwards' increasingly poor health, which resulted in a debilitation in June. Taken as a whole, however, this composition suggests that Edwards was also experimenting, not so much with changing the formal structure of the sermon itself, but with his own powers of memory and association, as well as with how to produce sermons more efficiently.

<!-- p. 375 -->

### The Threefold Work of the Holy Ghost

John 16:8> *And when he is come, he will reprove the world of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment*.

Christ for some time had been talking with his disciples like one departing, one that was going to take his farewell of them; he had been giving of them his dying counsel and instructions. And, as he takes notice, they were filled with sorrow upon this occasion. They had left their business that they formerly were wont to follow. The fishermen had left their nets at Christ's call, they had left their friends, yea, they had left all to follow Christ, with that belief that he was the Messiah and with that expectation that he would never leave them, but would always be with them, and that when he set up his kingdom, they should be advanced and should be great gainers by their being his followers.

They had not yet right notions of the Messiah's kingdom. They still entertained carnal and childish thoughts about the matter, as appears by the discourse of some of them after he was crucified, particularly of those that were going to Emmaus [Luke 24:13–35]. With these thoughts prevailing, they had now followed Jesus and kept close to him for three or four years, and had suffered without doubt very much in their temporal interest, and had suffered abundance of reproach and contempt from their countrymen, and particularly from the scribes and Pharisees and the chief men of the land.

And they all but Judas, who was now absent, had a true and dear love to their Master. And therefore, now to hear so much of his leaving them, to hear him speaking to 'em like a man departing and taking his leave of them, and giving his last counsels to 'em, surprised them and filled them with sorrow.

Besides this, amongst other things, he had told them of persecutions and such hard things that they were to suffer after he was gone. And particularly in this chapter, [the] second and third verses, "They shall

<!-- p. 376 -->

<!-- p. 377 -->

put you out of the synagogues: yea, the time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service. And these things will they do unto you, because they have not known the Father, nor me."

Page one of sermon on John 16:8, 1729. Courtesy of Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University.

Christ himself took notice how they seemed to be affected by these things. John 16:6, "But because I have said these things unto you, sorrow hath filled your heart."

Christ had said many things to comfort them in this their disconsolate condition. But the principal thing he insisted, was that when he went away, he would send the Comforter. And he tells 'em in the verse foregoing the text that it will be better for them than if he stayed with them.[^018-note3] "Nevertheless I tell you the truth; it is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you."

In our text, he tells them what the Comforter will do when he comes, what will be his work. He had told them before, and tells them further in the ensuing part of the chapter, what his work would be with respect to them. And his name, "The Comforter," signifies much of it.

In our text, he tells them what his work will be with respect to the world in general. And that consists in three things: reproving the world of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment. The word that is translated "reprove" is "convince" in the margin, and the marginal interpretation is now most commonly chosen by divines.[^018-note4] So that we may read the words thus: "He will convince the world of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment."

#### Doctrine.

#### The work of the Holy Ghost as Christ's messenger is to convince men of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment.

Before we come particularly to insist upon these several parts of the work of the Holy Ghost, we shall speak to two propositions.

*First Prop*. 'Tis the Holy Ghost that makes application of Christ's redemption. That is to say, that although Jesus Christ prepares the way for man's salvation by his righteousness and sufferings, yet 'tis the immediate work of the Holy Ghost actually to make men partakers of that salvation; 'tis he that doth the finishing stroke. Whatsoever Christ has done, yet if men were not brought to repentance, faith [and] union

<!-- p. 378 -->

with God and Christ, all would be to no purpose, and 'tis the work of the Holy Ghost to bring this to pass.

All the three persons are concerned in the salvation of man, as they were in his creation. When man was first created, there was a consultation among the persons of the Trinity. God said, "Come and let us make man in our image, after our likeness" [Genesis 1:26]. So it is in the work of redemption: the Father chooses the Christ, provides, chooses, sends and accepts a savior; the Son is the Savior who satisfies justice, and answers the law and brings redemption for his people; the Holy Ghost immediately confers the benefits of all this, and actually makes the elect partakers of the salvation Christ has wrought.

So that the several persons have their work according to the order of persons. The first things to be done with relation to men's salvation are to determine whether men shall be saved, and who shall be saved, and to contrive a way of salvation and to choose and send and accept a savior, and that is the work of the Father.

The next thing is to do the work of a savior, to purchase salvation, and that is the work of the second person.

The last thing to be done is to make the redeemed actually partakers {of the salvation Christ has wrought}.

The Holy Ghost don't only immediately apply Christ's redemption, but 'tis he that does what is necessary to be done upon men's hearts in order to [it]. What Christ does immediately is not upon men's souls, but for them, which yet their souls would never be the better for, were not something done immediately upon their souls. Whatsoever in the work of redemption is done immediately in or upon men's souls is the work of the Spirit, whether it be actually making them partakers of this redemption, by converting them and uniting them to Christ, and carrying on {grace in their hearts} and making of them perfect in holiness in heaven, and filling them with happiness; but also convincing men of sin, making of them sensible {of their unworthiness}.

*Second Prop*. What the Holy Spirit doth in order to men's salvation, he doth as Christ's messenger. All that he doth amongst men since the Fall is as applying Christ's redemption, or some way in order to the application of it.

The Holy Ghost dwelt in the hearts of men before his fall, and moved and influenced not through a savior. So the angels…. But since the fall, men are never any way made partakers of the Spirit but it is through a mediator, through the Son of God.

The Holy Ghost is Christ's messenger, not exclusive of the Father. The Father and Son are equally concerned in men's salvation, and he

<!-- p. 379 -->

that sent the Son to purchase redemption, he also sends the Holy Ghost to make application. And as the Holy Ghost proceeds both from the Father and the Son equally, so he is sent by both into the world to influence the hearts of the children of men to their salvation. Therefore Christ says he will send him from the Father (John 15:26), and that the Father will send the Comforter (John 14:26).[^018-note5]

### Reasons

1. *Negative*. Not because the Holy Ghost is inferior to the Son. Though in the Trinity there is such a thing as prior and latter in order, yet there is no such thing as degrees of dignity or excellency. Though one proceeds from another, yet one is not inferior to another. The Son is not inferior to the Father; he thought it no robbery to be equal with God. It is said, though he proceeded from the Father, the Holy Ghost is in nothing inferior to the Father or the Son, though he proceeds from both [John 15:26].

It no ways argues the Son to be inferior to the Father, that he was sent by him. So neither is it any argument {that the Holy Ghost is inferior}.

The reason is because they all are the same God, and it is therefore impossible there should be any {inferiority}. They all are the same substance, the same divine essence; and therefore whatsoever perfection, dignity or excellency belongs to the divine essence, belongs to every one of them. There are none of the three persons can have any more excellency or perfection or dignity than what belongs to the divine nature; and each one must have so much because each one has the divine nature, each one is the divine nature. Whatsoever power or wisdom or holiness, etc. belongs to the divine nature, still belongs to the same divine nature in whatsoever person it subsists, whether it subsists in the {Father, Son or Holy Ghost}.

2. *Positive*.

(1) 'Tis agreeable to the order of persons in the Trinity and their manner of subsisting. The Father subsists of himself; he is neither begotten nor proceeds. 'Tis suitable therefore that he should be first in relation to what is done in the work of redemption, that he should be first orderer, provider, etc. The Son proceeds from the Father; 'tis suitable that he should be sent by him. The Holy Ghost proceeds both from the Father and the Son. He proceeds from the Son as well as Father, and so is sent by him as well as by the Father.

<!-- p. 380 -->

'Tis evident, because he is called "the Spirit of the Son." Galatians 4:6, "God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts." Romans 8:9, he is called "the Spirit of Christ." Again, all things that the Spirit hath, he hath as well from the Son as from the Father (John 16:14–15).

And then he breathed the Holy Ghost into his disciples. John 20:22, "And when he said this, he breathed on them, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost." Which shows that the Holy Ghost proceeded from him, as well as his breath.[^018-note6]

River of water of life (Revelation 22). Living water is explained of the Holy Ghost (John 7:38–39).[^018-note7]

(2) The holy Trinity saw it meet that he that had been at so great cost to purchase salvation should also have the disposal of it. Whatsoever is done concerning man's redemption, is done as it were by consultation and agreement amongst the persons of the Trinity. There was as it were an eternal consultation and agreement about it, and whatsoever is done by each person is done by the consent and concurrence of all.

Christ was the person that was pitched upon to be the purchaser, and he was the only person that suffered. And all that great labor and suffering that was to be gone through in order to it, he undertook it: he put himself in men's stead; he took their burthen, their punishment, upon himself.

And therefore they saw it meet {that Christ should be the Savior of mankind}. It was looked upon but a suitable reward {for Christ's suffering}. For this reason, God gave Christ "power over all flesh, that he should give eternal life to as many as he hath given him" (John 17:2). And Matthew 11:27, "All things are delivered unto me of my Father: and no man knoweth the Son, but the Father." John 5:26–27, "As the Father hath life in himself; so hath he given to the Son to have life in himself; and hath given him authority to execute judgment also, because he is the Son of man."

(3) The Holy Ghost is the messenger of Jesus Christ {unto the elect}, that Christ may be a complete savior. The holy Trinity saw it meet that Christ, the second person of the Trinity, should be the Savior of mankind, and that he should be a complete [savior]; that he should have in his power everything that belonged or related to the salvation of mankind; that men's eyes might be to him, that they might look to him and

<!-- p. 381 -->

trust in him, etc.; that the faith of God's people might be encouraged and strengthened… and that Christ might have all the glory.

For this end, God the Father appointed him ruler of the world, head over all things to the church, [and] gave the kingdom of providence into his hands. John 17:2, he gave him "power over all flesh, that he should give eternal life to as many as he hast given him."

And for this end, the Holy Ghost became in this work subordinated to the Son, that Christ might [have] the whole work of salvation in his hands. Now the salvation of a sinner don't only consist in…

Thus we have shown {what the Holy Ghost doth in order to men's salvation as Christ's messenger}. We now proceed particularly [to] the several parts of the work of the Holy Ghost as Christ's messenger, and as carrying on the design of the salvation of men, as they are laid down in the text.

[*Prop*.] I. And we shall insist upon that work of [the] Spirit of God's convincing men of sin. And,

*First*, we shall show that 'tis the Holy Ghost that convinces men of sin in order to their salvation.

*Second*. We shall show what conviction of sin that is that the Spirit of God is the author of in order to men's salvation.

*Third*. [The] manner [of it].

*Fourth*. The means of this conviction of sin.

*Fifth*. The end of it.

*First*. 'Tis the work of the Holy Ghost to convince {men of sin in order to their salvation}. So dull and stupid are the souls of men naturally,[^018-note8] so under the power of that blinding, stupefying thing sin, that even natural conscience is lulled asleep and the natural reason is kept from a free exercise by it, so that they will not be sensible, etc. Experience. Instances in Scripture manifest it. Peter's sermon [Acts 2]. Jailor [Acts 16:27–34].

'Tis not ministers or providences without it.

*Second*. What that conviction of sin is that {the Spirit of God is the author of in order to men's salvation}.

1. The Holy Ghost makes them see that they are very sinful, brings them to compare themselves with the law of God, brings to mind God's commands. They often heard them before, but never thought much of them, never applied them to them or thought of them as what they were [in] any great matter concerned with.

<!-- p. 382 -->

Insensible sinners don't so much as seriously turn in their thoughts how contrary their hearts and lives are to God's law. When they perpetrate these and those acts of wickedness, when they are guilty of profaneness or lasciviousness, they don't stand to think how contrary is this {to the law of God}, how provoking must it needs be {to God's justice}.

He shows them and makes them to consider how very contrary {their hearts and lives are to God's laws}, and not only so, but how provoking those things that are so contrary must be to God's {justice}.

Before, they did not think with themselves what it was to slight the commands of so great and mighty a God.

They heard the commands of God before, but the voice was so low that they did not regard it. Now they hear them as it were with the thunderings of Mount Sinai: they are the commands of a mighty and terrible God.

The Holy Ghost makes men [sensible] how sinful their lives are, brings sin to remembrance. They little regarded how many sins they had committed, but now they are brought to reflect. Their sins are set in order before their eyes. Psalms 50:21, "I will set these things in order before thine eyes."

[The Holy Ghost] brings the aggravation of them to mind. They think how that at such a time they sinned against such convictions, such warnings of ministers, after such other sins.

Their sins, as attended with those aggravations, appear to [them] sometimes in so black a hue that they are ready to say that never was [there] any so great sinners.

The Holy Ghost convinces men of the sin and wickedness of the heart, makes them see what a fountain of corruption there is there. The Holy Ghost makes them reflect upon the wickedness of their evil thoughts and desires, makes them see how averse they are to duty, how opposite to God and Christ, how hard-hearted in that they are no more affected by [it], etc.

God turns their hearts as it were inside out to them, and there is no sight so frightful to a sinner as {a sight of his own heart}.

2. The Holy Ghost convinces men of the dangerous nature of sin. Not only the sins themselves, but they are made to have a lively apprehension of the punishment and misery that follows.

They are made to reflect not only on the commands themselves, to see how contrary their hearts and lives {are to God's laws}, but upon the threatenings also. Unawakened men don't regard those threatenings nor their danger. Sinners are in exceeding great danger. Awakened

<!-- p. 383 -->

sinners see it, see God's anger flaming, they themselves hanging over the pit, God's sword drawn, his bow bent.

They are made to think in what danger they daily walk,[^018-note9] how uncertain their lives [are], etc.

They are made to think how great [is] the misery of hell, what it is to die and to be judged.

They are made so to hear the voice of God's threatenings that they tremble. Preaching makes them tremble. Providences.

They see the necessity they are in of help, some way or other. Acts 2:37–38, "Now when they heard these things, they were pricked in their heart, and said, Men and brethren, what shall we do? Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost." Acts 9:6, "And he trembling and astonishing said, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?" Acts 16:29–30, "And he called for a light, [and sprang in, and came trembling, and fell down before Paul and Silas, And brought them out, and said, Sirs, what must I do to be saved?"].

3. The Holy Ghost convinces [men of their] helplessness[^018-note10] in any way of their own contriving. There are many ways that sinners under awakenings hope to help themselves, to escape their danger.

When they see the danger they are in, the souls in the next place naturally bend themselves to seek help.

Help in friends.

[They] lay obligation upon God, upon his justice, upon his honor. By his Word. Declarations of mercy. Promises. Providence. Showing mercy to others.

By righteousness. By prayers. Pitiful cries, etc. They think to help themselves by strength. Converting themselves.

They endeavor to find help in atheistical thoughts.

But the Holy Ghost convinces {them of their helplessness in any way of their own contriving}. [He convinces them] that friends can't help. He [is] under no obligation, etc. 2 Corinthians 10:4, "The weapons of our warfare are mighty through God for the pulling down of strong holds." Luke 15:16, "And he would feign have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: but no man gave unto him." In the

*Third* place, as to the manner, I shall speak to that in answer to this question, viz.:

<!-- p. 384 -->

*Inq.* Wherein lies the difference in the manner of the Holy Ghost's influencing of sinners in conviction and the saints?

We don't inquire what is the difference between the influence and operation itself {in influencing of sinners}.

By the tenor of the Scripture, it seems that the saints only are those that have the Spirit of Christ. They only are baptized with the Holy Ghost and with fire, that have his Spirit poured upon them; they only that are taught of the Spirit, that are led by the Spirit.

And yet it appears by the same Scripture that the same Spirit of God does some way influence even wicked men. Otherwise, how do we read of their resisting the Holy Ghost? [Acts 7:51]. And Hebrews 6:4, of some that fall away, that yet are made partakers of the Holy Ghost?

Therefore, why can't unbelievers be said to have the Spirit of Christ as well as believers? Why mayn't they be said to be baptized {with the Holy Ghost}? Wherein lies the difference {in the manner of the Holy Ghost's influencing of sinners in conviction and the saints}?

*Ans*. The Holy Ghost influences the souls of believers as an indwelling principle. But not [that] the Holy Ghost not moves upon the hearts of saints as an external agent, but he takes up his abode in the hearts of believers. They are the temples of the Holy Ghost. 1 Corinthians 3:16, "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" So we read of Christ dwelling in them. 'Tis by his Spirit.

The Holy Ghost is in them as a principle. John 4:14, "[A] well of water springing up." 'Tis in them as a principle of life and a principle of action. Galatians 5:25, They live in the Spirit and walk in the Spirit. And becomes as it were a principle of nature; thereby, they are of a new nature, and 'tis by this means they are partakers of the divine nature. But with respect to unbelievers, 'tis not so. [In the]

*Fourth* place, [the] means [of conviction]. The principal law of God. We cannot be saved by the works of the law. [The principal law is] abrogated as to our immediate concern with it, as containing the condition to be performed by us.

The principal use of it now is to convince of sin.

The precepts of the law convince of our sinfulness and vileness.

The threatenings of our danger.

The strictness of our helplessness.

Romans 3:19–20, "Now we know whatsoever things the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God. Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the

<!-- p. 385 -->

law is the knowledge of sin." Galatians 2:19, "I through the law am dead to the law."

Other means are used, as providences, etc. But they work by the law in subordination.

*Fifth*. As to the end.

1. To fit for Christ. [The] law [was our] schoolmaster (Galatians 3:24). How is it necessary.

2. That God's mercy may be the more prized. The more he is made sensible of his misery.

3. That the glory of free grace might be the more acknowledged. The more he is first made sensible of his deserts.

4. In them that yield not to its strivings, to harden and condemn them. We read of some that resist (Acts 7:51). At last often quench it. How many ways they quench it. 'Tis to harden and condemn them, Hebrews 6:6–8, "If they shall fall away, to renew them again unto repentance; seeing they crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame. For the earth which drinketh in the rain that cometh oft upon it, and bringeth forth herbs meet for them by whom it is dressed, receiveth blessing from God: but that which beareth thorns and briers is rejected, and is nigh unto cursing; whose end is to be burned." He hardens not by immediate efficiency, but by withdrawing, as fire hardens iron.[^018-note11]

### Application.

Application of the first part.

*Inf*. I. How wicked [and] stupid a time soever it may be, yet we have no reason to despair or draw up conclusions.

How long soever. How firm-rooting, wicked practices have soever by custom and habit. Or by being countenanced and encouraged by men. Great men.

[We] have no reason to despair concerning a particular place. Concerning the world.

Prayers of God's people should therefore be encouraged.

How has it been in times past, in times of most remarkable effusions. How in Christ's time. How in Luther's time. And prophesied concerning the times of future effusions of God's Spirit. Luke 18:8, "Shall he find faith?"

<!-- p. 386 -->

No reason to despair concerning particular persons, though less likely concerning some than others.

Apply the doctrine to several sorts of persons:

*First*, [to] unawakened sinners. I shall recommend several things to your consideration.

1. That you are in a state of condemnation. Dying in the state you are now in, it would be impossible but that you should be damned.

The flames of God's wrath, that are as hot as hell fire, bear against you. Psalms 7:11, "[God is] angry [with the wicked] every day."

You belong to the devil. "Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do. He was a murderer from the beginning, and abode not in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it" (John 8:44).[^018-note12]

The law of God is against you. His truth is against you. His justice.

You hang over hell. You hang by a slender thread. It may be you flatter yourself that nevertheless you shall not drop, but most that hang by that thread do drop.

2. 'Tis one of the most uncertain things in the world whether ever you will get into a better state. There is hardly anything we are concerned in in our business in the world more precarious. No prudent man would venture the smallest interest upon such an uncertainty.

You are of that kind of men that are most remote of all from salvation.

You not only have no foundation of certainty, but not so much as any for any conjecture in your favor. If you say you live under great advantages, and that is for you, your sinning willfully and continuing stupid is much more against you. If you say you are born of parents dear to God, that pray for you and advise you…[^018-note13]

And if we go to fact, and would guess by the numbers that are brought out of such a state, etc. Where there is one, that is, there are many that are not.

3. Consider that you every day make it less and less probable that ever you will be saved. [You] daily harden your heart, fortify yourself against everything, whereby you make God the more displeased. [You] take all methods to provoke him to give you over, or soon to cut you off.

The devil gets abundantly the advantage by your delays.

<!-- p. 387 -->

You can't be saved without convictions, and you fortify yourself against them.

You grow old, and an old, stupid sinner is the most forlorn, deplorable creature in the world, especially under great light.

[*Inf*.] II. To such as are awakened: first, by way of direction; and second, encouragement.

[*First*, by way of *Dir*.]

*Dir*. 1. Avoid all those things by which convictions may be stifled. How great need you have of them. How doleful your case would be if you should lose them and backslide.

By no means suppress convictions, however uneasy they may be to you. Not for the world go contrary to convictions of conscience in yielding to any temptation. Carefully avoid and strive against all murmuring and quarelling.

[*Dir*.] 2. To the utmost, improve convictions. Strive with God's Spirit. Use the means of God's appointment unweariedly, with that resolution that you will maintain that course.

[*Dir*.] 3. Be watchful against the first beginnings of declining. When you first begin to be more careless and less intense, strive and pray against them.

[*Dir*.] 4. Beware of going on in any way of self-confidence. When you pray, and when you weep, take heed how you drink in that notion that God must needs be affected and his heart drawn.

Remember that after you have done all, God may stop his ear justly. See that ben't the foundation of your encouragement, that if you do so and so, God can't find [it] in his heart to [reject you]. And don't think ever to be able to open your own eyes.

[*Dir*.] 5. Take heed that you don't lay hold of a false hope, and take up with some common impressions, as though [you are able to open your own eyes]. Don't presently think that you have true repentance because you weep for your sins and [have] every affectedness of mercies for true love.

[*Second*.] To encourage those that are under conviction of sin to go on seeking mercy.

When God's Spirit is striving, then God is nigh. Isaiah 55:6, "Seek the Lord while he may be found, call upon him while he is near." Then it's an accepted time, a day of salvation. 2 Corinthians 6:2, "Behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation."

God now stands at the door and knocks.

<!-- p. 388 -->

'Tis matter of great encouragement for you to strive while God is striving with you.

Draw up no dark conclusions against yourself. Don't give yourself over when God has not given you over.

Persons under great awakenings are apt oftentimes to fall into discouragement and a despairing way, but 'tis very unreasonable. But 'tis a temptation with many, that they doubt whether their concerns are from the Spirit of God or no. I shall therefore speak something to the following,

*Inq.* How may it be known whether the concerns that persons are under about the state of their souls are from the Spirit of God, and are such as persons may take encouragement from?

Before I directly answer, I shall

*Premise*

*First*. That sinners may experience fears and concerns relating to their souls that are not from God's Spirit. Though they have reason for the greatest fear and concern, yet they may have many fears and anxieties that are not just.

Many things they are frighted at that there is no occasion for.

Terrors of the damned.

So I don't see that any can affirm that persons never have any terrors in this world through fear, etc. That is only part of their punishment.

But then it has no other effects than some such like as the terrors of the damned. They are terrors that work that way.

Though God may make what he doth not to issue in good, though [not] directly tending to ill.

*Second*. That at the same time that the Spirit of God is at work with men, awakening and convincing of them, commonly Satan also is very busy.

All that persons experience at such times must not be looked upon as the operation of the Spirit of God.

Satan is roused by his fear of losing the soul that he has had in possession. When God's Spirit strives, he leaves nothing undone. He'll endeavor to turn awakenings and fears of hell to an ill effect, to discouragement, to hard thoughts. While the Spirit of God sets in with the Word, Satan also will set in with it, to pervert it to his own use.

While the Holy Ghost encourages, he will endeavor to turn it to security and negligence.

When God's Spirit moves to diligence, he'll endeavor to turn it to self-righteousness.

<!-- p. 389 -->

The Holy Spirit has his fears and terrors, and Satan his fears {and terrors}. The Holy Spirit has his encouragements, [and Satan his encouragements]. The Holy Spirit has his directions, [and Satan his directions].

Satan often very much stirs up corruption at such times. [He] sets in with tempting occasion.

*Third*. 'Tis no certain sign that impressions made upon the mind are from the Holy Ghost because they are occasioned by a place of Scripture coming into the mind, or something in the preaching.

Satan is transformed into an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14). 'Tis his way to appear in disguise. We have no promise that Satan shall not make use of God's Word to tempt. 'Tis frequent with him: so he did with Christ. Matthew 4:6, "For it is written, He shall give his angels charge." Nor if they are without places of Scripture in an extraordinary manner coming {into the mind}, is it any sign of the contrary.

The Word of God, whenever it comes into the mind, or is read or heard: we need not trouble ourselves how it comes to us, but we are to improve it as the Word of God. We can't say that because it comes suddenly into our mind, that therefore it was sent from heaven as declaring our case, etc. We have no rule for these things. And if we make such things our rule, we shall be likely to be deceived and ensnared.

*Fourth*. 'Tis no sign that the concern persons are under about their salvation is not from the Spirit of God, that it arises from consideration that they put themselves upon.

Many have that thought that 'tis wholly they themselves. They think they are not like others because they feel no extraordinary, sudden impressions that others tell of.

'Tis not the less from God's Spirit because [it comes] in that way, nor has it the less good tendency. The Spirit of God makes use of reason—what first set men to considering or made them design it. There is [a] difference in the manner of the Holy Ghost's operation: sometimes more sudden and surprising impressions, sometimes more in concurrence with natural powers, secretly moving and assisting them.

But to speak more directly to the inquiry:

*General Rule*

Whatsoever convictions and awakenings are agreeable to truth, and make men more careful to avoid sin and to use the means of God's appointment for salvation, there need be no scruples.

When we say "agreeable to truth," we mean when they are sensible

<!-- p. 390 -->

they are in that danger they are indeed in; when they are concerned and terrified upon true grounds, having God's Word for the ground of [it]; when the conviction of truth is the foundation of it.

Persons that are afraid, though they have grounds enough to be afraid, are oftentimes terrified upon any grounds, as for fear they have committen sin against [the] Holy Ghost, because they think they heard a voice, etc. or because such a place of Scripture came to their minds. And then the other thing is when it works the right way, makes men more careful, etc.

Sometimes terrors persons have, though they have reason to be terrified, yet [they] don't work the right way: sometimes to utter despair, blasphemy, etc. Much like those in hell. And we can't say God don't never leave men to that punishment in this life. Upon their death beds.

Men, when they see their danger, would blaspheme if not restrained by God's Spirit. And we can't say Satan don't earn[^018-note14] for that end, to torment 'em and cause 'em to blaspheme.

When convictions are thus according to truth, etc. they are according to the Word of God. What is according to God's Word, we may conclude is from God and not from Satan.

The Word of God is our only rule and touch stone in all such matters: what is according to that need not be scrupled. That Spirit that saith the same that the Word says, and promotes the same thing that the Word of God promotes, is the Spirit of God. The spirit of Satan, so grand an enemy, doth not thus. Mark 9:40, "For he that is not against us is on our part."

This was the rule that God gave to know the spirits of pretended prophets. Deuteronomy 13, at [the] beginning, and so in the New Testament, 1 John 4:2–3.

Satan has no [such] disposition. 'Tis against his interest.

Therefore, so far as {convictions and awakenings are agreeable to truth}, you may undoubtedly [trust], but no farther.

Persons, when they are under terrors of conscience, are oftentimes [under] fears and terrors about that that there is no occasion for.

Unpardonable sin.[^018-note15]

No hopes of salvation.

Day of grace past.

<!-- p. 391 -->

They ben't as others are.

These are not from the Spirit of God, any otherwise than as they, by a sight of their real danger, are put into a frightful posture, are easily frighted where no fear is. But their fears arise more directly from some other cause. Oftentimes [their fears] are occasioned by their ignorance, from wrong thoughts of God, from Satan's suggestions. Such terrors have no good tendency: [they] tend to the person's destruction rather than salvation.

It behooves persons carefully to distinguish who they have convictions [of] according to truth and that work, so they may conclude they are not given over. Yet we must not build too much upon it: you sin enough every day to provoke God to take away his Spirit.[^018-note16]

### [Doctrine Resumed.]

We have spoken of the first part of his[^018-note17] work, viz. convincing men of sin. That work of the Holy Ghost is only preparatory to those two that follow: convincing men of righteousness and of judgment. These two latter comprehend those convictions and that saving light that are given in conversion, when the soul is first [brought] out of a state of sin, is brought to Jesus Christ the Savior.

There are indeed saving convictions of sin that are given in true repentance, but it seems that those that respect is had to in this place are those that are given before conversion, by the illustration in the ninth verse: "Of sin, because they believe not on me." Which seems to intend these two things, viz.:

1. That they are convinced of sin, and have a sense of guilt lying upon their souls because they believe not in Christ; whereas if they did believe in [Christ], that guilt, and also the sense of it, would be removed. Those fears and terrors would vanish, and there would be no occasion for 'em. And,

2. They are convinced of their sin of unbelief, which is that which under the gospel brings the most guilt upon the soul, and is peculiarly aggravated and provoking, and what greatly strengthens and aggravates all other sins.

But the conviction of righteousness and judgment that follow are plainly such as are given when that great and wonderful work of conversion is wrought and a saving change made. By "righteousness"

<!-- p. 392 -->

here is undoubtedly meant the righteousness of God in Christ, or the righteousness of Christ as mediator, or his having answered the law and having done all that needed to be done in order to the reconciliation and acceptance of sinners. This is evident by the illustration of it in the tenth verse, "Of righteousness, because I go to my Father, and ye see me no more," that is, "Because I ascend into heaven, enter into the holy of holies, go to my heavenly Father to sit at his right hand."

This points forth two things:

1. As the exaltation of Christ, or his ascending into heaven and going to the Father, is a principal means whereby believers are made partakers of the benefits of Christ's righteousness, and that fulfillment of the law which he has performed.

Christ ascended into heaven for our sakes, as the high priest went into the holy of holies for the people. Christ, having performed perfect righteousness by his obedience and suffering, is gone to heaven, there to plead what he has done and suffered. He is entered with his own blood, he is gone there to produce as it were his righteousness for us, to make intercession for us and, as he says, "to prepare a place" [John 14:2].[^018-note18]

And then by his going to heaven, he makes us partakers of the benefits of his righteousness another way, and that is he thereby ascends his throne and takes possession of his [inheritance], has all things given into his hands, that he may distribute of the benefits which he by his righteousness has purchased to as many as God has given. For Christ to work out righteousness for us here upon earth only, that were not enough. But it was needful in order to our being the better for it, that he should make presentation of his meritorious sacrifice in heaven for [us] to the Father; and not only but that he should himself, in the exercise of his power given him in his exalted state, confer his righteousness on all that believed on him. For the great God don't see meet to have anything to do in a way of mercy with fallen men but through a mediator; so that the Mediator must not only work out righteousness, but must himself make men partakers of it.

Therefore Christ's going to the Father is here mentioned as the finishing stroke, as what crowns all that he did as our righteousness, and the last thing needful to be done by the Mediator in order to the making his righteousness ours: a crowning thing that renders him a complete object of the faith of believers, the last thing needed in order

<!-- p. 393 -->

to there being sufficient grounds for the world's being convinced of the sufficiency of his righteousness. Therefore it is he shall convince the world of righteousness, "because I go to my Father."

2. Christ's going to the Father is mentioned as being a principal argument whereby he does convince men of Christ's righteousness, not only as the means of our justification before the Father, but a principal means of convincing of 'em of the sufficiency of Christ's righteousness.

Christ's exaltation, viz. his rising from the dead and his ascending into heaven, is often insisted on in the gospel as being the great evidence that what Christ had done and suffered was sufficient for us. So it is, Romans 8:34, "Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us." So it is said, "Christ was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit" (1 Timothy 3:16), i.e. God justified him as mediator, declared by opening his prison doors that what he had done was sufficient. It was the highest demonstration that could be given: for Christ put himself in our stead, and took upon him our sins and became responsible for all. And God by…

Therefore Christ's going to the Father is here mentioned as an argument by which the Holy Ghost convinces the world of righteousness: for the Holy Ghost convinces by arguments; he enlightens the reason, and makes use of the gospel. The Word is the sword in the hand of the Spirit [Ephesians 6:17].

Christ's going to the Father seems here to be mentioned upon another [occasion] by our Lord, that is, to convince the disciples of the necessity [of] his going away. They were filled with sorrow.

By "righteousness" here seems to be meant the way of the justification of sinners by Christ. 'Tis not only meant Christ's active {righteousness}: a great deal more is intended than that. So by the term "righteousness," when it is spoken with respect to the Mediator in Scripture, is almost always thus to be taken. Christ is called "the Lord our righteousness," that is, he is he in whom we have justification. So it is said, in the Lord Jehovah we have righteousness and strength [Isaiah 12:2, Isaiah 26:4], that is, in him we have acceptance with God as righteous. We read, Romans 4:11, that circumcision was the seal of the righteousness of faith, i.e. a seal of the way of justification by faith; and [in the] thirteenth verse, that the promise that Abraham should be heir [of the world] was through the righteousness of faith. So, very evidently, it is to be understood, Romans 3:21–22 and Romans 1:17. It is not to be understood of

<!-- p. 394 -->

the holiness of God's nature, or the personal holiness or innocence of Christ, but God's way of justifying man.

So we understand the term "righteousness" in our text.
