His way of governing the hearts of his people is wonderfully gracious. He don't force them, but sweetly inclines their wills to the most excellent things and to their own happiness. He overcomes them by his love; he governs them by infusing his love into them, and so inclining them to obedience. His dominion over his people is by mutual love and esteem. He is therefore deservedly called "the prince of peace."

And when Christ judges his people, he will wonderfully make his grace to appear by the wonderful free reward he will give. He will take them to himself, that where he is, etc.

*Third*. The genuine fruits of this conviction {that are evidential of it}.

1. Trusting in him in dangers and difficulties. When afraid of Satan [or] beset with temptations. When burdened with indwelling sin… When in great affliction and adversity… When they don't know what to do. When their wisdom is nonplussed.

When afraid of death or in death.

Trust his power in weakness. His wisdom in ignorance and difficulties. His grace in unworthiness.

2. A rejoicing under his rule and government. That is great cause of joy to a true Christian, that Christ reigneth, and especially that he reigneth over him. Isaiah 52:7, "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!" Revelation 19:6, "And I heard as it were the voice of a great multitude, and as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of mighty thunderings, saying, Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth." It was the blessedness of Israel that Balaam took notice of, Numbers 23:21, "The Lord his God is with him, and the shout of a king is among them."[^018-note43] There is nothing that is greater cause of rejoicing and shouting for Christ's sincere servants, than that Christ is their king.

3. An entire subjection unto Christ, and an universal and willing obedience to all his commandments. All those that have truly seen the glory of Christ as the Lord of his people and captain, this will be the

<!-- p. 428 -->

effect. Therefore all such [as] live a holy and a Christian life, observing the precepts of the gospel, walking according to those excellent rules, and have respect to all {God's commandments}, they take Christ's yoke upon them and are his steady followers.[^018-note44]

### Improvement

We are now come to the improvement of this part.

I. Hence we learn how holiness of life and good works is secured by the gospel. Good works are not what men are justified by, but men are justified freely by faith in Jesus, through whom God justifies the ungodly. And God has promised that whosoever believes in Christ shall be saved: if he has once believed in Christ, he is sure of heaven; and it is impossible he should miss of it, how many sins soever he has been guilty of before, and though he falls into great sins afterwards.

Now some may be ready to say, if it be so, what need we trouble ourselves about good works, and what provision is there made for the holy living of believers? If they have believed in Christ, they may live as wickedly as they please, and enjoy the pleasure of sin as much as they please. They are sure they should go to heaven when they die notwithstanding, because they have believed in Christ and trusted in him for salvation; and then the gospel will be nothing else but an encouragement to licentiousness, and opens a door for all manner of wickedness.

The like objection is proposed and answered by the Apostle (Galatians 2:17).

But I say by this proposition, how the gospel secures good works, though men are justified only by faith and not by the works of the law: for the work of the Holy Ghost in conversion don't only consist in convincing men of righteousness, but also of judgment. He don't only show them the sufficiency of Christ's righteousness to justify 'em and so make 'em receive him as a savior from punishment, but also shows the glory of Jesus Christ as Lord and king, and makes them to receive him heartily and entirely as their Lord and king, their lawgiver, their deliver from the power of sin and Satan; that is, he makes them to submit to his rule and government, to yield themselves up to him as his servants and followers, and to trust in him to mortify and subdue sin, and deliver them from that as well as from punishment.

<!-- p. 429 -->

Conviction of righteousness and judgment always go together: the Holy Ghost don't give one without the other. The preceding conviction of sin is in order to both [of] these, and these are always given together in concurrence. And evermore when Christ is received as priest, he is received as king also; when his righteousness is received, his government or judgment is also received.

And they that are thus convinced of the glory and excellency of Christ as Lord and king, they are the most likely to yield a hearty and universal and careful obedience to God's commands and to bring forth good works. This is the most effectual means for this end; and this is an effectual means, a means that evermore has the effect and obtains the end.

Indeed, the more they have of this conviction, the less is their obedience from a principle of slavishness.[^018-note45] But the more it is from a more noble principle, even from love, esteem, and honor and gratitude— which principles alone can make obedience acceptable to God—this is to serve God in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.

They that serve God only from fear of his wrath, their service is not a service of heart or of the spirit, but only external. Fear will never make a man hearty and spiritual, though it may influence the outward actions; but he that serves God from an high esteem and supreme love and thankfulness, he serves God with the heart.

So that the gospel is so far from being an encouragement to sin, and Christ the minister of sin, that there is nothing else that lays a foundation for a true and upright obedience.

II. Hence we learn how vain the hopes of such persons are that think that they have trusted in Christ's righteousness and yet don't live a life of universal holiness. There are some such: they pretend that they trust in Christ, and that they depend only on Christ's righteousness and have no dependence on their own righteousness, that yet show by their lives that they never were convinced of judgment. They'll tell a very formal story about the light and discoveries they had: how they first see their own hearts; and that it would be just with God to cast 'em off; and afterwards, what a wonderful discovery they had of Christ from such and such places of Scripture. But they never were in concert with Christ for their king; they never liked his government, as is very

<!-- p. 430 -->

evident, for they don't walk according to the rules of the gospel. They'll do some things perhaps, but they live in the neglect of others. There is some lust or other that they indulge; there is some sin that they practice and that they plead for.

They are not just and upright in their dealings, or they live in some way of sensuality. They ben't of a spirit to take up their cross and follow after Jesus Christ. They won't deny themselves for Christ's sake; they ben't of a spirit to suffer for Christ. They regard their pleasure or their money or their neighbor's good will more than they do Christ Jesus and submission to his government.

There are some that don't observe those rules of charity and forgiveness that Christ so much insisted upon: they are all for themselves, and none for anybody else; they are proud, spiteful, revengeful sort of men; they lay up the remembrance of injuries forever in their breasts.

There are some of these that tell of their experiences that are not heavenly minded; they mind earthly things. Covetousness is a ruling principle in them.

It would be endless to mention all the particulars, but surely they are far from that holy, Christian walk which is the proper evidence of submitting to Jesus Christ as their Lord and king and deliverer from sin as well as punishment.

[III.] I shall conclude the improvement of this proposition by directing of you to some heads of consideration and meditation in order to your being convinced of {the glory and sufficiency of Christ as Lord and deliverer of his people}, and your being brought to an entire, cheerful and joyful yielding of yourself to Christ as your king.

*First*. Consider how proper it is that Christ should have dominion and power, who is the great God's only Son and heir. If it be fitting that those that are nobly descended and are of royal blood should have honor and rule (Ecclesiastes 10:17), how well doth the kingdom and power and glory suit with Christ, the natural Son of God himself, who han't the blood of earthly kings but the nature of the eternal God in him.

And [Christ] is not only his own natural Son, of the same nature with him, but is his only begotten Son, infinitely more honorable than the highest descended of mortal worms. Psalms 89:6, "There are none amongst the sons of the mighty can be likened unto the Lord."

And as Christ is the only Son of God, so he is the heir of all things. Galatians 4:7, "If a son, then an heir." Hebrews 1:2, "God hath spoken to us by his Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things."

O how honorable a king have we over us! He is not one of least

<!-- p. 431 -->

descent, a mean, obscure person that will be a disgrace. But we are the kingdom of the Son of God; we are the citizens of that city that God's heir reigns [over]. How great an honor is it to us to have such an one become our king, and captain of our salvation! And what a great privilege is it that we enjoy, that this heir of God should choose us, the poor children of men, to make more especially his kingdom!

*Second*. Consider what it was that moved him ever to become the king of the children of men. No profit… It was his love and pity to us that moved him. He saw us from the heights of his glory, poor worms enslaved to Satan and under the power and dominion of that ever-cruel tyrant and enemy, in a deplorable and miserable condition, and he pitied us. His heart earned towards us; it was a time of love with him. Being of an infinitely gracious nature, [he] was pleased to love us with a very dear love; his delights were with the sons of men (Proverbs 8:31).

And that was what moved him to become our head and king, and he set up his government over us: it was that he might be our deliverer. It was a thing well-pleasing to him, to think of reigning over such a miserable, deplorable company, that he might bring them from [being] miserable to the highest heights of happiness.

*Third*. Consider that Christ lays the foundation of this kingdom of his in his blood. He went through great, unheard of labors and sufferings to redeem us out of the hands of Satan, to bring [us] from our lost estate, so that we might be brought to him and become his church and kingdom.

He has purchased us to be a peculiar people to himself, for him forever to rule over. Never any king obtained his kingdom at so dear a rate. Many kings have gone through many dangerous battles and great hardships and vast difficulties to obtain their kingdom, but never any did or endured such great things to obtain their kingdom as Christ to obtain his kingdom of grace. Acts 20:28, "The church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood."

Christ condescends to esteem his church his riches, his treasure, his crown of rejoicing. And he has won this crown at the price of his own life; he waded through a sea of blood to come at it.

*Fourth*. Consider the excellency of the laws and rules by which Christ's kingdom is governed. The rules of his kingdom might all be resolved into these two: to be excellent, and to be happy. Christ our king requires us to be of a divine and heavenly temper, to be, as much as our limited natures will allow, like God our heavenly Father, and to

<!-- p. 432 -->

act and behave ourselves after the most divine and heavenly manner that we can; to be pure in our thoughts and affections, to be amiable in our actions, to follow after "whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report" [Philippians 4:8].

If we do these things that Christ requires of us, we shall but make ourselves shine with God's image, and shall have a luster and brightness upon our souls superior to that of Moses, full superior to that of the sun in the firmament.

All that is required of us by Christ may be summed up in that one thing, even love: that we should be filled with that divine principle; that we should love God and exert all suitable acts of love towards that infinitely lovely object; that we should love Christ Jesus our savior, the Son of God; that we should love one another even as ourselves.

How excellent a condition is that kingdom, in that [it] is subject to such laws. Obedience to these rules makes a man more excellent than his neighbor, makes a man as a jewel amongst rubbish.

*Fifth*. Consider the excellent and gracious manner of Christ's governing his people by communicating vital influences to them and governing their hearts. His powerful, inward influence is exceeding pleasant. The soul is never so happy as when it is under the strongest influences of Christ, and his heart is most irresistibly governed by him. Christ don't drive, but he draws the heart; he draws by light and love.

There is the greatest liberty in this his government. Men ben't forced and compelled, but they follow the sweet and gracious influences of Christ upon the will; they are not abridged of anything.[^018-note46] Christ rules over his subjects as a father amongst his dear children; he governs them by paternal respect and esteem and love. His commands are but fatherly counsels.

Christ's kingdom is his spouse. He is espoused to every soul that is his subject. They stand in the nearest relation to him. Yea, Christ's kingdom is his own body.

*Sixth*. Compare this dominion of Christ that believers are under to the tyranny of that master that the rest of the world are under.

*Seventh*. Consider the end of Christ's rule and dominion over his people in another world. What great advantage to his subjects. How glorious will Christ's kingdom be in its perfect, complete state.

*Eighth*. The angels count it their happiness that Christ is king over

<!-- p. 433 -->

them. How they sing. Revelation 5:11–12, "And I beheld, and I heard the voice of many angels round about the throne and the beasts and the elders: and the number of them was ten thousand times ten thousand, and thousands of thousands; saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing."

### General Improvement.

I shall conclude this discourse and what I have to say from this text in a few words of general improvement of this whole doctrine.

[*Use*] I. If it be so that 'tis the work of the Holy Ghost thus to convince men of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment, then we learn where ministers should have their dependence in their endeavors, even upon the Holy Ghost.

The Word of God indeed is sharp as a two-edged sword, and is quick and powerful, but it is so only through the cooperation of that Spirit that gave the Word. The Word alone, however managed, explained, confirmed and applied, is nothing but a dead letter without the Spirit. The weapons of their warfare are indeed mighty, but it is only through God (2 Corinthians 10:4). And then only can they hope to have [the Word of God] to success or to come in the fullness of the blessing of the gospel of Christ, but when they go forth in Christ's strength. That is all the encouragement ministers have that Christ has promised them, that he will be with them, i.e. by his Spirit, to the end of the world. Matthew 28:19–20, "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost: Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world."

Ministers therefore ought not depend on their learning or eloquence, nor upon their diligence, or the greatness of their endeavors to promote the good of souls. If they take never so much pains, they should not trust to that. Nor ought they to depend on their own experiences or the goodness of their preparations. But their eye should be to their master that sent them, to make their labors successful through his Spirit.

They should have their eyes to him. Public. Private. Not discouraged when without success. [Not] exalted by success or attribute it to themselves, or think themselves better or wiser than other ministers that have not success.

<!-- p. 434 -->

Their eyes should be to God to reform men that are vicious in their lives, however established and confirmed they seem to be in vicious courses. Convince secure [men]. Savingly to bring men to Christ… To direct them aright…

And therefore, 'tis ministers' duty to be much in prayer to God for this end. They should be as earnest with God in prayer as he is with the people in counsel, advice and warning.

[*Use*] II. We may take notice of the wisdom of God in so ordering that each person should have such a share in the work of redemption. We have often observed that it was in this work more especially that God designed to glorify himself[^018-note47] from all eternity, and he had this principally in view in the creation of the world and in all the great works of providence from the beginning.

And seeing God subsists in three persons that are the same in essential glory, it was seen meet that in this great work they should all of them have their particular glory manifested with a brightness and luster answerable to their equal, essential glory; that not only the perfections of the divine essence common to all might be manifested therein, but that glory of God be shown which consists in the deity's subsistence in three persons and their particular manner of subsistence; that the respect of the creatures might be equal to each of them who are in themselves equal; and that the creature's absolute dependence might be upon each of 'em respectively in this great affair, which is the greatest concern—and indeed the all—of the creature. And also that the glory of each of them might with a suitable luster [appear] to the angels in this work, which the angels desire to look into.

Now 'tis worth our while to consider how this matter is ordered. The Father manifests his glory by entertaining thoughts of mercy towards men after their rebellion, and that he should give his own Son, infinitely dear to him, for this end; and giving all the elect to him to be taken care of by him, and have their selection secured, and in accepting what Christ did, and justifying believers for his sake and taking of them into favor.

The Son, he is the Redeemer. He is he that actually procures salvation, that lays down his life; he redeems by merit, as he is the high priest, and by power, as he is the king of his church.

The Holy Ghost is he that, after salvation is procured, immediately possesses them of it all. Though Christ procures all, he confers all; 'tis

<!-- p. 435 -->

he that converts the sinner, that brings him out of darkness; 'tis he unites to Christ. He gives holiness and he gives the happiness purchased; he enlightens [the] understanding and renovates the will, elevates and purifies the affections. He gives the heart all comfort and all spiritual blessing in this world; he preserves to the end and fits for glory.

And not only so, but 'tis he that immediately gives eternal life also. 'Tis he that perfects holiness, and 'tis he that perfects the spiritual happiness of the soul. Then they will be perfectly holy and happy forever, because the Holy Spirit fills them.

Now I think it can hardly be said which of the persons in the Trinity has the greatest share in this work of redemption: it's all from every one of them. It's all from God the Father, for he is the person that determines whether or no there shall be any salvation at all: he provides the Savior, by whom all salvation is procured, and he accepts him, and he sends the Spirit; so that it is all originally from the Father. It is also all from the Son, for he procures it all; he is the medium of it all. And it is all from the Holy Ghost, for he applies it all; he possesses of it all. Therefore the glory of all that happiness which we have by redemption is to be given to each of them, and our absolute dependence in the whole affair is to be upon each of them. And glory will be given in heaven forever to the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost with equal ardor, exaltation and gratitude. As the wisdom of God appears in abundance of other instances in this work of redemption, so this is one remarkable instance for which this work is worthy to be admired by us.

[*Use*] III. From this doctrine we learn how we ought to be affected towards the Holy [Ghost], and what glory we should give. The doctrine teaches us our concern with him and our dependence upon him, how he is the immediate light of the soul that enlightens it and fills it with divine light and saving knowledge, and how he makes application thereby of the benefits of Christ's redemption.

There belongs to him therefore our dependence upon him, as being him by whom we nextly and most immediately have all spiritual blessings. We should look for life and holiness and comfort from the Father, through the Son and by the Spirit. So we should look for sanctifying influences, for supports under temptations and afflictions, for eternal life and heavenly glory from the Father, through the Son and by the Spirit. And as we glorify the Father for {providing the Savior}, and the Son for {procuring salvation}, so we ought to glorify the Holy

<!-- p. 436 -->

Ghost as he that, by coming into our souls and dwelling there, gives light and knowledge, gives us holiness and makes us happy.

As he is the source and fountain of all holiness, so he is called the Holy Spirit, and upon that account he should be acknowledged and glorified by us. As he gives us those saving convinctions and divine light, so he is called the Spirit of Truth, and should be admired and glorified by us upon that account. As 'tis he that gives all spiritual comfort and delight, so he is called the "Good Spirit" and "the Comforter," and so he should be {glorified by us upon that account}. We ought to be filled with gratitude to the Spirit of God for his wonderful condescension and beneficence in coming to take up his abode in such {poor creatures}, and so honoring of us as to make us his temple and filling of us with such unspeakable riches, such glorious light and precious grace and sweet counsels. And we should glorify him abundantly upon the account of those more perfect degrees which we expect in another world, when his light will be full and like the noonday sun.

*Use* IV. Of *Exam*. By this doctrine, let all try their state. Have you…

[*Use*] V. Let us do what in us lies to be filled with the Spirit, seeing that 'tis by him immediately, and by him only, that those great blessings {are given}. Let none content themselves without having his indwelling {presence}, without having such a glorious principle of life and action in their hearts.

And let us strive for greater and greater degrees of it. Let it be considered that he that has most of the Spirit will have most {of God}. He that hath most of the Spirit, hath most of God, is most like Christ, has most comfort and joy in the world, and lives most to God's glory; and not only so, but he that hath most of the Spirit here in this world, and has most of the exercises and fruits of it, will have most of it also in the other world. Though there all will have it to such perfection as to exclude anything of the contrary, yet some will have it in greater measure than others, and those that have [it] in greater degree then will shine brightest, "as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever" [Daniel 12:3].[^018-note48]

That we may so be, let us carefully avoid all things by which it may be quenched. Let us long and thirst for it. Let [us] cherish and yield to and follow all his motions. Let us pray for the Spirit.

<!-- p. 437 -->

See also no. 32, written later that year, in which JE refers to his explanation of John 16:8 under a definition of justifying faith (ibid., 608–John 16:09). [^018-note6]: JE deletes: "and was his Spirit as much as his breath was his."

### The Sacrifice of Christ Acceptable

This piece is a christological statement that asserts Christ's obedience and death, and not good works or natural virtue, as truly atoning for sin. It is part of Edwards' effort to refute anti-trinitarian arguments against the divinity of Christ that denied the need for atonement by the death of an infinite being, as well as the Arminian view of works and grace.[^019-note1] He does so by exploring the meanings of Old and New Testament sacrifices, specifically the "legal sacrifices" under the covenant of works and the sacrifice of Christ that initiated the covenant of grace.

Edwards begins this sermon with what is for him an unusually long and detailed explication, based on his glosses on the text of this sermon in the previously written "Notes on the Scripture" nos. 62 and 171, in which he explains the ancient Jewish custom of a slave who loved his master's service having his ear "bored" in the presence of judges. Edwards points out that the slave was a type of Christ, in that Christ willingly became God's servant. While other commentators take notice of Christ's voluntary consent, Edwards gives the passage a distinctive interpretation by stating that Christ's offering himself freely was his "highest act of obedience."[^019-note2]

In the first proposition, Edwards demonstrates why Old Testament sacrifices were not in themselves acceptable. Sacrifices under the Old Testament dispensation, or "the law," were not proper atonement for sins because in offering animals the Israelites were only offering to God what was his already. In addition, there was no "moral goodness" in such sacrifices; they could not make atonement for sins and could not merit God's blessing. Why then, Edwards asks, did God bother with having the people of Israel sacrifice at all? If legal sacrifice was not efficacious, he explains, it was at least symbolic. Sacrificing according to the law demonstrated obedience, kept the memory of sins alive,

<!-- p. 438 -->

taught that the offense of sin could only be effaced by suffering, represented God's willingness to be reconciled to sinful humankind, and typified the sacrifice of Christ.

With the incarnation of Christ, however, a new and efficacious sacrifice was offered. Drawing on numerous "Miscellanies" entries on "Christ's Righteousness" and related topics (including nos. 381, 385, 387–88, 398–99, and 402–03) and "Faith" no. 32, [^019-note3] as well as on his investigation into the nature of the Trinity instanced most prominently in *The Threefold Work of the Holy Ghost*, Edwards here explores the work of Christ in offering himself as a sacrifice. Christ's sacrifice or obedience was acceptable because it was holy, propitiatory, and meritorious. First, it was holy by virtue of Christ's divine nature and union with the Father and Holy Spirit. Second, it was propitiatory because Christ offered to God the Father that which he did not already have: an infinitely meritorious sacrifice to match all of the sins of humankind. Christ's offering of himself was not obligatory or compelled; rather, he did it voluntarily, as the servant who had his ear "bored." Thus, Christ was able to satisfy the Father's offended sense of justice and answer the law. Finally, it was meritorious because it not only paid the debt of sin, it also secured the "positive blessings" of grace.

In Edwards' view, offering legal sacrifices is synonomous with offering merely moral behavior as a plea for redemption. Anything that human beings render in the way of sacrifice or obedience to the law, apart from Christ, is worthless. Edwards likens the unconverted to those under the Old Testament dispensation who offered "slain beasts," whereas those who are converted are under the New Testament, the new covenant, and can plead the sacrifice of Christ.

Edwards made a note to himself in the manuscript that indicates when the sermon was preached. At the end of the first preaching unit, he wrote "Sheldon," referring to Elisha Sheldon (b. 1707), who was to be admitted to full church membership in the near future, in all probability the coming sacrament day.[^019-note4] Sheldon's name also appears at the end of the sermon on 1 Peter 3:4 (133), which was most likely delivered on October 26, 1729, the Sunday before the November 2 sacrament sermon, *Glorying in the Savior*. This means that Edwards probably began

<!-- p. 439 -->

to preach *The Sacrifice of Christ Acceptable* on the lecture day of the intervening week.

∗ ∗ ∗

The manuscript consists of sixteen duodecimo leaves. There are two preaching units in this sermon, the second beginning at the second proposition.

Besides writing the name of Elisha Sheldon at the end of the first preaching unit, Edwards also wrote "Baptism" as a reminder to himself either to perform that sacrament following the service or to announce that it would be administered the next sabbath.

<!-- p. 440 -->

### The Sacrifice of Christ Acceptable

Psalms 40:6–8> *Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required. Then said I, Lo, I come: in the volume of the book it is written of me, I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart*.[^019-note5]

This psalm was probably sung by David upon occasion of some remarkable deliverance from his enemies. He here praises God that he had heard his cry and brought him out of an horrible pit, and put a new song into his mouth, and that his thoughts of mercy towards him and his people could not be reckoned up nor numbered.

Now it was usual upon experience of [a] very singular mercy to offer sacrifices of peace offerings unto God, which is the occasion of the Psalmist's saying here as [he] does, "Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required."

The Psalmist knew that that was not the thing that God principally required or expected of his people of such occasions. He says much to the same purpose in the fifty-first Psalm, sixteenth verse.[^019-note6] There was something else that God expected from his people that was a more acceptable manifestation of their gratitude and respect after the receipt of mercies, and another sacrifice that he had respect to, for the sake of which he laid aside his wrath and received the sinner into favor.

We may consider these words two ways: either as they more immediately relate to David himself, or as the Holy Ghost in them has a more principal and ultimate respect to Christ, the spiritual David. For in many passages in the Psalms, the Psalmist has a more immediate respect

<!-- p. 441 -->

to himself in those things which he speaks; but yet the Holy Ghost has a principal aim at the Christ, the son of David. Whether David himself had an aim to Christ or no, the Holy Ghost might have a further aim in those words which he dictated to David, than David himself had: for as the Apostle teaches us (2 Peter 1:20–21),[^019-note7] the prophecy of Scripture is not "of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost"; i.e. it was not what the penman thought of {in composing it}.

And there is no difficulty in supposing that the prophets themselves sometimes did not fully understand their own prophesies. They did not know everything that the Holy Ghost had in view in the words which they spoke or wrote. It is evident by Numbers 12:6–8, "And he said, Hear now my words: If there be a prophet among you, I the Lord will make myself known unto him in a vision, and will speak unto him in a dream. My servant Moses is not so, who is faithful in all mine house. With him I speak mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches; and the similitude of the Lord shall he behold: wherefore then were ye not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?" By which it is evident that it was God's usual manner not to speak apparently but in dark speeches to ordinary prophets.

If[^019-note8] we consider the words as they respect David, they are a profession of his willing obedience to God. God often declared that obedience was better than sacrifice. The Psalmist is here declaring his giving of it the preference in his practice; he did not rest in sacrifices or look upon his duty as consisting mainly in them. But he was willingly obedient to God's law; he delighted to do God's will. God had opened his ear. It might have been translated, "Mine ear hast thou bored." It is in the original, "Mine ear hast thou digged," alluding to the law (Exodus 21:5), by which it was appointed that if the servant loved his master's service and freely chose it, his master should bore his ear through with an awl.

"Burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required. Then said I, Lo, I come"; as a willing servant[^019-note9] says when he is called.

"In the volume of the book it is written of me." There is the greatest

<!-- p. 442 -->

difficulty[^019-note10] in understanding this clause. It is generally understood [as] the book of God's decrees,[^019-note11] that Christ came to do God's will, as it was written of him in the book of the decrees, or in the book of scripture. But this is what seems to me to be the meaning of it (every one may judge for himself): viz. that the Psalmist still alludes to that law and custom about the servant that chose his master's service forementioned, and that by the "volume of the book" is meant the public records. The servant in that case was to be brought unto the judges and was to declare his choice, and his ear was to be bored before them that those public officers might be witnesses of it. Now we may conclude that there was a record written of it, that it might be known what servants had thus done, and that they by that record, as a public evidence of their act, might be obliged by it. It was the custom amongst the Jews to keep records of other things of this nature, as of the conveyances of land, as we have account. Jeremiah 32:10, "I subscribed the evidence of it"; it is in the Hebrew, "I wrote in the book." So the Psalmist is still carrying on the same comparison of a servant that had his ear bored. [The record is] called "volume of the book," that is, "roll."[^019-note12]

But the Psalmist here doubtless speaks prophetically and as representing Christ. Christ freely and willingly became God's servant by becoming incarnate, by taking flesh upon him. And therefore instead of the words, "Mine ear hast thou bored," in the New Testament we have this text quoted: "A body hast thou prepared me" (Hebrews 10:5). And as the servant that had his ear bored [learned] obedience by the things that he suffered—it was a testimony of his real desire to serve his master, that he was willing to suffer this in order to it—so did Christ learn obedience by the things that he suffered. The offering up his body a sacrifice was his highest act of obedience.[^019-note13] So when it is said, "Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire," it is as much as if he had

<!-- p. 443 -->

said, "Those sacrifices of beasts, etc. are in themselves worthless. God did not require them for their own sake; but my body crucified is the true sacrifice that God delights in." I have been the longer in opening these words,[^019-note14] it being so remarkable a text.

#### Doctrine.

#### The sacrifice of Christ is the only sacrifice that is upon its own account acceptable to God.

The sacrifices that are of God's appointment are either Christ, the true sacrifice, or the typical sacrifices under the Old Testament. We find in Scripture that thanksgiving is sometimes called a "sacrifice" and "obedience" and a "broken heart," and our bodies—that is, our persons—when offered to God, are called "a living sacrifice." But these are only called "sacrifices" metaphorically; they are not proper sacrifices.

A sacrifice is something offered to God, which by its suffering and death makes atonement and procures acceptance for them that it is offered for. The sacrifices under the law did not truly do this, but they did it typically. And therefore Christ, according to the language of Scripture, may be called the true sacrifice, in distinction from all other sacrifices; and his altar, the true altar; and the tabernacle he officiated in, the true tabernacle. Hebrews 8:2, "A minister of the sanctuary, and the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched, and not man"; and Hebrews 9:24, "For Christ is not entered into the holy places made with hands, which are the figures of the true."

Here are therefore these two propositions to be considered:

I. That the sacrifices of the Old Testament were not in themselves and upon their own account any way acceptable to God.

II. That the sacrifice of Christ was in itself and upon its own {account acceptable to God}.

*Prop*. I. The sacrifices of the Old Testament were not {in themselves acceptable to God}.

*First*. They were not acceptable to God as gifts that he received anything by. The sacrifices are called "gifts." Exodus 28:38, "That Aaron may bear the iniquity of the holy things, which the children of Israel shall hallow in all their holy gifts." They are not so-called because they were not proper gifts to God; they were God's own already. As David

<!-- p. 444 -->

said when he made such large offerings for the house of God, "Of thine own have we given thee" (1 Chronicles 29:14). But they were types of Christ's sacrifice, that was properly a gift.

God stood in no need of their sacrifices. They were of no manner of advantage to him. Psalms 50:7–10, "Hear, O my people, and I will speak; O Israel, and I will testify against thee: I am God, even thy God. I will not reprove thee for thy sacrifices or thy burnt offerings, to have been continually before me. I will take no bullock out of thy house, nor he-goats out of thy folds. For every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills."

God is self-sufficient, and cannot stand in need of anything. Acts 17:25, "Neither is worshipped with men's hands, as though he needed anything."

God received neither profit nor pleasure from such gifts. Isaiah 1:11, "I delight not in the blood of bullocks, or of lambs, or of he-goats."

The heathen had a notion that the gods were pleased with the scent of their sacrifices, with the smoke that ascended up from off their altars. And the sacrifices under the law are said to be made by fire for a sweet savor unto the Lord [Leviticus 3:5]: they were offered with burning of incense, which made a sweet and fragrant smell. But it was only to represent the acceptableness of Christ's sacrifice, which was indeed a sweet savor, and was that in which God was well-pleased and delighted.

*Second*. The sacrifices of the Old Testament were not acceptable as having any moral goodness in their own nature. There is no moral goodness in offering of slain beasts unto God; the law of nature required no such things. We can't infer that this is one kind of worship [that] is due to God, merely from the consideration of God's nature or attributes, or his relation to us. We may infer our obligation to prayer and praise and other duties of natural worship.[^019-note15] They were not required to attend it because it was in itself naturally a fit and becoming thing that reasonable creatures should [worship] in this way; and therefore in the twelfth [chapter] of Romans, first verse, the offering ourselves a living sacrifice is called a "reasonable service" in very way of distinction from the sacrifices under the law, because reason and the nature of the thing obliged us to offer this sacrifice, which it did not [in] the sacrifices of beasts. So this is there said to be holy and acceptable to God in contradistinction to them, because they had no moral

<!-- p. 445 -->

holiness in them; nor were they acceptable to God upon any such account. Micah 6:8, "He hath showed thee, O man, what is good."

The obligation to offer those sacrifices arise only upon God's positive and arbitrary institution. There was no other holiness in them than in their holy places, which was not a moral holiness, but what was typical and depending on positive institution.

*Third*. Those sacrifices were not propitiatory. They did not nor could not make atonement for the soul; they made no satisfaction to divine justice. How could the burning of the flesh of beasts make any satisfaction for the debt which the sinner had contracted to divine justice by his sins? How was there any compensation for the injury done to the divine majesty by the killing of a beast? The value of the thing offered could not be equivalent to the debt contracted, nor could the suffering of the beast be equivalent to the deserved sufferings of the sinner. And therefore, as the Apostle says (Hebrews 9:9), those gifts and sacrifices "could not make him that did the service perfect, as pertaining to the conscience."

And this same doctrine God taught his people under the Old Testament. When he required that they should offer sacrifices for him, yet he taught them at the same time that they could not make atonement. Micah 6:6–7, "Wherewith shall I come before the Lord, and bow myself before the high God? shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves of a year old? Will the Lord be pleased with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of rivers of oil? shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?"

And David, when after he had been guilty of his adultery and murder and was brought to repentance of it, he says, by the Spirit of God, "Thou desirest not sacrifice; else would I give it: thou delightest not in burnt offering" (Psalms 51:16). Much less,

*Fourth*, were they meritorious of God's favor or any positive blessing. The sacrifice of Christ was not only propitiatory, but meritorious, as we shall endeavor to show afterwards. But the legal sacrifices were not so. It is said of Noah's sacrifice (Genesis 10:21) that God smelled a sweet savor, and said in his heart that he would no more curse the ground; but it was not because that sacrifice had drawn and inclined God's heart to Noah and his posterity, but it was the respect which God had to the great sacrifice which that was the shadow of that made God thus propitious. It was the substance, and not the shadow, that sent forth that sweet savor.

<!-- p. 446 -->

*Inq.* Of what use were the sacrifices of the Old Testament, or in what respect were they acceptable to God?

It is evident they were of divine institution: they were so from the beginning of the world. Sacrifices did not begin in the church upon God's giving the Law at Mount Sinai, but they were of longer standing. We read frequently of the patriarchs building altars and offering sacrifices unto the Lord: so Noah, he offered sacrifices; so we read that Abel brought of the firstlings of his flock, and of the fat thereof, and his offering was accepted; and it is supposed that those skins that God clothed Adam and Eve with were skins of sacrifices.

And from sacrifices being of such early institution, it doubtless came to pass that the custom of sacrificing became so universal all over the world amongst the heathen. They had it by tradition from their ancestors, from Noah and his sons, or else how should they come all to agree in it?

Seeing therefore this custom was in use in the church from the beginning of the world, it is worthy of inquiring of what use it was of in the church. Those sacrifices, when offered in a right manner, were acceptable to God. So we read (Genesis 4:4) that God had respect to Abel and his offering. Therefore I answer:

*First Ans*. The sacrifices of the Old Testament were acceptable to God as they were done in obedience. One end of the ceremonial law was to exercise and try the obedience of his people, as it was of all the laws that God gave at Mount Sinai. When God descended on Mount Sinai, Moses said to the people, "Fear not: for God is come to prove you, and that his fear may be before your faces, that you sin not" [Exodus 20:20]. That is what God tells the children of Israel was the end of the Law when he gave it. Deuteronomy 6:1–2, "Now these are the commands, the statutes, and the judgments, which the Lord your God hath commanded to teach you, that thou mightest fear the Lord thy God, to keep all his statutes and his commandments." To the same purpose is that in Jeremiah 7:22–23, "For I spake not unto your fathers, nor commanded them in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices. But this thing commanded I them, saying, Obey my voice."

The law of sacrifices and the rest of the ceremonial law was very burdensome. It required a considerable expense, and also a great deal of care and exactness, in order to its being duly attended.

And when sacrifices were offered to God according to the law, out of

<!-- p. 447 -->

a spirit of obedience and from a sincere respect to that authority that instituted them, they were acceptable to God.

*Second* [*Arts*.] Another end was to bring their sins to their remembrance. By their so often offering sacrifices for sins, they were put in mind of their sins anew. They had their yearly sacrifices. Hebrews 10:3, "But in these sacrifices is remembrance again made of sins every year." Every year they had a day of atonement. They had their monthly sacrifices: they were to offer a special sacrifice to God at the new moon at the beginning of every month (Numbers 28:11). And they had also a weekly sacrifice to be offered every sabbath (in the same chapter, Numbers 28:9). And then they had their daily sacrifice, morning and evening, as in the beginning of that chapter, to the ninth verse. Which was to teach them that they were continually sinning against God every year, every month, every week and every day.

There were sacrifices to be offered at the birth of every child, to teach them that they came sinful into the world, besides other sacrifices for sin that were to be offered upon special occasions: as their feasts at the consecration of priests, special judgments of God or particular transgressions, sins of ignorance and against light, etc.

Hereby they were taught that they were depraved, sinful creatures, that they had sinful natures and were always a-committing sins for which God might justly[^019-note16] be angry with them.

*Third* [*Ans*.] It was to teach them the necessity of satisfaction for sin by suffering. They were taught the necessity of justice being satisfied by a suffering of the penalty. They saw that without shedding of blood, there was no remission (Hebrews 9:22). By the sufferings of those beasts there being slain, they were put in mind that the wages of sin was death; and by their being burnt in the fire, they were taught how they deserved to suffer God's fiery wrath for their sins, and that God would not pardon sin without suffering, without its being punished.

This put them in mind of the evil nature of sin and taught them the holy jealousy of God, and how that he would in no wise clear the guilty. And so this type and shadow, together with God's declarations of his being a holy and jealous God that would in no wise clear the guilty, secured the honor of God's jealousy and justice, and tended to bring off the sinner from a trust in his own righteousness. It taught him the strictness of the law, that sin must be suffered for notwithstanding all that he could do to make amends.

<!-- p. 448 -->

*Fourth* [*Ans*.] They were hereby taught God's willingness to be reconciled. They were by this institution taught both God's justice and his mercy at the same time that they were hereby led to a sense of God's jealousy and severity. They were also led to [a] sense of his free grace, which must always be together in true faith. At the same time that the sinner trusts in God's mercy, it must be with a sense of his awful majesty and justice, or else his trust is presumption and not faith. His faith is not true, because it believes a thing that is false: it believes that God will pardon sin without justice being satisfied. Therefore God so contrived the matter in those days of the church, when so little was known of the true sacrifice, that his people might be led both not to trust in themselves and also to trust in God's mercy.

*Fifth* [*Ans*.] And lastly, it was to typify the sacrifice of Jesus Christ and to lead men to trust in him. Christ was the end of all the ceremonial observances of the law; he was the sum and substance of all. By this ceremonial law, the gospel was preached to them; though they had not the direct light of the sun of righteousness, yet they had it reflected from those typical ordinances.

Those sacrifices were to point forth Christ and to lead them to trust in him, to prepare the church for the reception and entertainment of him when he came. They would more readily receive the mystery of Christ's satisfaction by his death, for having been so long taught the necessity of sacrifices in order to purge away sin.

And this institution of sacrificing prepared even the heathen world for the entertainment of the gospel, although they changed the sacrifices of divine institution into sacrifices to devils. So however they thereby received this notion that there was need of sacrifices in order to remission, that suffering and shedding of blood was needful in order to appease the gods, so that when the gospel of Christ's sacrifice came to be preached amongst them, they doubtless the more readily entertained it.

And it is of great use and service even to the Christian church now those sacrifices are abolished, for the now seeing those shadows, and seeing the wonderful agreement between them and the antitype, tends to confirm our faith in Christ [and] our belief of the gospel. And there is abundance of instruction in them; they are full of gospel doctrine.[^019-note17]

<!-- p. 449 -->

*Prop*. II. The sacrifice of Jesus Christ is in itself and upon its own account acceptable unto God. When it is said, "Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire, a body hast thou not required," it is as much as to say, "The sacrifices of beasts didst thou not desire, but the sacrifice of my body thou didst desire. In burnt offerings and sin offerings thou hast no pleasure, but thou hast pleasure in my coming to do thy will." That was the will of God, that Christ should come into the world and lay down his life for sinners. And therefore he says, when the time drew nigh, "Not my will, but thine be done" (Matthew 26:39); and Matthew 26:42, "O my Father, if this cup may not pass away from me, except I drink it, thy will be done."

God is well-pleased with Christ as mediator; he is well-pleased in him as high priest and sacrifice upon his own account. As Christ tells us, God loveth him upon this account (John 10:17). Here,[^019-note18]

*First*, the sacrifice of Jesus Christ was in itself most holy. The sacrifices of the Old Testament, as we showed, have in their own nature no moral goodness. We find them called in the Law, "most holy" things [Leviticus 6:17]. According to the Hebrew it is "holy of holinesses," but their holiness was but typical. But the sacrifice of Christ is properly most holy; there is a transcendent holiness in it, and therefore it must be very acceptable to God.

Now in order to see how holy the sacrifice of [Christ is], there are three things to be considered: the holiness of the thing offered; the holiness of the altar, for Christ tells us the altar sanctifies the gift (Matthew 23:19); and the holiness of the act of sacrificing.

1. The thing offered was most holy, for he made his soul an offering for sin (Isaiah 53:10). He offered up himself; he gave himself for us. Now the soul of Christ was a most holy thing. Christ was perfectly innocent: he was born perfectly free from any stain of original sin; on the contrary, he had a holy nature. Therefore the angel, when foretelling Mary of her being the mother of Christ, calls him "the holy thing which shall be born of thee" [Luke 1:35]. His soul was the holiest of all creatures. This was that which was offered up in sacrifice to God. [In the] offerings of beasts [there was] no holiness.

<!-- p. 450 -->

2. The altar, viz. the divine nature of Christ. And then with its relation to the divine nature of Christ, it may be looked upon as infinitely holy: for the soul of Christ that was offered up is personally united to the eternal Word, the second person in the Trinity, who is an infinitely holy person. And 'tis that that gives this sacrifice an infinite value in the sight of God. The divine nature of Christ is that altar that sanctifies the gift, supposed to be typified by the altar in the tabernacle and temple: which altar had no real holiness, for what holiness can there be in stones or brass? Now this altar so sanctifies the gift, that it gives it an infinite holiness.

3. There was a transcendent holiness in that act of Jesus Christ in offering up himself a sacrifice to God, and that two ways:

(1) As it was done to vindicate the majesty, holiness and justice of God, injured by the sins of men. Christ by that act testified an infinite regard to God, that when he desired to save sinners, he had rather die than that that salvation should be any injury to his majesty, justice and law.[^019-note19] He had rather be at infinite expense, for it was an infinite expense that Christ was at; it was an infinite price that he paid. And this he paid that men's salvation might not be with any injury to the glory of God's attributes, and thereby not only testified his love to men, but an infinite regard to the glory of God, and showed his infinite love to God. And therefore as Christ's act of offering up himself a sacrifice was an exercise of so great love to God, so it was a transcendently holy act. Now sacrificing under the law had no holiness in it this way, viz. by the offerer's subjecting himself to death for the vindication of God's justice: for it was not he that suffered, but the beast that was slain. And then,

(2) The act of Christ's subjecting himself to death was transcendently holy, as he did [it] in obedience to the Father. He voluntarily subjected himself to this extreme suffering because he delighted to do God's will, which likewise showed an infinite regard to God and his commands, that he would obey it in so suffering; which also rendered that act of his an act of transcendent holiness. The sacrifices under the law were offered by God's people in obedience, but we speak here of Christ's obedience in suffering as a sacrifice. They under the Old Testament did not obey so.

*Second*. The sacrifice of Jesus Christ was a sacrifice properly propitiatory.

<!-- p. 451 -->

It did indeed make atonement for sin; thereby satisfaction is made for the injury done to God. The Old Testament sacrifices, ten thousand of 'em, were not sufficient to make atonement for one sin; but there is sufficient in Christ's sacrifice to make satisfaction for the sins of the whole world.[^019-note20] In order to our seeing how the sacrifice of Christ doth properly atone for men's sin, consider,

1. What Christ offered in sacrifice to God was that which was in Christ's own power. Christ was under no obligation to offer it till he became mediator, not till he had undertaken to be our surety; indeed, consider him as having already undertaken and having become mediator. And so he became the Father's servant: he was subject to his command, and it was in obedience to his command that he laid down his life. But he was under no obligation to become mediator: that was what he freely consented to in the covenant of redemption.

So that Christ, in offering up his life, in spilling his blood, offered that that was in his own power, in his own right. It was a gift that he freely offered to the justice of God.[^019-note21]

Now the sacrifices under the Old Testament, as we observed before, were not so. When they offered beasts in sacrifice, they offered to God that which [was] in God's power and not their own. They were not arbitrary disposers of what they offered, for all the beasts of the field were God's, and the cattle upon a thousand hills, and it is impossible that atonement should be made for an injury done to God by offering that to him which he before had an absolute right to.

We are infinitely inferior to God; [we] are his creatures, his subjects and servants, his possession. We are God's, and all that we have is his, so that [if] we should offer, as the Prophet says, the fruit of our bodies for the sin of our souls [Micah 6:7], or if we should offer our own blood, we should offer God his own.

But 'tis not so with Christ: he is the Son of God. He is not his servant only, as he voluntarily made himself so, as the servant that had his ear bored; but he is in himself God's equal, his fellow. Zechariah 13:7, "Awake, O sword, against the man that is my fellow." When Christ therefore offers his life, he offers his own and that which he is the true disposer of.

<!-- p. 452 -->

2. What Christ offered in sacrifice to God was equivalent to what justice demanded of us for our sins.

The desert of our sins may be considered as a debt that we owed to divine justice. And therefore if atonement is indeed made, it must be by the offering of something whereby the debt may be paid, which can't be except that [the] thing offered be equal to the debt, except it be of the same value.

Now the demerit of sin in infinite. [The punishment] that we had deserved by our sins is death, that is, eternal destruction, which is infinite suffering.

But the sufferings of Christ were equivalent to this. The suffering was the same in kind, so far as it was possible for the suffering of one that was perfectly holy to be of the same kind with the damnation of the ungodly. Christ suffered the death of his body with extreme outward pains, and he suffered in his soul great darkness from God's withdrawing his comfortable presence and extreme agonies as the effects of God's wrath against our sins that were laid upon him.

Christ had not despair as the damned in hell have; and in some other respects, wherein it is impossible that an innocent person should suffer the same as the guilty, Christ's sufferings were different from those of the damned. Christ was a green tree, and the wicked are the dry tree; they are both cast into the same fire, though the fire has not exactly the same effect upon both.

And though Christ's sufferings were but temporal, yet they were equivalent to our eternal sufferings by reason of the infinite dignity of his person. Though it was not infinite suffering, yet it was equivalent to infinite suffering, for it was infinite expense. His blood which he spilled, his life which he laid down, was an infinite price because it was the blood of God, as it is expressly called. Acts 20:28, "The church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood." His life was the life of that person that was the eternal Son of God, though it was the life of the human nature.

Now upon this account, the price offered was equivalent to the demerit of the sins of all mankind, [and] his sufferings equivalent to the eternal sufferings of the whole world.[^019-note22]

<!-- p. 453 -->

But how far otherwise is it with respect to the legal sacrifices. There were nothing of an equivalent offered in them. If the angels of heaven had died and were made sacrifices for men, that would not have been equivalent to men's eternal sufferings, much less the death of goats and calves.

3. Christ, that gave himself in sacrifice, is so united to them he died for, that it may well be accepted as their sacrifice. It may well be accepted of God as if we had offered that price, and justice in Christ's suffering may well be satisfied for our sins; it may be looked upon as though we had suffered, because Christ is as we. He laid down his life out of love to us; he has been pleased to unite himself to us in his heart, to love us so as to put himself in our stead in the most extreme case.

And he is appointed hereto of the Father. God chose him for our mediator; he is God's elect, and his anointed and sealed. And therefore God looks upon him as our head, and the head being united to the members, the sufferings of the head may be looked upon as the sufferings of the members. The husband being united to the wife, the debts of the wife may be looked upon as his debts, and his goods as her goods. But there was no propriety in looking upon the sufferings of the beasts slain in sacrifice, as though they were the sufferings of him that they were offered for, for there was no union of this nature between them.

4. By the sacrifice of Christ the law was answered with respect to our sins, for the law admits of the sufferings of a surety that are equivalent. The threatening of the law is thus: "In the day that thou sinnest thou shalt [surely die]." Now according to the tenor of the covenant of works, when it is said, "In the day that thou sinnest," it means, "Thou or thy representative": for these words were not only spoken to Adam, but to all his posterity. So that as they are spoken to us, they are to be thus explained: "In the day that thou eatest, or thy surety." Therefore the last clause, which is no more personal than the first, will as fairly admit of a like explanation: "thou shalt die," that is, "Thou or thy surety shalt die." So that as we sin in a representative according to the tenor of the covenant of works, so we may die by a representative according to such an interpretation of the covenant, as the words will fairly admit—that is, provided there can any representative be found

<!-- p. 454 -->

whose sufferings shall be equivalent to our eternal sufferings, that shall undertake for us and God shall appoint.

But the sacrifices of the Old Testament no way answered the law. They could not be said to die in the death of slain beasts, much less be said in them to suffer a death equivalent to an eternal death, which was what the law threatened.

Thus we have shown how the sacrifice of Christ is properly a propitiatory sacrifice.

*Third*. It was a meritorious sacrifice. That is, the sufferings of Christ did not only satisfy justice for our sins, but merited God's favor. Merely by our sins being done away, we stood entitled to no positive blessing at all: we were only freed from obligation to punishment. But Christ's sufferings have not only satisfied and appeased God's anger, but they merited God's favor and eternal life.

The end of sacrifices under the law was not merely typically to atone for sin and appease God's wrath, but to procure positive blessings. They were for a sweet savor to God, to procure his favors: this was often the end of those sacrifices that were vows. They were vowed in order to the obtaining of some special favor or blessing of God.

So the blood of Christ was not only a price to pay a debt, but it was also a price to buy positive blessings with. Christ hath purchased the church with his blood (Acts 20:28); the purchased possession is purchased by Christ's blood.[^019-note23]

But the sacrifice merits positive blessings by the holiness of the act, [as it was] an expression of respect to the Father's righteousness. Christ's submitting [to] shed his blood was the principal act of his obedience, as is intimated in our text: he delighted to do God's will, and had his ear bored. This was a command that he received of the Father, viz. to lay down his life. John 10:18, "I lay down my life, and have power to take it again. This commandment received I of my Father." And Philippians 2:7–8, "He took upon him the form of a servant, and became obedient unto death."

This was a most glorious act of obedience because it was so expensive. Christ therein showed an infinite respect to God's commands, in that he would obey it at such infinite expense. And it was therefore meritorious because Christ was not obliged to it: he was not obliged to

<!-- p. 455 -->

appear in the form of a servant in such a manner to obey God. It is an act of obedience of infinite value in God's account, and a price sufficient to purchase all those eternal blessings which are promised in the gospel to believers. It is so sweet a savor unto God, that he has complacency in Christ for it. John 10:17, "Therefore my Father loveth me," and delights in all that are Christ's upon the account of it.

### Application.

*Inf*. I. Hence learn the reason why this sacrifice is but once offered: because it is the true sacrifice, a sacrifice truly acceptable to God as a propitiation for sin. That sacrifice that truly makes atonement for sin has no need to be offered more than once. If it won't make atonement for sin by once offering it, it will not, though it be offered never so [many times];[^019-note24] but if sin be atoned for by once offering, what need is there of its being offered up again? Hebrews 9:25–28, "Nor yet that he should offer himself often, as the high priest entereth into the holy place every year with blood of others; for then must he often have suffered since the foundation of the world: but now once in the end of the world hath he appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself. And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment: so Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many; and unto them that look for him shall he appear the second time without sin unto salvation."

Now the sacrifices of the Old Testament, they were offered up often: they were offered daily; and the high priest every year entered in once into the holy of holies with the blood of bulls and goats, and there was a remembrance again made of sins. It was because they were not able to take away sins, as the Apostle argues in the beginning of the Hebrews 10: "For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect. For then would they not have ceased to be offered? because that the worshippers once purged should have had no more conscience of sins. But in those sacrifices there is a remembrance again made of sins every year. For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins." And Hebrews 10:11–14, "And every priest standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins: but this man, after he had offered one

<!-- p. 456 -->

sacrifice for sins forever, sat down on the right hand of God; from henceforth expecting till his enemies be made his footstool. For by one offering he hath perfected forever them that are sanctified."

The Papists, they hold that the sacrifice of Christ is to be offered often. They suppose that their priests make a new offering of the body and blood of Christ every Mass, which they hold to be a propitiatory sacrifice and the same that Christ offered upon the cross, which is very contrary to the holy Scriptures.

[*Inf*.] II. Hence we learn why the legal sacrifices do now cease: because they were not the true sacrifice. They were not upon their own account acceptable to God, had no moral goodness in their own nature and were only shadows of the sacrifice of Jesus Christ. They were to point forth that, and prepare the church for the reception and entertainment of it. And now that true sacrifice has actually been offered: Christ, the true high priest, has come into the world and offered up himself; he bore our sins in his own body on the tree; he was a minister of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched and not man, and has entered into the true holy of holies, even into heaven, with his own blood. And this sacrifice of his is published and declared in the gospel, which is commanded to be preached to every creature under heaven.

And the substance being come, there is no further occasion for the shadows; they all vanish. When we have the direct light of the Sun shining above the horizon, we have no further occasion for his light reflected from the moon.

*Inf*. III. How great is the sacrifice of Christ, that was the sum and substance and the end of all the sacrifices that were in the church since the beginning of the world. Sacrificing always till Christ came was made a very great part of outward worship; it was so both before and after Moses, and all was only to point forth the sacrifice of Jesus Christ, and to lead the church to that.

This sacrifice of Christ is surely a thing that God makes much of, that he took care to have it represented so soon in the church, even immediately after the Fall; and appointed so many different kinds of sacrifices in the law of Moses; and set apart one family, and even a whole tribe, to be concerned about this business of sacrificing. God took care to have this sacrifice of Christ represented every day, week, month and year, besides abundance of special occasions. A great part of the law of Moses is about sacrificing, and all to shadow forth Christ's sacrifice. How much doth this argue that God made of this sacrifice.

Great part of the worship of the heathen world consisted in sacrificing,

<!-- p. 457 -->

which though it was from the devil as they used it, yet as it was from tradition from Noah and his sons, it shows the greatness of the sacrifice of Christ, for he was the only true sacrifice.

How many thousands and hundreds of thousands of beasts have been slain to represent this. At one time, at the dedication of the temple, two and twenty thousand oxen and an hundred and twenty thousand sheep (1 Kings 8:63).

[*Inf*. IV.] *Exh*. Let this sacrifice be acceptable unto us. If this was that which was represented and [shadowed forth] by all other sacrifices, if this be the substance, if this be so holy a sacrifice, if it be truly propitiatory and meritorious, let it be that which we look to and trust in.

Let that be what we seek to see, the excellency, suitableness and sufficiency of it. If it be a truly propitiatory [sacrifice], and sufficient to make atonement for all our sins, let us go to Christ, betake ourselves to the Lamb slain for satisfaction for our sins.

Consider:

*First*. Necessity.

*Second*. The excellency.

[1.] The holiness.

2. The love of Father and Son. The freeness. The wisdom. The glory of Christ's person. How much all God's attributes are glorified by it.

*Third*. 'Tis the only way to find rest of heart with respect to the conscience, [the] only way to cast off those burthens, to be freed of that dreadful sound. Matthew 11:28, "Come unto me, all ye that labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."[^019-note25]
