### Glorying in the Savior

In this sacrament sermon, Edwards shows how believers are brought together to constitute the invisible church, of which Christ is the head. Formerly, Edwards notes in the explication, only Abraham's seed was the subject of God's favor. But Israel was a "typical nation" and represented "the true people of Jesus Christ in all ages." It is through Christ that Abraham's spiritual seed is justified.

After distinguishing the people of Christ from unbelievers in the Doctrine, Edwards dwells on what it means for the blessed to glory in Christ, and why they should do so. Glorying in Christ means having a sense of the great privileges bestowed by God and declaring that sense. Believers should boast of Christ's excellencies and glory in their dependence on him and in his honor because he is the most righteous, just, and gracious Lord. As they are redeemed sinners, believers should praise God (for instance, with "divine song") and not glory in their own pride or think they can be saved through their own self-righteousness.

From the beginning of the sermon, Edwards takes aim at what he perceives to be the superficial religion of many of his parishioners. Though many may "profess a better religion," yet they "improve" it so little that they should be ashamed. He criticizes hypocrites whose "tongues and outside" belong to Christ, but not their hearts. The doctrine, he states, "reproves" those who "value and esteem themselves" because of any "natural qualification" they may have. Challenging his listeners' assumptions about their status as saints, Edwards goes on to denounce any who "glory" in their "party among Christians" and in their "profession," which has gained them admittance to the sacraments.

We can surmise that *Glorying in the Savior* was preached for the sacrament service, most likely held on November 2, 1729, that was announced at the conclusion of the sermon on 1 Peter 3:4 (133). In the first head of the first proposition, Edwards refers to attending on the ordinances of Christ, and in the Application he exhorts his listeners, "Particularly

<!-- p. 459 -->

endeavor that you may attend on this ordinance of the Lord's Supper with the spirit of true glory."

∗ ∗ ∗

The manuscript consists of eight duodecimo leaves. Edwards repreached the Sermon in February 1754. He made some minor additions and deletions in a later ink, but gave no indication of whether he repreached the whole or part of the sermon. Portions of the sermon are outlined, particularly the latter part of the second and the whole of the third propositions, as well as the final exhortation of the Application.

<!-- p. 460 -->

### Glorying in the Savior

Isaiah 45:25.[^020-note1]

> *In the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified, and shall glory*.

In this latter part of the chapter, we have a prophecy of the calling of the Gentiles, or of their becoming of God's people, beginning with the twentieth verse: "Assemble yourselves and come; draw near together, ye that are escaped of the nations: they have no knowledge that set up the wood of their graven images, and pray unto a god that cannot save." In the twenty-second verse, Christ invites the Gentile nations to come to him and be saved: "Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else." And in the twenty-third verse, he declares his immutable will of making the whole Gentile world acknowledge him by an oath: "I have sworn by myself, the word is gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and shall not return, that unto me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear." In the twenty-fourth verse, 'tis foretold how he shall be acknowledged and trusted in: "Surely, shall one say, in the Lord have I righteousness and strength: even to him shall men come; and all that are incensed against him shall be ashamed." And then we have an account, first, of the confusion that shall be brought upon his enemies; and second, of the great advantages and happiness which shall anoint those that are his people: the first of these in the latter part of the twenty-fourth verse, "All that are incensed against him shall be ashamed"; the latter in our text, "In the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified, and shall glory."

In the words we may take notice,

1. Of the subject spoken of, the seed of Israel. In the foregoing verses, it is prophesied that the Gentiles should look to Christ and [be][^020-note2]

<!-- p. 461 -->

saved, and that unto him their knee should bow and their tongues swear, and that in him they should say, "I have righteousness and strength." So that being justified and glorying is not here appropriated to the seed of Israel according to the flesh, but 'tis the spiritual Israel that is spoken of; not those that are of the loins, but those that are of the faith of Abraham. If they are Christ's, then they are Abraham's and Israel's seed. The nation of Israel was a typical nation; they were a type of the invisible church, the true people of Jesus Christ in all ages.

2. Two things spoken of them. The first, the act of God relating to them: "They shall be justified"; the last, an act of theirs: they "shall glory." Which is the opposite to being ashamed, spoken of in the last words of the foregoing verse: they "that are incensed against him shall be ashamed." But these, on the contrary, shall glory. 'Tis the last of these things predicated of the seed of Israel we shall insist on at this time.

3. Who is the foundation of this justification and glorying of the seed {of Abraham and Israel}. "In the Lord[^020-note3] shall all the seed of Israel be justified, and shall glory." By which Jesus Christ is meant: for 'tis he that is spoken [of] in the preceding verses, in whom one shall say, he has righteousness {and strength}, and every knee [should] bow (Philippians 2:10–11).

#### Doctrine.

#### The people of Jesus Christ have great cause to glory in their Savior.

I. Who are meant by the people of Christ.

II. What is implied in glorying in Christ.

III. What cause they have to glory in him.

I. Who are meant by the people of Christ.

*First*. Not all those that are called Christians, or are his professed and visible people. They are not all Israel that are of Israel; there are multitudes of those that have Christ living that will [not] be owned by him.

There are great multitudes of those that call themselves "Christians." The part of the world that is called "the Christian world" is very large, comprising many whole nations. But Christ's flock is but small in comparison of [these]: they are but a handful; they are but thinly sown here and there in the Christian world.

<!-- p. 462 -->

That which is commonly called "the Christian [world]"[^020-note4] in distinction to the heathens, Jews and Mahometans is a mixed multitude of every kind, good and bad, drunkards, lascivious, covetous…. But the people of Christ, they are of one kind: the prevailing dispositions of their hearts are the [same],[^020-note5] and their main work is the same.[^020-note6]

'Tis not all those that make a more particular profession of godliness. Many of these have no cause at all to glory; though indeed they profess a better religion, and enjoy greater light and have higher privileges, yet they so improve [them], that they have so much the more reason to be ashamed.

But,

*Second*, those whose hearts are truly united unto Christ, and who love and follow him. Those are truly Christ's people whose hearts—and not they whose tongues and outside—are his. The whole Christian world have a[^020-note7] seeming union with Christ; they [have] a seeming subjection to him.[^020-note8] They separate from the heathens and Mahometans and Jews, those open enemies, and profess to be on Christ's side; they have those outward and visible appearances of union with him, in that they go with God's people [and] attend on the ordinances[^020-note9] of Christ; they seem to be his disciples, in that they outwardly hear his instructions, and seem to be his subjects, in that they hear his commands.

But God looks at the heart, and they only are indeed the people of Jesus Christ and of his flock that have given their hearts to him and serve him: such as have received him by faith, that really have been so convinced of the reality and sufficiency and excellency of Christ as a savior, and have entirely inclined and drawn the heart to him, to choose and acquiesce in him;[^020-note10] such as love in truth, that have seen his

<!-- p. 463 -->

excellency and desirableness; such as have subjected themselves to him and chosen him for their king; such as have indeed given themselves to him; such as have admitted Christ into the heart and placed him upon the throne there; such as have been begotten by the Spirit of Christ, been born of God, and been made partakers of Christ's nature and temper.

And such whose hearts have left all other things for his sake, and such as do forsake other things and cleave to him in their practice; such as are not of the world, but leave the world for Christ: such as these are the true Israel; these are the peculiar people of God. Israel of old was separated from all other nations; they were not reckoned among the nations. So these are not of the world: their hearts have left it for Christ, and they follow him and not the vanities of the world.

II. What is implied in the people of Christ glorying in Christ.

To "glory" is for a person to express his high esteem of his own advantages of excellency, honor or happiness above others. The word in the text in the original signifies to show forth one's own praise, or to exalt oneself with one's own praises. Therefore boasting or glorying is generally taken in an ill sense, as an expression of a haughty disposition.[^020-note11] Thus when the Apostle, when he is setting forth the exceeding great wickedness of the heathen, he mentions this, amongst other things, that they were "boasters" (Romans 1:30). Self-praise is spoken of, as by the wise man, as a foolish thing. Proverbs 27:2, "Let another praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips."

But there is one sort of glorying that is no manifestation of pride, but the contrary, and is most consistent with prudence and but this one sort.[^020-note12] 1 Corinthians 1:31, "Let him that glorieth, glory in the Lord."

Glorying in Christ contains these:

*First*. A humble and joyful sense of mind of the great privilege and happiness they have above others in the interest they have in Christ. Those that are so highly favored and privileged of God, God expects that they should be sensible of it: insensibility of it argues stupidity and ingratitude. 'Tis but a thing becoming one so favored, that he should be sensible how greatly he is distinguished from others. It becomes them to have a very high esteem of their own privilege in being in

<!-- p. 464 -->

Christ Jesus; they should esteem themselves more happy in having an interest in Christ, than if they had the whole world in possession.

It becomes them to admire their own happiness, and their sense of it should excite exultation of heart and joy of soul. Christian joy is a principal part of the disposition exercised in glorying in Christ.[^020-note13]

*Second*. In declaring before others that joyful sense and the grounds of it. As it becomes a Christian that his heart be full of a joyful esteem of its own privilege and happiness, so it is becoming that [that] sense should be manifested and declared.

This joyful sense ought to be manifested in the behavior. A cheerful obeying of Christ's commands and adherence to him through all, even the greatest difficulties—enduring the cross and despising the shame, neglecting with contempt all other pleasures and profits and honors that are set before him to allure him—is the best way of manifesting that he esteems the happiness.

This is very proper to be done in divine songs. We find the Psalmist was very much in his divine songs enjoyed in glorying in his God; so was Moses, Deborah, and Hannah and the blessed Virgin.

And particularly at the Lord's Supper. 'Twas designed partly for this end, that we might, by celebrating this ordinance, give testimony of our sense of our own happiness.

And upon occasion, it is very proper for Christians to declare their sense of their superior happiness, particularly to those of other religions, as the children of Israel were wont to glory in their God. "Their rock is not as our Rock," say they [Deuteronomy 32:31]. They should likewise express it to one another.

Its being in Christ implies three things:

1. To glory of him. To boast of his excellencies and beauty, to speak of or otherwise to declare in a joyful, triumphant manner of his transcendent beauty and glory, as the spouse doth. Canticles 5:16, after describing him, she says: "This is my beloved, this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem." To boast of the acts of Christ, of his works, especially towards them in saving and redeeming of them, his wonderful love in doing and suffering so much for them.

To boast of his relation to them, as the spouse does. Canticles 2:16, "My beloved is mine, and I am his."

To glory [in][^020-note14] the promises of Christ.

<!-- p. 465 -->

2. To glory in a dependence on Christ.[^020-note15]

3. To glory in his name and for his honor, and of their own honor, only as they are in him. 'Tis not so much a love to their own honor that disposes them thus to glory, as the glory of Christ. Psalms 115:1, "Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory, for thy mercy, and for thy truth's sake." The believer aims therein at the glory of Christ; he boasts and glories in Christ's name, because he would have all to see and own the glorious excellencies of Christ.

And he aims at his own honor only secondarily, as he is a member of Jesus Christ or a partaker with him in his glory. As the parts of the body partake with the head, there should be such an union of the believer's heart with Jesus Christ, that whatsoever honor Christ has, he ought to feel affected with joy as other men do when they themselves are honored, and they are to account it their own honor. But he should seek his own honor, considered as in this glorying in Christ, considered as separate from him.[^020-note16]

III. We are come now to inquire what cause they have thus to glory in Christ.

*First*. They have a more glorious Lord. Christ is the most glorious king: there are none of the sons of the mighty can be compared unto him. He is KINGS OF KINGS [Revelation 19:16], which phrase not only signifies that he rules over other kings, but that he is the most excellent king, as "Song of Songs" signifies the most excellent song.

He is a king of higher descent. Others are sons of nobles, but he is the Son of the Most High God; others have royal blood, but he has the divine nature.

His kingdom is of greater extent, who rules over heaven and earth; whose dominion is over the angels of heaven as well as over the potentates of the earth; who sits in heaven as his throne; whose kingdom is of greater duration, being an everlasting kingdom, and his dominion without end. He is a king of greater wisdom and strength.

He is a "King of righteousness" (Hebrews 7:2) who is perfectly just in his government. He is the "Prince of Peace" [Isaiah 9:6], a king of the most unparalleled clemency and grace. Never was any kingdom[^020-note17] ruled by a government so mild and gentle and gracious.

He is exceeding gracious in the manner of his ruling his people by sweetly and powerfully influencing their hearts by his grace: not governing

<!-- p. 466 -->

them against their wills, but by powerfully inclining their wills. Psalms 110:3, "Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power." The laws of his kingdom, they are most excellent; his commandments are pure and righteous, altogether exceeding perfective of our nature, and such as above the laws of all other governments tend to the peace, the flourishing, the beautiful order, the excellency and the happiness of his people.

The invisible church of God is by far the most happy kingdom in the world. He that is their king is their father, their brother and husband, one that has a love stronger than death to his people, has infinite wisdom to guide him in governing of [them and] infinite strength to defend them. The citizens of Zion have great cause to glory in their king, agreeable to Balaam's observation of them, Numbers 23:21, "The shout of a king is among them."

How much a more glorious Lord have they over them than wicked men, who are under the prince of the power of the air, whose hearts are under the dominion of Satan, who have their reason and all their other faculties lorded over by impure lusts and vile affections.

How much a more glorious God have they than the heathen. How much [a] more glorious head of their religion have they than Mahometans. Psalms 149:2, "Let Israel rejoice in him that made him: let the children of Zion be joyful in their King."

*Second*. They have a far better savior. Indeed, he is the only true Savior. But there are many other things that men are trusting in to be saviors to them, but Jesus Christ is far the best. All other confidences will fail: they will prove but broken staves, [a] false foundation; they will not be able to accomplish salvation for those that trust in them. But Christ fully and completely finishes that work of salvation for all that trust in him.

He has more worthiness than other saviors. He is infinitely worthy, being a divine person and infinitely near and dear to God. He has that advantage that no other savior has, that he is in the bosom of the Father. He is so worthy and excellent in the sight of God, that God is always well-pleased in him and cannot fail of accepting all that are in him for his sake. The worthiness of other saviors, if it comes to be inquired into, will be found to be nothing; their excellency will prove deformity and loathsomeness.

Christ has a better righteousness. Christ performed a glorious righteousness for his people, perfectly fulfilled the law, being obedient unto death, and by his sufferings has fully satisfied divine justice and answered the law. 'Tis an infinitely more glorious righteousness than

<!-- p. 467 -->

that that many other men trust in, even their own righteousness, which is as filthy rags; 'tis a righteousness that will justify 'em. They shall be justified, and therefore shall they glory.

More strength. All dangers and enemies. Help in all difficulties. Others trust in an arm of flesh. But these rejoice or glory in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence {in an arm of flesh}. More grace.

*Third*. They have a far better portion. Christ is above all others excellent, fairer than the sons of men, altogether lovely. Rose of Sharon [Canticles 2:1].[^020-note18] How highly privileged are they that are united to so excellent a person, that have such an one for their best friend, and to be enjoyed by them forever.

They that have Christ, they have a soul-satisfying portion. They have the truest pleasures and comforts. Here is to be found the proper happiness of the soul. Least liable to accidents and change… Here is the best employment for the understanding…. Such as have Christ, they have better and greater riches than others…. Better honor… Far better pleasures than sensual men. The joys are more exquisitely delighting than ever was enjoyed by the greatest epicure. [There are] no pleasures like those that are by the enlightenings of the Spirit of Christ, the discoveries of the beauty of Christ and the manifestations of his love.

Their portion will be of longer duration. Others' portions will fail, but…[^020-note19]

They have upon these accounts great reason to glory:

1. Before the devil, their grand enemy. Satan to his utmost seeks the misery of mankind, and to his utmost endeavors to afflict God's people. But God will give them to truimph over him: glorying is included in triumphing. They shall tread upon the lion and adder, the young lion and dragon shall they trample under foot [Psalms 91:13].

After Satan has done his utmost, they are still out of his reach because they are in Christ. They are happy, and will be so to all eternity, and he most miserable.

2. Before wicked men, such as have their portion in this life, that think themselves much happier in the enjoyment of their worldly and sinful enjoyments than those that deny [them], that are proud of their wealth and honor and prefer themselves before [God].

Hypocrites that trust in their own righteousness and have dependence on what is outward.

{They have great reason to glory}, particularly,

<!-- p. 468 -->

3. Before their persecutors. They may triumph over them. They can't hurt them, because they are in Christ Jesus. With all the mischief they can do them, after they have exerted themselves to the utmost to render them miserable and to make themselves happy, yet they are happier than they. By reviling.

A martyr in the flames may triumph over their persecutors, as many of 'em have done.

Though their persecutors may be their judges, and may have 'em in their power, may lord it over 'em, yet they are above 'em.

### Application.

[*Use*] I. What reason have we to praise God, who has given us so much cause to glory in Christ Jesus, that we that deserve so much shame should have so much cause to glory. We were in a forlorn condition: we were depressed to the lowest depths of misery and wretchedness; we were filthy and abominable, had made ourselves viler than the earth, and deserved nothing but shame and everlasting contempt; we had nothing to glory in, but all the circumstances of our case were such as administered to us just cause of shame and confusion of face.

But God has been pleased to provide one for us to take away our guilt and disgrace, and to be the glory in the midst of us; to put great honor upon us, to be as a covering to hide our nakedness, and not only so, but to adorn us and make us glorious; to be to us wisdom, to bring us from our shameful ignorance and darkness; to be our righteousness for the removal of our guilt and to procure acceptance with God for us; to be our sanctification, to change [us] from sinful and loathsome to holy and amiable; to be our redemption, to deliver us from all trouble and danger, and make us happy and blessed forever; to bestow upon us gold tried in the fire, that of poor we might become rich, and that he might exalt us from the dunghill and set us among princes. That God should take us, who were under bondage to sin and Satan, and give us such a glorious victory over our adversaries, and cause us thus to triumph over those that had us captives and were so much stronger than we; that God gives [us] so much greater privileges than others, that we should have such a king, {is reason to praise God}.

*Use* II is of *Reproof* to all such as glory in anything else but in the Lord. Such as glory in themselves, that highly value and esteem themselves upon the account of anything of theirs, any natural qualification, acquired advantages or any of their own actions.

<!-- p. 469 -->

It reproves all sorts of pride. Such as are lifted up with their own natural abilities, are proud because they have better sense [and] more wit than their neighbor. Such as are proud of their riches, and glory in their being in high and honorable stations or any outward advantages. Such as trust to these things. Jeremiah 9:23–24, "Thus saith the Lord, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches: But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the Lord which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the Lord."

It especially reproves such as trust in their own righteousness. This is most directly contrary to glorying in Christ Jesus, that is, to set up ourselves as saviors to glory in instead of Christ.

And then the doctrine reproves such as glory in their being of such and such a party among Christians, that highly value themselves in a profession and outward advantages. Such as these have confidence in the flesh.

*Exh*. [I.] Counting all other things as loss and dung, strive to win Christ. Consider on the one hand, how worthless all those things are which men are wont to set their hearts upon, and on the other hand, what great cause of rejoicing and glorying.

You have nothing to glory in while you are out of Christ. Forsake all, sell all, that you may have this pearl of great price. Choose the better part that shall not be taken away from you.

*Exh*. II. Let the people of Jesus Christ be exhorted to glory in Christ Jesus. 'Tis a most becoming thing in the blessed people of Christ—for his people are a blessed people—for them to rejoice and glory in their King, their Savior and their portion. 'Tis a becoming thing that the shout of a king should be heard in that glorious city of Zion. 'Tis a most becoming sight to see that company of the redeemed of the Lord to be humbly triumphing over the world. Endeavor to obtain this spirit, which will be obtained only by obtaining much of the Spirit of Christ.

Particularly endeavor that you may attend on this ordinance of the Lord's Supper with the spirit of true glory.

In order to this, three things must be done:

*First*. Strive to see more of the excellency of Christ and of the happiness of having an interest in him. Consider of the glories of Christ's person. [The] glories of his benefits.

*Second*. Strive to get assurance of your interest in Christ. By having grace strong and lively.

<!-- p. 470 -->

*Third*. To be more sensible of your absolute dependence on Christ. 'Tis a humble sense of this that is in the first place necessary in order to a right glorying in Christ Jesus, or else you'll glory in yourself, and in you own name and for your own honor. To be of a spirit of humility and dependence is the way to have the Spirit of God and of glory rest upon you.

<!-- p. 471 -->

### God's All-Sufficiency for the Supply of Our Wants

In this thanksgiving-day sermon, Edwards turns what would appear to be an expected sort of message for such an occasion—God's bounty toward humankind—into a meditation on the wonders of creation. The sermon seems to have had its immediate inspiration in an effort to explain how God "orders" rain to fall on a drought-stricken land. This question irresistibly leads Edwards to explore the interconnected workings of the cosmos. In doing so, and in keeping with his deliberately "modest" literary style, he hides a great deal of learning in his statements, particularly his exposure to the works of scholars such as John Ray and Thomas Burnet, who were interested in demonstrating how God's wisdom is evident in nature.[^021-note1]

Edwards also demonstrates his concurrence with a preeminent theological assumption of the eighteenth century by assuming that the laws of nature and the laws of reason are one. There is a universal harmony, he maintains, created and supervised by God, that exists between all things for the benefit of humankind. This sermon therefore reflects Edwards' interest in natural philosophy, evident in such early writings as "Of Being," "Of Atoms," and "The Mind."[^021-note2] Yet Edwards distinguishes himself from other evangelical apologists in the debate against natural theology by his dispositional ontology. A universal harmony prevails because God, who is omnipotent and consonant, communicates himself in the manifold aspects of creation. Edwards states that God's "fullness of power" is such that, "let things be great or small, they are all one to his power." Herein Edwards imparts his personal vision of the magnificence of God.

Though Edwards was fully acquainted with the Copernican view of

<!-- p. 472 -->

the solar system as well as the works of Newton and his expositors, he nonetheless retains references in this sermon to the Ptolemaic cosmology.[^021-note3] Why Edwards does this is uncertain; perhaps his congregation was still not ready to accept modern theory,[^021-note4] or perhaps he deliberately subordinated scientific fact to the theological truth that humankind is the focal point of creation and that God arranges everything for humankind's benefit. However, Edwards does incorporate current learning, such as Newton's *Optics* (1686) and Locke's *Essay Concerning Human Understanding* (1690), when in his discussion of the human body he calls sight the chief of the senses.

In the manner of John Flavel, Richard Steele, and Cotton Mather,[^021-note5] Edwards spiritualizes reality as he tries to show how meaning can be drawn from "the book of nature" as well as "the book of grace." Psalms 65, the text of the sermon, was probably written after the end of a drought; in New England, it seems, the year 1729 was without rain. Several sermons besides this one use imagery that testifies to such a condition.[^021-note6] The sun's heat and light, the seasonal growth of vegetation, and the flowing river have for Edwards particular spiritual significances, as recorded in "Images" nos. 13–15, written shortly before or concurrent with this sermon. In addition, the significance of the yearly propagation of vegetation, as explored in "Images" no. 19, is also

<!-- p. 473 -->

discussed here. Yet Edwards, whether talking about hellfire and an enraged God or about the bounty of nature and a benevolent God, always ends up at the same point: the free mercy of God to a sinful people. All humankind, he concludes, can and must drink at God's overflowing fountain of grace.

The date of the colony-wide thanksgiving for 1729, the occasion for which this sermon was most likely preached, was November 13. As was his habit, Edwards only implies the occasion by making a passing mention in the Application to "the custom of the country to have a day of thanksgiving once a year."

∗ ∗ ∗

The manuscript is composed of eight duodecimo leaves, with one under-sized fragment appended on which Edwards completed the application. This fragment is part of a letter cover addressed on one side "To the Rev. Mr. Jonathan Edwards at Northampton."

Though the regular separation of Explication, Doctrine, and Application obtains, the sermon is structurally distinctive for its lack of detailed, formal analysis of propositions in heads and subheads. In this regard, the sermon verges on being an essay.

<!-- p. 474 -->

### God's All-Sufficiency for the Supply of Our Wants

Psalms 65:9> *Thou visitest the earth, and waterest it: thou greatly enrichest it with the river of God, which is full of water: thou preparest them corn, when thou hast so provided for it*.

This psalm seems to be written upon occasion of some special mercies being shown to the children of Israel, in answer of prayers, after some great and general calamity. And, by the latter part, it seems to have been the sending of rain and giving fruitful seasons after some great drought or famine. This mercy is elegantly described in our text and the following verses.

He "enricheth the earth with the river of God, that is full of water"; that is, God never wants water to supply the clouds and to pour upon the dry and thirsty ground. God's river is always full: he can, when he pleases, cause the heavens to yield a plentiful supply for the earth. The water is continually, from year to year, from the beginning of the world to the end, coming down upon the earth; but yet God's river is not empty, but is as full as ever. God's wisdom has so contrived for the continual supply of the earth, and his goodness is so abundant in it, that it is like a river ever-flowing.

This is a beautiful representation not only of [the] greatness, fullness and constancy of God's bounty in giving rain, but also in other things, in the yearly and daily mercies which he bestows upon us.

#### Doctrine.

#### God, by the exercises of his common bounty towards men, shows that he has an all-sufficiency for the supply of their wants.

I. He thereby shows the sufficiency of his power to provide for mankind all that they stand in need of. We may justly argue from the

<!-- p. 475 -->

greatness of God's power appearing in providing those things that are for the support and comfort of our lives, that he is able to do every-thing that we need. His power in those things appears plainly infinite.

He shows his infinite power in creating those things which subserve to our necessity and delight: in creating the earth for us to dwell upon, and the air for us to breath in and water for our drink; in creating the visible heavens and heavenly bodies to shed down their influences upon [us]. He stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and spreads them out like a tent to dwell in [Isaiah 41:22]. God's power as easily extended that vast expanse of the starry heavens as we can spread a curtain, or as a man can set up a tent. Job 26:7, Job 26:13, "He stretcheth out the north over the empty place, and his hands have formed the crooked serpent"; that is, the constellation in the heavens called "The Serpent."[^021-note7]

He shows his almighty strength in forming and fixing those vast globes over our heads, that are many of them far greater, and some of 'em a thousand times greater, than the whole globe of the earth; in fixing a tabernacle for the sun, as it is expressed (Psalms 19:4); and in forming that endless variety of creatures that subserve to our benefit.

And God shows that nothing is too hard for him to do for us by the strength [of his arm] in so ordering, moving and directing those things so as to make them administer to our good, particularly in moving and managing the heavenly bodies so that they may be under advantages in the best manner to diffuse their light and heat all over the face of the earth. What a mighty strength is required to manage the system of the world, to fix the ordinances of heaven and keep the mighty heavenly bodies in their swift and regular courses! God moves those huge globes and keeps [them] in play in their appointed circles from age to age, from one thousand years to another, only by the word of his power. Though they are such vast things, yet they are not unwieldy in God's hands; though their course is so mighty swift, yet God easily keeps them within their bounds and makes them observe his rules.

The sun, at God's command, "is as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, and rejoices as a strong man to run his race. His going forth is from the end of heaven, and his circuit unto the ends of it"; and by this means, "nothing is hid from the heat thereof" (Psalms 19:5–6).

God commands the morning, and by his mighty power makes the dayspring to know its place (Job 38:12). And he turns the earth to the

<!-- p. 476 -->

sun as clay to the seal, and the things that are upon it stand as a garment (Job 38:14)—that is, in the night the face of the earth is undistinguished, all confused, like clay before it has had the impression of the seal, without those various and beautiful appearances which are seen upon it when the sun comes to shine upon it and as it were like a seal impresses those figures upon it—and then those appearances of the green fields and trees, they appear as a beautiful garment to cover the earth.

God by his mighty power orders the various seasons. When the sun has got to its appointed bounds towards the north or south, at God's command it returns again; it never transgresses his law. God by his power doth that which none other can do: he binds the sweet influences of Pleiades and looses the bands of Orion (Job 38:31). 'Tis by his power that the bands of the winter are loosed in the spring, and the snow and ice are dissolved. And the earth, which before was as a stone, is opened and mollified, and the sweet influences of Pleiades are shed abroad, and the earth brings forth; the pastures are clothed with green grass, and the trees bud forth and put on their beautiful garments, and all nature is renewed and revived. And again, those sweet influences, they are bound again when winter comes on with the bands of Orion by God's mighty power, and for the good of mankind and in fulfillment of his gracious promise to Noah and his posterity. Genesis 8:22, "While the earth remaineth, seed time and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease."

God shows his great power in sending abroad at such a prodigious distance so powerful a light and heat from the sun, which is so great in its influences all over the face of the earth. How mighty and powerful is that globe of fire through so vast regions of the universe, and shows the all-sufficient power of him that kindled it, and that maintains its light and heat![^021-note8]

God shows his great power in ordering of the atmosphere, or that body of air that encloses this globe and the things contained in it, for our good, as in raising and sustaining in the air such vast quantities of water in the clouds. He calls for the waters of the sea, and the waters of the sea obey him and mount up at[^021-note9] his command, and he poureth it out on the dry land. Amos 5:8, "Seek him that maketh the seven stars

<!-- p. 477 -->

and Orion, and turneth the shadow of death into the morning, that maketh the day dark with night: that calleth for the waters of the sea, and poureth them out upon the face of the earth: the Lord is his name."

God shows his great power in the winds, in moving such great portions of the atmosphere with such rapidity, whereby he fans and cleanses the air; and wafteth to and fro the clouds, those great quantities of waters above the firmament, whither he pleases they should go. Proverbs 30:4, "Who hath gathered the winds in his fists?"

He shows his mighty power in thunder and lightning, whereby he cleanses and sweetens the air. Job 26:14, "The thunder of his power who can understand?"

God shows his great power in moving and managing the sea, that huge collection of waters, for the good of mankind, especially in the tides. He hereby shows he has his way in the sea, and his path in the great waters (Psalms 77:19).

God, by these and other exercises of his power for our good, shows that he has a fullness of power. He that can do these things, he can't want any power: he shows that he has all creatures in his hands and at his dispose; he shows that, let things be great or small, they are all one to his power; he shows that his power is sufficient to supply all our wants, because when we stand in need of so many and so great things as those that have been mentioned for our support and comfortable subsistence, he that has done and daily doth such great things for us is doubtless able to [do] all other things.

II. God, by the exercises of his common bounty towards men, shows that he has a fullness of wisdom to prepare and order all things for us as we stand in need. As God has shown infinite power in the creating [of] those things that minister to our advantage, so he has shown an equal wisdom in contriving and ordering of them. Infinite wisdom has been set an work how to provide for men in abundance of instances.

Thus when God was about to create man, and it appeared needful to him that he should have light—mankind could not subsist in perfect darkness—then the question was, How mankind should be provided with light that should sufficiently enlighten the habitable world? And God's wisdom contrived the sun, a vast globe and fountain of light, so placed and ordered that it should enlighten one half of the globe at once. But then here would be another question: How all parts of the globe of the earth should be provided with light? And God therefore contrived the diurnal revolution of the sun round the earth in perpetual

<!-- p. 478 -->

successions, which also served many other purposes: it avoided the fatal inconvenience that would have arisen from the sun's always standing over one side of the earth; it would have burnt it up. And then by those revolutions, man had a more convenient time for that rest and sleep which God saw needful for man. And because it would be inconvenient for man to be wholly without light in the night, God therefore contrived the moon and stars, which should give so much light as to serve the necessary occasions that man might have of passing to and fro in the night, and yet not interrupt his quiet rest.

When God saw it necessary that the body of man should be continually recreated by proper nourishment, then God contrived a way that the earth should bring forth all things suitable to that. So the earth by God's wisdom brings forth abundance of [all] kinds of things for his nourishment and refreshment, some meet to be received immediately, others first to be turned into the flesh of other animals and so be prepared for man's food.

And when God saw it necessary that these fruits of the earth should be propagated to all ages of the world, God contrived that when one plant had brought forth its proper fruit, it should bring forth also a seed, from whence another might spring of the same kind. And God, seeing that those seeds would not spring and grow and bear fruit without some heat and warmth to quicken and enliven it and put it forward, God therefore for this end contrived the sun, which by its heat should cause the grass, herbs, and corn and trees to flourish and grow.

And when God saw that it was not sufficient that there should be merely warmth without moisture,[^021-note10] now the question was, How the whole face of the earth should be watered from time to time in a convenient manner? In order to this, there must be some way or other contrived how vast quantities of water might be suspended up at some distance above the face of the earth, and might be carried about hither and thither according as God saw meet. And God has contrived a wonderful way for this purpose: he contrived the sun, that by its heat it might cause the water to ascend from the sea in great quantities and to be so purified that it might be suspended in the air, and collected in clouds and condensed in them, and from them descend upon the earth to water it. And God hath so contrived that the water should [not] come down in such great bodies, which would be very incommodious

<!-- p. 479 -->

and would dash in pieces the fruits of the earth; but that it should distil gently in drops so that we can walk amongst it, and the fruits of the earth are not hurt, Job 36:27–29, "He maketh small the drops of water: they pour down rain according to the vapor thereof; which the clouds do drop and distil upon man abundantly. Also can any understand the spreadings of the clouds, or the noise of his tabernacle?" Thus, according to the text and context, God visits the earth and watereth it and greatly enriches it with the river of God, which is full of water, and prepares corn when he has so provided for it; he waters the ridges thereof abundantly; he settles the furrows thereof; he makes it soft with showers; he blesses the springing thereof [Job 36:9–10]. And very wonderful must the inward make and formation of the plant itself be, that only with those influences of the sun and rain, etc. it should of itself grow in such form and produce such fruit, and bear also another seed that should produce the like again, and so forever.[^021-note11]

God saw that man and beast would stand in necessity of water where they dwelt. And God therefore, besides the rain, contrived that water should be distributed in springs and rivers all over the face of the earth.

And in order to there being a sufficient supply for the clouds and rivers, God saw it needful that there should be a vast collection of waters. God hath therefore provided the seas, which are also exceeding convenient to mankind for transportation and upholding a communication with the distant parts of the world. And that this great body of waters might not grow corrupt by stagnation, and so by infecting the air become fatal to the inhabitants of the earth, God contrived that the sea should be salt and be kept in continual motion by the tides.

And because God saw that the water of the rain and that which is for ordinary use of man and beast should be fresh, God therefore hath contrived that although the most from whence all comes is salt, yet that the waters should be made fresh in the clouds and springs.

God saw that we should for many ends stand in necessity of something else of a very different nature for the preparing of our food, and

<!-- p. 480 -->

the defending of us from the cold, and many other uses. And God's wisdom invented for us that wonderful thing, fire.

And God hath shown a marvelous wisdom in providing for us in the make of our bodies. God saw it necessary for us in this world that we perceive things at a distance from us, and he hath contrived those wonderful organs, the eyes, which are most curious pieces of divine workmanship.[^021-note12] And not much less wonderful are those organs by which we perceive sounds, even the ears; very wonderful is God's contrivance for the conveying of sounds. And so God hath contrived organs of speech for the expedite communicating of our thoughts one to another. And every part of the human body is of a piece with these: the body of man is a world of wonders, and has more contrivance in it than all the pieces of human art that ever were in the world put together.

But it would take up volumes to mention the tenth part of the instances of wonderful divine wisdom that are to be seen in the provision God has made in his works for the good of man. But by this specimen, we may see reason to be convinced that nothing is too hard for the wisdom of God that we stand in need of.

III. God hereby shows that he has all-sufficiency of goodness for the supply of our wants. If God has shown such an all-sufficient power and wisdom in thus providing for us, then surely his goodness is all-sufficient, that inclined thus to exert his power and wisdom for our good in so many wonderful instances. But here,

*First*, the plenty and variety of the common bounty of God to us shows the all-sufficiency of his goodness. Heaven and earth is full of God's bounty: when we look upon the sun, moon and stars, we may behold them as so many wonderful gifts of God to us. The earth and sea are themselves gifts of God's bounty to mankind, and all the fullness of them. The face of the earth is covered with a vast variety of the gifts of God to us, and the sea is filled with them, and the bowels of the earth. What a vast plenty and variety is there for our necessity and delight!

Here is enough for the supply of all mankind, the many millions of

<!-- p. 481 -->

men that are in the world. Yea, there is an abundance; there is more than enough. We are needy, empty creatures; we are full of our wants. But yet there are none of the needs of this life but that are provided for. God brings it out of his treasures. God's river is full of water, and not only so, but it overflows all its banks. All the many thousands and millions of mankind may drink and quench their thirst at this river.

*Second*. By the constancy of the supplies which he grants, he shows by this that his goodness is everlasting; it endureth forever. God is never weary of being bountiful. In this respect, his goodness is very fitly compared to a river. A river is never weary of flowing: although it empties vast quantities of water every day, yet there seems to be never the less to come. One may live by a river and be supplied with water one's whole lifetime; there is no danger of spending of it up, or of its running all away.[^021-note13]

How constantly does God supply the wants of mankind. It is wonderful to consider in some instances, as in that instance of the sun's light and heat. The sun has been sending out its rays and shedding of them abroad in vast profusion from the beginning of the world, and yet its rays ben't spent; it is as full of them, probably, as ever; it shines with a constant and uninterrupted brightness, continually still. As this is a notable effect of the fullness and everlastingness of God's bounty, so 'tis very much of an image of it: for God is "the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning" [James 1:17].

Again, how unwearied is the sun in its course. Though the world be so wicked and so full of provoking rebels against heaven, yet God don't cease to cause the sun to arise upon them, which ariseth on the just and unjust. How unwearied is the earth in bringing forth for men's food and clothing: if it were not for God's power and efficiency, it would soon cease.

### Application.

I. How greatly are the generality of men to blame, that they reflect so little upon the daily goodness of God to 'em. If God shows so much power and exercises so much wisdom in so plentifully, variously and continually providing for us, as we have now heard, how stupid are we, that we have no more thought about it. How seldom does it come into our thoughts when we look abroad in the world, and see the light of the sun and see the trees and fields, that these things are what God has

<!-- p. 482 -->

taken care to provide for the benefit of mankind? When we see the variety that there is upon the face of the earth of different sorts of good things suitable to our different needs, how seldom does such a reflection as this come across us? What care has God taken of mankind, that they should not want anything that [is] for their convenience.

And when we gather in the fruits of the earth, and when we eat and drink, how insensible are [we]. How seldom do we think on't that it was God's wisdom that contrived this for our comfort? Yea, are there not some that breath and walk and eat and drink like beasts, and don't think seriously of its being God's goodness that they live upon not once in a week?

If a king should take a poor man from the street that had nothing to eat or wear, and should build a stately house for him with everything convenient for his necessity and comfort within doors and without, and should every day, as duly as the day came,[^021-note14] send him provision and everything he needed, and so as long as he lived: would it not be a stupid thing in the man if he never or seldom reflected upon it, that it was this king's gracious kindness that he lived upon?

The very cattle and dogs and other brute creatures seem to be more sensible of man's kindness to 'em, than some men do of the kindness of God. Isaiah 1:3, "The ox knows his owner, and the ass his master's crib: but Israel doth not know, my people doth not consider."

'Tis true, 'tis a general custom for men to return thanks after they have set down to meat, and 'tis the custom of the country to have a day of thanksgiving once a year; but how little does it signify if it be nothing but a mere formality, and done with as little reflection of mind and motion of heart about the goodness [of God] as a harp or flute, or something that makes a sound without life?

II. From this doctrine we learn what improvement we should make of the works of nature. We should improve to learn the all-sufficiency of God: it appears both in the works of nature and the works of grace, and the book of nature and the book of grace [and] of revelation both teach us this lesson. We should therefore read in both of them.

We may find suitable matter enough to employ our thoughts at all times, wherever we turn our eyes. When we are travelling, or when at work abroad, we should still be a-reading to learn God's all-sufficiency.

III. If God by the exercises of his common {bounty towards men

<!-- p. 483 -->

shows that he has an all-sufficiency for the supply of their wants}, then what encouragement is here to look to God and trust in him for whatever we stand in need of. God shows us every day, if we did but consider it, by his daily goodness to us, that he is able to do everything for us that we have need to have done, and that he is wise enough to contrive for us in all difficulties and good enough to give us sufficient for our needs. He shows that he delights in goodness and in providing for the good of man. We see the daily fruits of it, besides what we are taught about it in the Word of God.

Therefore whatever your wants are, be directed to go to this fountain. If your wants are outward, if you stand in need of things for your comfortable subsistence, go to him who hath promised that all those things should be added to you if you seek first the kingdom {of God}. If you want health, if you want ease, if you want for yourself, if you want for your children, go [to] that river of God's bounty that is so full of water. Don't be anxious about those things, but go to God and leave your case with and cheerfully wait in a way of well-doing for what he shall see meet to provide for you.

If your wants are spiritual (as all our souls are in themselves exceeding poor, necessitous things), here is encouragement to go to him and trust in him. Those manifestations of power that were mentioned, as his {plenty, abundance, constancy and all-sufficiency}, may convince us of his ability to redeem our souls from all adversity.

And his wisdom in so contriving {for the supply of our wants} may convince us of the sufficiency of his wisdom to contrive for us and guide us in the way of peace. And he whose goodness provided in such plenty and vast variety for our bodies, though we are sinful creatures, shall he not much rather provide for our souls, our more necessitous parts?

The sun's fullness of light is but an image, a faint resemblance of God's fullness of grace. As the sun's light and influence endures, so God's grace is forever and ever.

IV. We should be stirred up by this doctrine to a constant serving of God and seeking his glory. He that is continual and constant and abundant {in supplying for our wants} abundantly deserves our hearty and cheerful service, and that we should [do] with all our hearts. If God so greatly and so variously improves his power, we should [improve] our power. If God so exercises of his wisdom, if God so constantly and richly gives us his goodness, we should serve him without intermission and perseveringly through all difficulties.

<!-- p. 484 -->
