And his divine nature will then also be present, which is united to the human nature; and it will be by the wisdom of that divine nature that Christ will see and judge.

*Inq.* Why is Christ appointed to judge the world rather than the Father or the Holy Ghost?

We cannot pretend to all the reasons of God's dispensation. God is not obliged to give us an account. But so much [as] we may learn by divine revelation, as to discover to us a marvelous wisdom in what he determines and doth with respect to this matter, we learn by God's Word.

*First*. God saw meet that that person that was in the human nature should be the judge of those that had the human nature. John 5:27, "And hath given him authority to execute judgment also, because he is the Son of man." Seeing that there is one of the persons in the Trinity united to the human nature, God chooses in all his transactions with mankind to transact by him. He did so of old, in his discoveries of himself to the patriarchs and in giving the Law, and leading the children of Israel through the wilderness and in the manifestations he made of himself in the tabernacle and temple: when, although Christ was not then actually incarnate, yet he was so in design; it was ordained and agreed in the covenant of redemption that he should be. And since Christ's incarnation, God governs the church and the world by Christ. And so he will also at the end of the world judge them by him. They shall be judged by God, and yet at the same time by one of their own nature.

God sees fit [that] those that have bodies, as all mankind will have at the day of judgment, that they may then see their judge with their bodily eyes and may hear him with their ears. If one of the other persons of the Trinity was appointed as judge, there must be some extraordinary outward appearance made on purpose as a token of God's presence, as it was of old, before Christ was incarnate. But now there is no need of that: now one of the persons of the Trinity is actually incarnate, so that God by him may appear to bodily eyes without the making any miraculous visionary appearance.

*Second*. Christ has this honor given him, to be {the judge of the

<!-- p. 519 -->

world}, as a suitable reward for his sufferings.See *Threefold Work*, p. 380, for sermonic precedent. This is a part of Christ's exaltation. The exaltation of Christ is given him in reward for his humiliation and sufferings. This was what was stipulated in the covenant of redemption, and we are expressly told that it was given him in reward for that. Philippians 2:8–11, "And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore hath God highly exalted him, and given him a name above every name: that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and under the earth; and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father."

God sees meet, that he that appeared in such a low estate in the world amongst mankind, without form or comeliness, having his divine glory veiled, should appear a second time amongst men in his own proper majesty and glory, without a veil; that those that saw him here at the first as a poor frail man, not having a place to lay his head, subject to much hardship and affliction, may see him the second time in power and great glory, invested with the dignity and glory of [the] absolute Lord of heaven and earth; that he that once tabernacled with men, and was despised and rejected of men, might have the honor of having all men arraigned before his throne and judging them with respect to their eternal state. John 5:21–24, "The Son quickeneth whom he will. For the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son: that all men should honor the Son, even as they honor the Father…. He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation."

God sees meet, that he that was once arraigned himself before the judgment seat of men and was there most vilely treated, being mocked and spit upon and condemned, and at last was crucified, that he should be rewarded by having those very persons brought at his bar, that they might see him in glory and be confounded, that he might have the disposal of them for all eternity according to his sentence; as Christ said to the high priest when before him, Matthew 26:64, "Nevertheless [I say unto you, hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power and coming in the clouds of heaven]."

*Third*.'Tis needful that Christ should be the {judge of the world} in order to his finishing the work of redemption. 'Tis the will of God, that he that is the Redeemer of the world should be a complete Redeemer,

<!-- p. 520 -->

and therefore should have the whole work of redemption left in his hands.

Now the redemption of fallen man don't consist merely in the imputation of righteousness by {Christ's death} or in the making way for it, but in the actually fulfilling of it in converting sinners: in carrying them on in a way of grace… and in at last raising their bodies unto life, and glorifying them and pronouncing the blessed sentence upon them, and crowning of them with honor and glory in the sight {of the world}, and completing and perfecting their reward. 'Tis needful that Christ should do this in order to his going through with the work that he has begun. Raising the saints from the dead, and judging of them and fulfilling the sentence, is part of their salvation; and therefore it was needful that Christ should be the judge of the world in order to his finishing his work. John 6:39–40, "And this is the Father's will which hath sent me, that of all which he hath given me I should lose nothing, but should raise it up again at the last day. And this is the will of him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life: and I will raise him up at the last day." John 5:25–30, "The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God: and they that hear shall live. For as the Father hath life in himself; so hath he given to the Son to have life in himself; and hath given him authority to execute judgment also, because he is the Son of man. Marvel not at this: for the hour is coming, in which all that are in graves shall hear his voice, and shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation. I can of mine own self do nothing: as I hear, I judge; and my judgment is just." The redemption of the bodies of the saints is part of the work of redemption: the resurrection to life is called a redemption of their bodies (Romans 8:23).

'Tis the will of God that Christ himself should have the fulfilling of what he died for and underwent so much for, that that he died for was the salvation of his people, which that which shall be done at the last judgment will be the finishing stroke to. 'Twas needful that he should be the judge in order to giving that finishing stroke.

When Christ had finished his appointed sufferings, God did as it were put the purchased inheritance into his hands to keep for believers and to be bestowed upon them at the day of judgment.

*Fourth*. It was meet that he that is appointed the King of the church should rule till he has put all his enemies under his feet, in order to

<!-- p. 521 -->

which he must be their judge. He must be the judge of his enemies as well as of his people.

One of Christ's offices as Redeemer is that of king. He is appointed King of the church, and head over all things to the church. And in order to his kingdom's being completed and the design of his reign's being accomplished, he must conquer all his enemies; and then he will deliver up the kingdom to the Father. 1 Corinthians 15:24–25, "Then cometh the end, when he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God, even the Father; when he shall have put down all rule and all authority and power. For he must reign, till he hath put all enemies under his feet."

That will be the final subduing of his enemies, putting of them [under his feet]: the bringing those that have denied, opposed him and rebelled against him to his judgment seat, and the passing and executing sentence upon them. That will the thing that will put a final end to the war.

Now 'tis suitable that he that now reigns and is carrying on a war against those that are of the opposite kingdom, should have the honor of finishing the victory.

*Fifth*. 'Tis the abundant comfort of the saints that Christ is appointed to be their judge. The covenant of grace, with all its circumstances and all those events that it has relation to, are every way so contrived of God as to give strong consolation to believers. For God designed the gospel for a glorious manifestation of his grace to them; and therefore everything in it is so ordered as to manifest the most grace and mercy.

Now 'tis for the abundant consolation of the saints that their own Redeemer is appointed to be their judge, that he, that same person that spilt his blood for them, has the determination of their state left with him; so that they need not doubt but they shall have what he was at so much cost to procure.

How will [it] be for their joy at the last day to lift up their eyes and behold the person that they have trusted in alone for salvation, whom they have fled for refuge to and built upon as their foundation for eternity, upon whose voice they have heard, inviting of them to him for rest and safety, coming to judge them!

*Sixth*. It will be for the more abundant conviction of the ungodly that Christ is appointed {judge of the world}. It will be for their conviction that they are judged and condemned by that very person that they have rejected, by whom they might have been saved: who shed his blood to give them an opportunity to be saved; who was wont to offer

<!-- p. 522 -->

his righteousness to them when they were in their state of trial; and many a time called and invited them to come to him that they might be saved.

How justly will they be condemned by him whose salvation they have rejected, whose blood they have despised, whose many calls they have refused, and whom they have pierced by their sins.

How much will it be for their conviction, when they shall hear their sentence of condemnation pronounced, when they reflect with themselves: "How often has this same person that now passes sentence of condemnation upon me, called by his messengers to accept of him, to give myself to him; how often has he knocked at the door of my heart; and how might I have had him [for] my Savior that is now my incensed judge, were it not for mine own folly and obstinacy!"

IV.JE inserted an opening bracket for repreaching at the beginning of the head. Describe it.

[*First*.] In the first place, Christ Jesus will in a most magnificent manner descend from heaven with all the holy angels. The man Christ Jesus is now in the heavens of heavens, or, as the Apostle expresses it, "far above all heavens" (Ephesians 4:10); and there he has been ever since his ascension, being there enthroned in glory in the midst of thousands and millions of angels and blessed spirits.

When the time appointed for the day of judgment comes, then notice will be given of it in those glorious regions; and Christ will descend from thence to the earth, attended with all those glorious hosts in a most solemn, awful and glorious manner. Christ will come with divine majesty; he shall come in the glory of his Father. Matthew 16:27, "For the Son of man shall come in the glory of his Father with all his angels."

'Tis but little we can now conceive of the holy and awful magnificence in which Christ will appear as he comes in the clouds of heaven, or the glory of his retinue. How mean and despicable is the splendidest appearance that earthly princes can make in comparison of it. There will a glorious and visible light shine round about him, and the earth and all nature shall tremble at his presence.

How vast and innumerable will that host be that will appear with him, when all the angels of heaven shall be with him. Heaven will be for the time deserted of its inhabitants.

We may argue the glory of Christ's appearance by his appearance at other times. When he appeared at his transfiguration, his face did

<!-- p. 523 -->

shine as the sun and his raiment was white as the light. The apostle Peter speaks magnificently of it long after. 2 Peter 1:16–17, "We were eyewitnesses of his majesty. For he received from God the Father honor and glory, when there came such a voice to him from the excellent glory." And his appearance to Paul; and to St. John, Revelation 1:13–17, "And in the midst of the seven candlesticks one like the Son of man, clothed with a garment down to the foot, and girt about the paps with a golden girdle. His head and his hairs were white like wool, and white as snow; and his eyes were as a flame of fire; and his feet like unto fine brass, as if they burned in a furnace; and his voice as the sound of many waters. And he had in his right hand seven stars: and out of his mouth went a sharp two-edged sword: and his countenance was as the sun shineth in his strength. And when I saw him, I fell at his feet as dead." We may conclude that his appearance at the day of judgment will be vastly more glorious than either of these, it being upon a so much greater occasion. And then, our nature in the present frail state could not bear the appearance of the glory that he will then be seen in.

We may argue the glory of his appearance from the appearance of some of the angels when they have appeared to men. The angel that appeared at Christ's sepulchre after his resurrection, "his countenance was like lightning, and his raiment white as snow" (Matthew 28:3).

The angels will all of them doubtless make as glorious an appearance at the day of judgment as ever; and then, how glorious will be his retinue, made up of so many thousands of them;MS: "him." and how much more glorious will Christ, the judge himself, appear that they attend upon. Doubtless, their God will appear immensely more glorious than they.

Christ will thus descend into our air at such a distance from the surface of the earth that everyone, when gathered together, shall see him. Revelation 1:7, "Behold, he cometh with clouds, and every eye shall see him." Christ will make this appearance suddenly and vastly to the surprise of the inhabitants of the earth. It is therefore compared to a cry at midnight, when persons are waked up in a great surprise [Mark 13:35–36].

*Second*. At the sound of the last trumpet, the dead shall rise and the living be changed. As soon as Christ is descended, the last trumpet shall sound as a notification to all mankind to appear, at which mighty voice shall the dead be raised and [the] living changed immediately. 1 Corinthians 15:52, "For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised

<!-- p. 524 -->

incorruptible, and we shall be changed." Matthew 24:31, "And he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet." 1 Thessalonians 4:16, "For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, and with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God." There will be some great and remarkable signal given for the rising of the dead, which it seems will be some mighty sound caused by the angels of God that shall attend on Christ.

Upon this, all the dead shall arise from their graves; all, both small and great, that ever have lived upon earth since the foundation of the world: those that died before the flood, and those that were drowned in that flood, and all that have been since or that shall die, to the end of the world. There will be a great moving and stirring upon the face of the earth and in the waters, bringing bone to his bone [Ezekiel 37:7], bringing together all the scattered particles of dead bodies and opening graves. The earth shall give up the dead that are in it, and the sea shall give up the dead that are in it [Revelation 20:13].

And, however the parts of the bodies of many are divided and scattered—many have been burnt, and their bodies turned to ashes and smoke and driven to the four winds; many have been eaten byMS: "with." wild beasts, and the fowls of heaven, and the fishes of the sea; many have had their bodies consumed away upon the face of the earth, and great part of their bodies ascended in exhalations—yet the all-wise and powerful God can immediately bring every part to his part again. Some shall rise to the resurrection of life, and others to the resurrection of condemnation. John 5:28–29, "All that are in the graves shall hear his voice, and shall come forth; they that have done good, to the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, to the resurrection of condemnation."

When the bodies are prepared by the mighty power of God, the departed souls shall [enter] again into their bodies and be reunited to 'em, now never to be separated more.

The souls of the wicked shall be brought up out of hell, though not out of their misery, and shall very unwillingly enter into their bodies, which will be but eternal prisons to 'em. Revelation 20:13, "And death and hell delivered up their dead which were in them." They shall lift up their eyes, full of the utmost amazement and horror, to see their awful judge, their bodies most loathsome and filthy….

The souls of the righteous shall descend from heaven with Christ

<!-- p. 525 -->

and the angels. 1 Thessalonians 4:14, "Them that sleep in Jesus will God bring with him." They shall be reunited to their bodies, that they may be glorified with them. They shall receive their bodies as glorious habitations, by the art [of] God prepared and beautified to be glorious mansions and habitations of pleasure and delight to all eternity. They shall be every way fitted for the uses and exercises and delights of perfectly holy and glorified souls. Their bodies shall be made with a superlative beauty, like to Christ's glorious body. Philippians 3:21, "Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body." Their bodies shall rise incorruptible, no more liable to pain or diseases, and with an extraordinary vigor and vivacity like to that of those spirits that are as a flame of fire. 1 Corinthians 15:43–44, "It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body."

With what joy will soul and body meet, and with what joy will they lift up their heads out of their graves to behold that glorious sight! And it will be a glorious sight to see those saints arising out of their graves, putting off their corruption and putting on incorruption and glory.

And then also at the last trump, those that shall be then living upon earth shall be changed; their bodies shall pass under a vast change, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye. 1 Corinthians 15:51–52, "Behold, I show you a mystery; we shall not all sleep, but we shall be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump."

The bodies of the wicked will be changed into such hideous things as are answerable to the loathsome souls that dwell in them, and such as shall be prepared to receive and administer eternal torments without dissolution.

The bodies of the righteous shall be changed into the same glorious and immortal form as those that are raised.

*Third*. They shall all be brought to appear before Christ, the godly being placed at the right hand, the wicked at the left. Matthew 25:31–33, "When the Son of man shall come in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then shall he sit upon the throne of his glory: and before him shall be gathered all nations: and he shall separate them one from another, as a shepherd divideth his sheep from the goats: and he shall set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left."

The wicked, however unwilling, however full of fear and horror, shall be dragged or drove before the judgment seat. However they may try to hide themselves, and creep into dens and caves of the mountains, and cry to the mountains to fall on them and the {rocks to hide them}

<!-- p. 526 -->

[Revelation 6:15], yet there must they come—there shall not one escape—and stand on the left hand with devils.

The righteous will be joyfully conducted, probably by the angels, to Christ Jesus. Their joy will as it were give them wings to carry 'em thither. They will with ecstasies and rapture of delight meet their friend and Savior, and come into his presence and stand at his right hand.

There seems also to be this difference, besides the one standing [at] the right hand and the wicked at the {left}: that when the dead in Christ are raised, they all shall be caught up into the air where Christ is, and shall be there at his right hand during the judgment. Nevermore shall [they] set their feet on this earth; whereas the wicked shall be left standing on the ground, to abide the judgment. 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17, "The dead in Christ shall rise first: then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall be ever with the Lord."

And what a vast congregation will there be of all the men, women and children that shall have lived upon earth from the beginning to {the end of the world}! Revelation 20:12, "And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God."JE ended the second unit of the sermon here, with a note to announce a baptism and sacramental lecture. He starts the third unit of the sermon with a recapitulation of the doctrine and propositions, which has been omitted.

*Fourth*. The next thing will be, the books will be opened. Revelation 20:12, "I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened." Which books seem to be these two: the book of God's remembrance and the book of Scripture; the former as the evidence of their deeds that are to be judged, the latter as the rule of judgment.

The works of both righteous and wicked will be brought forth, that they may be judged according to them; and those works will be tried according to the appointed and written rule.

1. The works of both righteous and wicked will be rehearsed. The book of God's remembrance will be first opened. The works of the children of men are by God as it were written in a book of remembrance. Malachi 3:16, "A book of remembrance was written before him." God don't forget any of the sins of ungodly men, however ready they may be to make light of ['em]MS dam. from stitch hole. and to forget 'em. Neither doth God forget any of the good works of the saints: if they give but a cup of cold water with a spirit of charity, God remembers it.

<!-- p. 527 -->

The evil works of the ungodly shall then be brought forth to light. They must there hear all of their profaneness, their unbelief, their abuse of ordinances, etc. with all their aggravation: how this man sinned after such warning and after the receipt of such mercies….

And they shall be called to an account concerning them, to see what answer they can make for themselves. Matthew 12:36, "But I say unto you, that every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment." Romans 14:12, "So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God."

The good works of the saints will also be brought forth as evidences of their sincerity and of their interest in the righteousness of Christ. As for their evil works, they will not be brought forth against 'em on that day; for the guilt of 'em will not lie upon 'em, being clothed with the righteousness of Jesus Christ. The judge himself is the person that took the guilt of their sins upon him. Their sins won't stand against them in the book of God's remembrance; their account will appear to have been canceled before that time. Their account that will be found in God's book will [be] not of debt but credit: God cancels their debts and sets down their good works, and is pleased as it were to make himself a debtor for them by his own gracious act.

And both good and bad will be judged according to their works. Revelation 20:12, "And the dead were judged out of those things that were found written in the books, according to their works"; and Revelation 20:13, "And the sea gave up the dead," and "they were judged every man according to their works."

Though the righteous are justified by faith and not their works, yet they shall be judged according to their works. Their works shall be brought forth as the evidence of their having believed. Their faith in that great day shall be tried by its fruits. If men's works have been bad, if their lives have been unchristian, that will condemn them without asking any more questions; but if their works, when they come to be inquired into and examined, prove good and of the right sort, they shall surely be justified. It will be taken and declared as a sure evidence of their having believed in Jesus Christ and being clothed with his righteousness.

But by works we are to understand all voluntary exercises of the faculties of the soul, men's words as well as what is done with their hands. Matthew 12:37, "By thy words shalt thou be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned." And not only outward acts, but also the thoughts and inward workings of the heart. "Man judgeth according

<!-- p. 528 -->

to the outward appearance but God trieth the heart" [1 Samuel 16:7]. Revelation 2:23, "I am he that searcheth the hearts and the reins: and I will give unto every one of you according to his works."In revising for repreaching, JE added: "Omissions. Matthew 25:42, etc."

Then, secret and hidden wickednesses will be brought forth to light, all the uncleanness, injustice and violence that men have been guilty of in secret. It shall then appear how this and that man has indulged himself in a way of wicked imagination. [Then], the good works of the saints that were in secret [also will be brought to light], the secret workings of their hearts.JE only sketched out this sentence with two short phrases and a blank line beneath each. He possibly intended to elaborate extemporaneously on each phrase.

2. The book of Scripture will be opened, and their works will be tried by that touchstone; their works will be compared with the Word of God. That which God gave them for the rule of their actions while in this life, shall then be made the rule of their judgment. God has told us now, beforehand, what will be the rule of judgment. We are told in the Scripture upon what terms we shall be justified and upon what terms we shall be condemned. That which God has given us to be our rule in our lives, he will make his own rule in judgment. But the rule of judgment will be twofold:

The primary rule of judgment will be the Law. The Law ever hath, and ever will, stand in force as a rule of judgment for those to whom the Law was given. Matthew 5:18, "For verily I say unto you, till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled." The Law will so far be made the rule of judgment, that not one person by any means shall be at that day justified or condemned in a way inconsistent with that which is established by the Law. As for the wicked, the Law will so far be the rule of judgment respecting them, that their sentence shall be the sentence of the Law. It will be the sentence of the Law that the judge will pronounce upon them. The righteous will be so far judged by the Law, that although their sentence will not be the sentence of the Law, yet it will by no means be such a sentence as shall be inconsistent with it, but such as the Law allows of: for it will be the righteousness of the Law that they will be justified by.

It will be inquired concerning every one, both righteous and wicked, whether the Law stands against him or no, whether they have a fulfillment of the Law to show. As for the righteous, they will have this to show: they will have it to plead that the judge himself has fulfilled the

<!-- p. 529 -->

Law for them; that he has both satisfied for their sins and fulfilled the righteousness of the Law for them. Romans 10:4, "Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth." And as for the wicked: when it shall be found by the book of God's remembrance that they have broken the Law and have no fulfillment of the Law to plead for themselves, they shall have the sentence of the Law pronounced upon them.

A secondary rule of judgment will be the gospel, wherein it is said, "He that believeth shall be saved; and he that believeth not [shall be damned]" [Mark 16:16]. Romans 2:16, "In the day when God shall judge the secrets of men by Jesus Christ according to my gospel."

It will be by the gospel, or covenant of grace, that believers shall have eternal blessedness adjudged to them. When it is found that the Law hinders not, that the curse and condemnation of the Law stands not against them, they shall have the reward of eternal life given them according to the glorious gospel of Jesus Christ: which gospel will be found, as well as the Law, to condemn the ungodly. They, being found not to have believed on the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, shall be condemned according to the tenor of that gospel.

*Fifth*. The sentence will be pronounced. Christ shall say to the wicked on the left hand, "Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels" [Matthew 25:41]. How dreadful will be those words of the judge to the poor, wretched, despairing souls on the left hand! How amazing will every syllable of it be, how will it pierce them to the soul!

The words of the sentence, they show the greatest abhorrence and wrath. Christ will bid them depart. He'll send them away from his presence, will remove them forever, far out of his sight, into an everlasting separation from God, as those [that] are most loathsome and unfit to be in his presence, and unfit for any sort of communion with him.

Christ will call them cursed: "Depart ye cursed," to whom everlasting wrath and ruin belongs; that are by your wickedness prepared for nothing else but to be firebrands of hell; that are the fit objects and vessels of the vengeance and fury of the Almighty.

"Into fire." He won't send them away only into a loathsome prison, a receptacle of the filth and rubbish of the universe; but they must be sent into a furnace of fire: that must be their dwelling place, to be there tormented with most racking pain and anguish.

And it is "everlasting fire." There is eternity in the sentence, which

<!-- p. 530 -->

infinitely aggravates the doom, and will make every word of it immensely the more dreadful, sinking and amazing to the souls that receive it.

"Prepared for the devil and his angels." Which will set forth the greatness and intenseness of the torment, as the other did the duration. It shows the dreadfulness of the fire they will be condemned to, that it is the same that is prepared for the devils, those foul spirits and great enemies of God. Their condition must be the same, in many respects, as the devils; they must burn in the same fire forever.

And this sentence will doubtless be pronounced in such an awful manner as shall be a terrible manifestation of the wrath of the judge. There shall be divine and holy and almighty wrath in the countenance and voice of the judge. And we now know not what other manifestation of anger there will accompany the sentence: it may be those words of the sentence will [be] accompanied with thunders and lightnings far more dreadful than were at Mount Sinai at the giving the Law.

And there will be answerable manifestations of fright and terror and horrible amazement in the condemned. How will all faces look pale, how will death sit upon their countenances when those words are heard! What dolorous groans and cries, what trembling and wringing of hands, and chattering of teeth and tearing of hair, will there be!

But Christ will, with the most benign aspect, in the most endearing manner and with the sweetest expressions of love, invite his saints on his right hand to glory: "Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world" [Matthew 25:34]. He will not bid them to go from him, but to come with him: to go where he goes, to dwell where he dwells, to enjoy him and to partake with him.

He calls them "blessed," and blessed of his Father, blessed by him whose blessing is infinitely the most desirable, namely, God.

"Inherit a kingdom." They ben't only invited to go with Christ and to dwell with him, but to inherit a kingdom with him; to sit down with him in his throne; to receive the honor and happiness of a heavenly kingdom.

"Prepared for you from the foundation of the world." Which denotes the sovereign and eternal love of God as the source of their blessedness. He puts them in mind that God was pleased to set his love upon them from all eternity, long before ever they had a being, and that God made heaven on purpose for them, fitted it for their delight and happiness.

<!-- p. 531 -->

*Sixth*. There will be immediately after this the execution of the sentence, as we are informed, Matthew 25:46, "These shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal." When the words of the sentence have once proceeded out of the mouth of the judge, then that vast and innumerable throng of ungodly men shall go away, shall be drove away, shall be necessitated to go away with devils; and shall be cast into that great furnace of fire, with dismal shrieks and cries, having the perpetual thunders and lightnings of the wrath of God following of them.

They must enter with their bodies into that furnace that they never shall come out of no more. But there they must spend eternal ages in wrestling with those torments, in crying out in the midst of those dreadful flames and under that insupportable wrath.

The righteous shall ascend with their glorified bodies, with Christ and all the angels, all that host that descended with him, up to heaven. They shall ascend in a most joyful and triumphant manner. And they shall enter with him into that glorious and blessed habitation that had for the time been empty of its creature inhabitants. Christ shall enter into heaven with his glorious church every way completed, and shall present them before the Father without spot or {blemish}, having given them that perfect beauty and crowned them with that glory and honor and happiness which was stipulated in the covenant of redemption before the world was, and which he died to procure for them.

And thus shall they be instated in everlasting glory, dwelling with Christ, who shall feed them and lead them to living fountains of waters. They shall have the full enjoyment of God, and shall spend their eternity in the most holy and glorious and joyful exercises.Here JE drew a closing bracket for repreaching.

V. [The fifth] thing under the doctrine [is], that all this will be done in righteousness. He will give to every man his due according to a most just and righteous rule. Those that are condemned will be most justly condemned: they will be condemned to that punishment which they have justly deserved. And the justice of God in condemning them will be then made most evident. Now God's justice in punishing wicked men, and in the degree of their punishment, is often blasphemously called into question; but then it shall be made clear and apparent to all. Their own consciences will tell them that the sentence is just, and all cavils will be put to silence.

And those that are justified and adjudged to eternal life will be most

<!-- p. 532 -->

justly so. Although they also have been great sinners and have deserved eternal death, yet it won't be against justice or the law for 'em to be thus justified, as they are in Christ. But the acquitting of them will be an act of justice; it will be but giving the reward merited by Christ's righteousness. Romans 3:26, "That God may be just, and the justifier of him that believeth in Jesus." He gives everyone their due proportion.

*First*. Christ can't fail of being just in judging through mistake. He can't mistake some for sincere and godly that are not so, or take some for to be hypocrites that have real sincerity in them. His "eyes are as a flame of fire" [Revelation 1:14], and he "searcheth the hearts, and trieth the reins of the children of men" [Revelation 2:23]. He can't err as to what is justice in particular cases, as human judges often do. He can't be blinded by prejudice, as human judges are very liable to be. Deuteronomy 10:17, "He regardeth not persons, nor taketh reward." He can't be deceived by the excuses and false colors and pleas of the wicked, as human judges. He can't err in assigning every one his proportion of reward and punishment according to men's wickedness or good works.

*Second*. He can't fail of judging in righteousness, through an unrighteous disposition, who is infinitely just and holy in his nature. Deuteronomy 32:4, "He is a rock, his work is perfect; all his ways are judgment; a God of truth without iniquity, just and right is he." 'Tis impossible that an infinitely powerful and self-sufficient Being should be under any temptation to be unjust. 'Tis impossible that an infinitely wise Being, that knows all things, should not choose justice; for he that perfectly knows all things, perfectly knows how much more amiable justice is than injustice.

VI. [The sixth] thing, and last thing, under the doctrine, is to consider those things that will be immediately consequent upon the day of judgment.

*First*. After the sentence is pronounced and the saints are ascended with Christ into glory, this world will be dissolved by fire. The conflagration will immediately succeed the judgment, when an end is put to the present state of mankind. This world, which was designed for their habitation during that state, will be destroyed; there will then be no further use for it. This earth, which has been the stage upon which so many things have been acted, upon which there have been so many great and famous kingdoms and great cities, where there has been so many wars, so much trade and business carried on for so many ages,

<!-- p. 533 -->

shall be destroyed. Those continents, those islands, those seas,MS: "those Rivers." Omitted as an intended deletion. those mountains and rivers shall be seen no more at all. All shall be destroyed by the devouring flames.

This we are plainly taught in the Word of God. 2 Peter 3:7, 2 Peter 3:10, "The heavens and the earth which are now, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men…. But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up."JE deletes: "This earth is not everlasting. 'It shall wax old as a garment; and as a vesture shall it be changed' (Psalms 102:26)."

*Second*.JE wrote much of the following four paragraphs on a salvaged prayer bid inserted into the duodecimal booklet. Because of the small size of the paper, he composed this section in sentence fragments, conjectures for the expansions of which have been inserted in brackets. An increase of the misery of the wicked and happiness of the saints [shall follow the day of judgment].

The misery of the wicked will be increased. [Their] bodies [will be] tormented.

Why [should the wicked] not [suffer torments] as well as "the devils, who believe and tremble" (James 2:19)? They are bound in chains of darkness to the judgment. 2 Peter 2:4, "For God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness to be reserved unto judgment." Therefore they cried out when they thought Christ was come to torment 'em (Matthew 8:29).

[The] happiness of the saints, it won't be complete before then. Therefore we are in the New Testament so often encouraged with the promises of the resurrection, and the day when Christ shall come the second time. It is spoken of as being the great object of the expectation and hopes of Christians. Their being united again to their bodies, their rising from the dead, [will then take place]. A state of separation is an unnatural state to human souls. [They will receive] glorious bodies.

And the occasion of happiness to the saintsMS: "soul." will doubtless be great. 'Tis compared to the marriage of the church and the Lamb (Revelation 19:7). Their reward will not be consummated before then.

Their joy will then be increased, because they will have new augments of joy. The body of Christ will be perfect: the church will then be

<!-- p. 534 -->

complete, all the parts of it in being, no parts of it under sin or affliction; all the members in a perfect state, all the parts together, none mixed with ungodly men. Then the church will be as a bride adorned {for her husband}; and therefore the church will exceedingly rejoice.

Then the Mediator will have fully accomplished his work, will have destroyed, and will triumph over, all his enemies. Then Christ will fully have obtained his reward. He will have fully accomplished the design that was upon his heart from all eternity. And then Jesus Christ will rejoice, and his members must needs rejoice with him.

Then God will have obtained the end of all his great works that [he] had been doing from the beginning of the world; all the deep designs of God will be unfolded in their events. Then his marvelous contrivance in his hidden, intricate and inexplicable works will appear, their ends being obtained. Then God's glory will more abundantly appear in his works, his works being perfected. This will cause a great occasion of happiness to the saints who behold it. Then God will fully have glorified himself, his Son and the elect. Then he will see that all is very good, and will rejoice in his own works, which will be the joy of all heaven.

Then God will make more abundant manifestations of his glory and the glory of his Son, and will pour forth more plentifully of his Spirit, and will make answerable additions to the glory of the saints, as will be becoming [to] the commencement of the ultimate and most perfect state of things and as will become such a joyful occasion as the completing of all things. And in this glory and happiness will the saints remain, forever and ever.At the end of the third preaching unit, JE announces a baptism. He begins the fourth unit of the sermon with a recapitulation of the text and doctrine, which has been omitted.

### Application.

*Use* I. Of *Instruction*. Hence many of the mysteries of providence may be unfolded. There are many things in God's dealings towards the children of men that appear very mysterious if we look upon them without having an eye to this last judgment, which, if we consider that, have no difficulty in them:

*First*. That God suffers the wicked to live and prosper in the world. The infinitely holy and wise Creator and governor of the world must necessarily hate wickedness, but yet we see many wicked men "spreading themselves as a green bay tree" [Psalms 37:35]. They live with impunity; things seem to go well with 'em, and the world smiles upon 'em.

<!-- p. 535 -->

Many that have not been fit to live, that have had God and religion in the greatest contempt and have been open enemies to all that is good, and that by their wickedness have been the pests of mankind—many cruel tyrants whose cruelties have been such that it would even fill one with horror to hear or read of—yet have lived in great wealth and outward glory, have reigned over great and mighty kingdoms and empires, and have been honored as a sort of earthly gods.

'Tis very mysterious that the holy and righteous governor of the world, whose eye beholds all the children of men, should suffer it to be thus, except men look forward to the day of judgment; and then the mystery is unraveled. Although God for the present keeps silence and seems to let them alone, yet then he will show himself with suitable manifestations of his displeasure against their wickedness. They shall then receive their condign punishment.

The saints under the old testament were much stumbled, [as] Job (Job 21), David (Psalms 73) and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 12). It was a great difficulty to them, because then a future state and a day of judgment was not revealed with that clearness that now it is.

*Second*. God sometimes suffers some of the best of men to be in great affliction {in the world}. The wicked rule, and they are subject and are trampled under their feet; the wicked are the head, and they are the tail. 'Tis a very common thing for the best men to be undermost in the present state of things. The ungodly rule and domineer, and they serve and are oppressed. This seems to be great confusion. When the wicked are uppermost, and the godly are oppressed by 'em, things are quite out of joint. Proverbs 25:26, "A righteous man falling down before the wicked is a troubled fountain, and a corrupt spring."

And if we look no further than the present state, it appears strange that God should suffer it to be so, so that sometimes one wicked man shall make many hundreds, yea thousands, of precious saints a sacrifice to his lust and cruelty, when he puts them to death for no other cause but for that which they ought above all things to be esteemed and commended for.

But when God shall put an end to the present state of mankind, these things shall be put to rights. The case won't be thus always; and though God suffers it for the present, yet 'tis but for a moment in comparison. When things come to be settled and fixed by a divine judgment, the righteous shall be exalted, honored and rewarded; and the wicked shall be depressed and put under their feet.

However wicked men seem now to prevail against 'em, yet they shall

<!-- p. 536 -->

at last have the ascendant and shall be conquerors. They shall see the just vengeance of God upon those that hate them.

*Third*.JE sketched out this paragraph in brief phrases only, intending to fill out his remarks extemporaneously; bracketed phrases are given as conjectures. It is another mystery of providence, that God suffers so much public injustice to take place in the world. How many unjust things [are] done. Many unjustly suffer and have [no] refuge, no appeals to make. [It is a mystery,] that he that is rightfully the supreme judge of the world and is by nature perfectly just, [suffers public injustice; but he will put all such things right].

*Use* II. Of *Awakening*. You that have not the fear of God before your eyes, that ben't afraid, consider seriously what you have heard from this doctrine concerning the day of judgment. Those things, though they are now future and unseen things, yet they are real and certain things.

If you are now let alone, if God keeps silence and judgment is not speedily executed, it is not because that God is regardless how men live and behave themselves.

Now indeed God is invisible, and his wrath is invisible to you; but at that day, you yourself shall see him with your bodily [eyes]. You shall not be able then to keep out of his sight, or to avoid seeing of him. Revelation 1:7, "Behold, he cometh with clouds, and every eye shall see him, and they also which pierced him." You shall see him coming in the clouds of heaven; your ears [shall hear] the last trumpet, that dreadful sound, the voice of the archangel; your eyes shall see your judge sitting on the throne. Your eyes will see those manifestations of wrath which there will be in his countenance; your ears shall hear him pronounce the sentence.

Consider seriously, if you live in ways of sin and appear at that day with the guilt of sin upon you, how you can bear the sight of those things; and whether or no horror and amazement will not be likely to seize you when you see the judge descending, etc. What account can you give, when it shall be required of you why {you lived as you did}?

What can you say for yourself, when it shall be asked why you neglected secret prayer, that you knew to be your duty?

Notwithstanding that you are so careless of your behavior, and make so light of sin—you sin freely, with little or no remorse or dread—yet you must give an account of every sin that you commit, of every idle word that you speak, of every sinful thought. Every time you deviate from rules of justice, or rules of temperance or chastity, or every time

<!-- p. 537 -->

you indulge a lust, whether secretly or openly, you must give an account of it. It won't be forgotten; it stands written in that book that shall be opened on that day. Consider the rules you must be judged by. Particularly, here consider:The next three subpoints are each followed by several blank lines, indicating JE's intent to explicate these point extemporaneously.

*First*. The judge will be your supreme judge.

*Second*. The judge will be omnipotent.

*Third*. The judge will be inexorable.

*Fourth*. The judge at that day won't mix mercy with justice. The time for mercy to be shown to sinners is past. Christ will now appear under another character: he'll lay aside those inviting {offers of mercy}. {He will demand} "the uttermost farthing" (Matthew 5:26). Revelation 14:10, "The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup for his indignation."

The punishment threatened to ungodly men is without any pity. Ezekiel 5:11, "Neither shall my eye spare, neither will I have any pity."

Vengeance shall come with its full weight. Here, all judgments have a mixture of mercy.Here JE drew a closing bracket for repreaching.

*Use* III. [I shall] apply myself more particularly:

*First*. To those that live in secret wickedness. Let them consider, that for all those things God will bring them into judgment. Secrecy is your temptation. Luke 12:2–3, "For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; nor hid, that shall not be known. Therefore, whatsoever ye have spoken in darkness shall be heard in the light; and that which ye have spoken in the ear in closets shall be proclaimed upon the housetops." Before human judges are brought only those things that are known. [Then] there will need [be] no other evidence but God and your own consciences.Eight blank lines follow.

*Second*. Such as are not just and upright in their dealings with men. Consider that all your dealings with men must be tried: they must [be] brought forth into judgment and there compared with the rules of the Word of God; your actions must be judged out of those things that are found written in the book of God's Word. If your ways of dealing with men don't agree with those rules of righteousness, they will be condemned as naught.

The Word of God directs us to follow that "that is altogether just" (Deuteronomy 16:20), and to do by others as we would that they should do unto

<!-- p. 538 -->

us. But how many are there, whose dealings with men, if brought [to] and strictly tried by those rules, would not stand the test? God has in his Word forbid all deceit and fraud in our dealings one with another (Leviticus 19:13); he hath forbidden us to oppress one another (Leviticus 25:14). How frequent are practices that are very contrary to these, and that won't bear to be tried by those rules? How common is fraudulency and trickishness in men's trading one with another; how will men endeavor to lead those they trade with on in the blind, so that they may make their advantage? Yea, lying in trading is too common a thing amongst us. How common are such things as that mentioned, Proverbs 20:14, "It is naught, it is naught, saith the buyer; but when he has gone his way, then he boasteth"; and other things of the like nature?

Many men will improve an advantage from another's ignorance to blind him and to advance their own gain to his wrong, and don't seem to scruple such things. There are many ways that men have of deceiving one another in trading, not by downright lying, that yet are not right in the sight of God and will appear to be very unjust when they come to be tried by the rule of God's Word at the day of judgment.

And how common a thing is oppression, a taking any advantage that they can anyways obtain, to get the utmost they can of their neighbor, and more than a suitable gain for what they have to spare and their neighbor stands in need of?

Let such consider that there is a God in heaven that beholds them and sees how they behave in their daily dealings one with another, and that he will try their works another day.

And justice will assuredly take place at last. The righteous governor of the world won't suffer injustice without rectifying of it; he'll rectify it by returning the injury upon the head of the injurer. Matthew 7:2, "With what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again."

*Third*. Let those that plead for the lawfulness of practices generally condemned by godly people consider that their practices must be tried at the day of judgment. Consider whether or no they will be likely to be approved by the most holy judge at that day. Proverbs 5:21, "The ways of man are before the eyes of the Lord, and he pondereth all his goings."

If you deceive your own hearts by your carnal reasonings, you will not be able to deceive the judge. He'll not hearken to your excuses, but will try your ways by the rule. He'll know whether they are straight or crooked.

When you plead for these and those liberties that you take, let it be considered whether or no they will be likely to be allowed of by the

<!-- p. 539 -->

judge at the great day. Will they bear to be tried by his eyes, that are purer than to behold evil and that cannot look on iniquity?

*Fourth*. [To] those that are wont to excuse their wickedness. Will the excuses that you make for yourself be accepted then? [If]MS damage (burn hole). you excuse yourself to your conscience by saying that you was under such a strong temptation as you could not withstand—corrupt nature prevailed and you could not overcome it; it would be so and so to your damage to have done otherwise; if you had done such a duty, you [would] have greatly [injured] yourself; you should have made a whip for your own back; you [would] have got the displeasure of such and such friends; you should have been despised and laughed at—or if you say, you did no more than it was the common custom to do, no more than a great many godly people have done, no more than such and such that are well accounted of; that if you had done otherwise, you must have been singular: will those excuses appear to be good when they come to be examined into at the day of judgment?

*Use* IV.JE bracketed the entire Use for repreaching. If there be a day appointed, let all persons be very strict in trying their own sincerity. God will discover the secrets of all hearts on that day.

The judgment of that day will be like fire that will burn up whatsoever is not true gold. Wood, hay, stubble and dross shall be all consumed by the scorching fire of that day.

The judge will be as a refiner's fire and fuller's soap, that will cleanse away all filthiness, however it may be colored over. Malachi 3:20, "Who may abide the day of his coming? And who shall stand when he appeareth? For he is like a refiner's fire, and like fuller's soap." And [Malachi 4:1, "For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven, and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble; and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the Lord of hosts."

There are multitudes of men that wear the disguise of saints, that appear like other saints; and their state is good in their own eyes and [in] the eyes of their neighbors. They have sheep's clothing. But there is no disguise that can hide [them] from the eyes of the judge of the world: his eyes are as a flame of fire that "search the hearts and try the reins of the children of men." He'll see whether they are sound or no; he'll see from what principles it is that they have acted.

A fair show will not deceive him, as it doth men here in this world. It will signify nothing to say, "Lord, we have eaten and drunk in thy

<!-- p. 540 -->

presence; and in thy name we have cast out devils; and in thy name have done many wonderful works" [Matthew 7:22]. It will signify nothing to pretend to a great deal of comfort and joy, and experiences of great religious affections, or a having done many things in religion and morality, without any greater evidences of sincerity.

Wherefore, let everyone take heed that they ben't deceived concerning themselves, that they don't depend upon that that won't bear examination at the day of judgment.

And don't be contented with having the judgment of men, the judgment of godly, experienced people, or of ministers. Consider that they are not to be your judges at last. Be often yourself in comparing your heart with God's Word, that is to be the rule of judgment by which you are to be tried then.

And try yourself by your works, by which you must then be tried. Examine whether you live a holy and Christian life, whether you perform an universal and unconditional obedience to all God's commandments, and whether you do it from a truly gracious respect to God.

And be much in begging of God the judge, that he would search you and try you now, and discover you to yourself, that you may see if you are insincere, and lead you in the way everlasting; that if you are not upon a good foundation, that God would unsettle you and fix you on a better path, after the example of the Psalmist. Psalms 31:1–2, "Judge me, O Lord; examine me, and prove me; and try my reins and mine heart"; and Psalms 139:23–24, "Search me, O God, and know my heart; try me, and know my thoughts; and see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting."

God will search us hereafter and discover what we be, to ourselves and to all the world. Let us pray that he would search us and discover our hearts to us now. We have need of divine help in this matter, for the heart is deceitful above all things.

*Use* V. If God hath appointed a day {to judge the world}, let us judge and condemn ourselves for our sins. This we must do if we would not be judged and condemned for them at that day.

If we [are to] escape condemnation, we must see that we justly might be condemned. We must be so sensible of our vileness and guilt as to see that we have deserved all that condemnation and punishment that is threatened; that we are in God's hands and that he is sovereign disposer of us.

Let us therefore be often reflecting on our sins, and be truly humbled before God for them, and confess them to God.

<!-- p. 541 -->

*Use* VI. Not to [be] forward to judge others, to judge others' thoughts, to judge their hearts upon particular occasions, to determine as to the principles, motives and ends of their actions.

This is to assume God's province, to set up ourselves as lords and judges. Romans 14:4, "Who art thou that judgest another man's servant?" And James 4:12, "Speak not evil one of another, brethren. He that speaketh evil of his brother, and judgeth his brother, speaketh evil of the law, and judgeth the law; but if thou judge the law, thou are not a doer of the law but a judge."

This is the way to be judged and condemned ourselves. Matthew 7:1–2, "Judge not, that ye be not judged. For with what judgment ye judge; ye shall be judged."

*Use* VII. Of *Consolation* to the godly.JE sketched out much of this paragraph, leaving blank lines between fragments; conjectures are given in brackets.

This day, which is so terrible to ungodly men, [will be the occasion of joy to the saints].

Though you meet with affliction now more than many wicked men, [then you will be vindicated].

If you are unjustly treated by wicked men and are reproached by them, what a comfort to the injured, that they [can] appeal to God, who judgeth righteously. The Psalmist often used to comfort himself with this.

Upon these accounts, the saints have reason to love the appearing of Jesus Christ. 2 Timothy 4:8, "Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give at that day; and not to me only, but to all those that love his appearing."

This is to the saints a blessed hope. Titus 2:13, "Looking for that blessed hope, and glorious appearing of the great God and our Savior, Jesus Christ."

It may well be the object of their longing desire. When they hear of the day of judgment, they may say, "Even so, come, Lord Jesus" (Revelation 22:20).

It will be the most glorious day that ever the saints saw in their lives, whether those that shall die before and their souls go to heaven, or those that shall then be found on earth. It will be the wedding day of the church.

## Appendix: Dated Batches of Sermons 1723–1729

Dating by Thomas A. Schafer

Sermons are listed according to approximate date of composition and the original Schafer number, followed by the title if printed, or by the Scripture text, a statement of the doctrine, and any other relevant information if unpublished. Within period groups, sermons are listed in canonical order. In some cases, more precise dating of a sermon consequent to its original numbering has been noted in its description. Sermon texts followed by an asterisk indicate those printed in previous editions. Unless stated otherwise, the manuscript is in the Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University.

One sermon on each proposition. Dwight ed., *8*, 355–78.

 81. *Living Unconverted Under an Eminent Means of Grace* (Jeremiah 6:29–30). Preached shortly after Stoddard's death. 82. Matthew 12:30. "There are no neuters in religion." 83. Matthew 13:22(a). "The cares of this life are what often hinders any saving effect of the Word of God." 84. *Profitable Hearers of the Word* (Matthew 13:23). Three sermons. 85. Luke 8:28. "There is no goodness in praying, though it be never so earnestly, merely out of fear of misery." 86. *The Spiritual Blessings of the Gospel Represented by a Feast* (Luke 14:16). Sacrament sermon. MS in Trask Library. 87. *The Torments of Hell Are Exceeding Great* (Luke 16:24). 88. Luke 17:34. "There will be a great difference made hereafter in the state of many that have lived together here." MS in Trask Library. 89. Luke 19:42(a). "If sinners outstand their day of grace, they will surely perish." 90. 1 Corinthians 16:22. "It's crime enough to render any man a cursed person, not to love Jesus Christ." 91. Galatians 2:20. "Christ had a particular respect to every believer, in what he did and suffered in the work of redemption." 92. 1 John 4:19. "God is first in love to his saints." 93. Isaiah 53:3(a). "Our Lord Jesus Christ, when upon earth, met with abundance of contempt and reproach." 94. Jeremiah 42:20. "There are some men do nothing but dissemble, in their pretenses of disposedness to their duty." Sacrament sermon. 95. Amos 8:11. "Spiritual judgments are the most terrible that can befall a people." Fast-day sermon for March 20, 1729. 96. *None Are Saved by Their Own Righteousness* (Titus 3:5).

Spring–Fall 1729 97. Exodus 20:24. "If we would be in the way of God's grace and blessing, we must wait upon him in his own way and in the use of his appointed means." 98. Psalms 66:5. "'Tis to the glory of God, that he is terrible in his doings towards the children of men." 99. Psalms 82:6–7. "Great men are as liable to death as others." 100. Proverbs 5:11–13(a). "Vicious persons, when once they come to taste the bitter fruits of their evil courses, will greatly lament their folly in not hearkening to the counsels and warnings that were given them."

 101. *The Threefold Work of the Holy Ghost* (John 16:8). 102. Romans 6:14. "The gospel, or new covenant, is eminently a dispensation of grace." 103. 1 Corinthians 1:9. "Christians have communion with Christ." Sacrament sermon. 104. 1 Peter 1:3. A sermon on the resurrection of Christ. Not extant but cited in "Miscellanies" no. 409. 105. Revelation 3:15. "A man had better be a heathen, than to differ from 'em only in common light and profession."

Summer 1729. 106. Deuteronomy 7:10. "God will not be slack in punishing wicked men."

Summer–Fall 1729 107. Numbers 23:19. "God never changes his mind." 108. Deuteronomy 32:35(a). "The punishment of wicked men generally comes upon them when they don't expect it." 109. 2 Samuel 23:5. "The covenant of grace is every way so ordered as is needful, in order to its being made firm and sure." 110. Job 31:3. "It is a strange punishment that God has assigned to the workers of iniquity." 111. Psalms 18:26. "They that contend with God, can expect no other than that God will contend with them." 112. Psalms 33:1. "The righteous, above other men, have reason to praise God." 113. *The Sacrifice of Christ Acceptable* (Psalms 40:6–8). 114. *God's All-Sufficiency for the Supply of Our Wants* (Psalms 65:9). Thanks giving sermon for Nov. 13, 1729. 115. *Sin and Wickedness Bring Calamity and Misery on a People* (Proverbs 14:34). Preached before the county court, probably in early December 1729. 116. Proverbs 23:5. "Earthly riches are of a very fleeting nature." 117. Canticles 5:1. "Persons need not and ought not to set any bounds to their spiritual and gracious appetites." Sacrament sermon. 118. Canticles 8:1. "The incarnation of Jesus Christ was a thing greatly longed for by the church." 119. Isaiah 3:1–2. "It's a manifestation of God's displeasure against a people, when he takes away from them many that have been useful and serviceable among them." Mentions Stoddard's ministry and death; possibly for a fast day. 120. *Glorying in the Savior* (Isaiah 45:25).

 121. Jeremiah 5:9. "'Tis unreasonable to think that God will take no care to punish the wickedness that there is in the world." 122. Jeremiah 17:5–6(a). "They that trust in the creature will be left in an utterly destitute and hopeless condition, and shall not see when good comes." 123. Jeremiah 17:7–8. "There are those that make an outward show of friendship to Jesus Christ, that at the same time act the part of enemies and betrayers." 129. John 8:44(a). Childlike respect to God should be the main principle of the Christian's obedience." Edwards makes two observations on the text but uses only the second as his doctrine; it is not clear whether there was a sermon on the first. 131. 1 Peter 1:8(a). 'Tis the part of wise and pious parents, to maintain a true concern of mind towards their children, lest they should fall into sin. 2. The commission of wickedness against light and

 knowledge has this tendency, to cause men to curse God in their hearts." Two short sermons, one on each observation.
